# Observations inbox

Raw observations land here as they are noticed, get triaged, and are handed to a worker session as a
grounded prompt. This file is the source of truth between sessions — an item that is only in a chat
transcript is an item that will be lost.

**How to use it.** Add anything to CAPTURED, however rough, without stopping to diagnose. Triage moves an
item into a bucket with a verdict. When a bucket is worth a session, a prompt is written from it and the
items are marked with the version that fixed them.

**Status vocabulary:** `captured` (raw) · `triaged` (understood, not started) · `assigned` (a session has
it) · `fixed vX.Y.Z` · `wont-fix` (with the reason).

| A1 | **Guide-tip header/footer banner does not reflow on resize — it is a BITMAP being stretched.** Scoped 2026-07-30. The banner is a canvas built by `drawHud()` (`lib/catalogue/infoCard.ts`) and drawn onto a full-frame quad, so once built the wrap points are baked in at that width and any size change magnifies the picture. The font sizing is innocent: `fontPx = max(12, min(viewW*0.011, viewH*0.026, 20))`, clamped 12-20px — nothing computes a giant font, a small canvas is being upscaled. **Scope is narrow: three call sites, two at risk.** (1) Player STARMAP, 2D and 3D, via `Starmap3DView.applyTips()` — ALREADY GUARDED, it re-measures the container on every build and carries a comment about this exact failure. (2) Player SYSTEM 3D via `catalogue/+page.svelte:600`, a reactive `hudCanvas = drawHud({...})` feeding `HoloView` — **prime suspect**, check whether its viewW/viewH refresh on resize. (3) DOCUMENT headers/footers (`document/blocks.ts`, `documentStyles.ts`) are a SEPARATE path doing real layout, not a bitmap — expected unaffected, confirm only. **Note the puzzle:** the reported screenshot is the STARMAP, which is the guarded surface — so either the player starmap does not go through `applyTips`, or there is a second stale-size source. Identify which surface actually drew it before fixing. Best fix moves the re-measure INTO `drawHud` so a third caller cannot reintroduce it. **Session notes (2026-07-31, v2.1.304):** could not reproduce headless (the automated pane stops compositing, which suspends the ResizeObservers under test). Reviewed all three sites: (2) the catalogue hudCanvas IS reactive on hudW/hudH and `setHud` re-sizes its quad on scene resize, so it should track a visible-window resize — same for the starmap scene. One real mechanism found and closed: RO notifications deliver BEFORE PAINT, so a resize landing while the window is not painting (minimised, background tab, other desktop) leaves a canvas at the stale size until something forces a render — the DOCUMENT view (path 3) now also re-measures on window resize + visibilitychange. If the screenshot came from a resize-while-hidden, that may be the whole story for path 3 but paths 1-2 would still bitmap-stretch until their next prop change. **ROOT CAUSE FOUND (live repro by Alex, v2.1.305): the rebuild always ran and never reached the screen.** Both scene setHud implementations swapped the rebuilt canvas into a live texture via `map.image = ...` -- and WebGL2 texture storage is immutable once allocated (texStorage2D), so uploading a DIFFERENT-SIZED canvas fails silently and the quad keeps stretching the stale bitmap. Every re-measure guard upstream was therefore working and irrelevant. Fixed by recreating the texture whenever the canvas dimensions change (system holo + starmap scenes), and the same trap closed in the label sprites (drawLabel resizes its canvas under a live texture on font/text change). The document view was never affected -- its setSource already recreates per frame. Followed by a fine-tuning pass centring the text within the band (v2.1.306). | fixed v2.1.304-306-beta |
| A2 | Player-view construct panel is anaemic — Blip-A shows Type / Orbit distance / Atmosphere, i.e. BODY fields, while the data holds crew, engines, fuel tanks, cargo and delta-v. Constructs need their own block in the document / DocPanel builder. **FIXED v2.1.325-beta.** **Root cause: there was no construct branch at all.** `bodyFacts` had exactly one construct-aware line — the Type label at `:70` — and a construct then fell through the whole body block, matching only the rows a ship happens to share with a world. Blip-A's three rows were Type, Orbit distance and Atmosphere, and the last one said "None". **Everything in the new block is READ from `calculateFullConstructSpecs`**, the existing derivation behind the GM's Construct Derived Specs panel, the transit planner, the autopilot adapter and the interstellar modal — nothing is recomputed, so the player block and the GM panel cannot print different numbers for one ship. Confirmed at the formatter too: the GM uses `fmt.speedMs`, which is `formatSpeedKmS(ms / 1000, …)`, character-for-character what the block now calls for Δv. Twelve rows for Blip-A: class, location, crew, supplies, dimensions, dry mass, cargo against capacity, total mass, power surplus, fuel by name, max acceleration, Δv. **The rule pack had to be threaded in, and that is the one structural change:** engine and fuel DEFINITIONS live in the pack, not on the node, and without them a tank has no density and an engine no Isp. `GuideDocOpts` and both consumers (`DocPanel`, `FilteredDocumentView`) take an OPTIONAL `rulePack`, passed at all six mount sites; the host is resolved inside the builder the same way the parent-nav row resolves it, so the two cannot name different parents. **The honest-degradation rule was applied twice after testing the no-pack path and finding it QUIETLY WRONG rather than merely short** — the same fault class as A5. A tank whose fuel is not in the pack contributes zero mass, so "Total mass" read 1,200 t instead of 2,300 t; and an unresolved engine has no power draw, so what was labelled "Power surplus" was really the plant's output (100 MW against a true 60). Total mass is now suppressed unless every tank resolved, and the power row is relabelled "Power output" unless every engine did. **Redaction: nothing new is exposed.** The boundary is node-level — `computePlayerSnapshot` drops hidden subtrees and `gmNotes`, and optionally `description`; every field this block reads (class, placement, crew, `physical_parameters`, `systems.life_support`, `power_plants`, `fuel_tanks`, `engines`, `current_cargo_tonnes`) already crossed to players. **One field deliberately LEFT OUT because it is not clearly player-safe: `cargoDescription`** — see [[A27]]. **Verified on all 26 constructs in the campaign** (the block reads sensibly for a 6-million-crew colony drum, a 1,000 km ring gate and two derelicts alike) and live on BOTH consumers with identical rows: `FilteredDocumentView`, reached by drilling Tau Ceti → Adrian → Blip-A, and `DocPanel`. **Not exercised on live data, said plainly: the `Status` row and a construct's `Tags` row** — no construct in the bundled campaign carries a `flight_state` (it is set at runtime by the transit planner) or a single tag. **One knock-on fixed in the same commit:** the panel subtitle appended the singular `class`, which only constructs carry, so with the class now properly in the Type row it read "Ship · Ship/Interstellar/Eridian". Suppressed for constructs; bodies are untouched. Also raised: [[A28]]. | fixed v2.1.325-beta |

| A4 | **GM starmap labels grow with zoom (system names, depth cues, placement ghost).** System-name font should stay a constant screen size as you zoom, not scale with the map transform. `Starmap.svelte` — the labels are inside the world transform, so they scale with it. (Compare: the 3D starmap uses sprites with an explicit `setLabelSize`, which is why it does not have this.) Each label font size and its offset from the marker now divide by the zoom, cancelling the one inherited factor. **Not covered — see A8:** route labels, the measure read-out and the multi-star `+` indicator still scale. | fixed v2.1.295-beta |

| A5 | **Stat block pairs two different temperatures in adjacent rows.** Pandora: "Surface temp 45 °C" against "Temp range -28 °C to -23 °C" — the mean sits 70 °C outside its own range. 45 °C is 318 K, the range is 245–250 K, and the ~71 K gap is the GREENHOUSE: the block shows the composed surface temperature on one row and the EQUILIBRIUM min/max on the next. A proper surface range already exists — `SurfaceTempProfile.totalMinK` / `.totalMaxK`, which is what the GM body panel decomposes by cause. Use that. Check every other paired figure in the same block while there. **FIXED v2.1.323-beta, exactly as scoped — and the SWEEP found a second row of the same class, which is the more valuable half.** Root cause confirmed at `bodyFacts.ts:92-93`: one row printed `temperatureK` (the composed SURFACE temperature) and the next printed `equilibriumTempMinK/MaxK`, which omit the greenhouse and every other heat term. Now `temperatureRangeK`, which `surfaceTempProfile` builds as `mean ± rss(swings)` and therefore brackets `temperatureK` **by construction**, not by luck. **Verified numerically over the whole bundled Sol map rather than on the reported body: 34 of 34 means sit inside the surface range; 11 of 34 sat outside the equilibrium range that was being shown** — Venus (754 K against "229–231"), Earth (287 against "252–256"), all four giants, Io, Europa, Titan, Mimas. **Degradation needed no fallback and this was checked rather than assumed:** `processEnvironment` returns early for stars (`SystemProcessor.ts:356`) so a star has NEITHER field, and `importFixup`'s `DERIVED_FIELDS` strips and re-derives both together — so there is no state where one exists without the other, and the row simply drops. Confirmed live: Sol prints "Surface temp 5,778 K" and no range row. **THE SWEEP, item by item, so the next session need not redo it.** (a) **"Surface liquid" was the second bug, same class, and is fixed in the same commit.** The row printed raw `hydrosphere.coverage` and hard-coded the word "liquid", while the PHASE is separately derived and published as a `hydrosphere/*` tag — so the block contradicted its own Tags row two lines below. Europa read "Surface liquid 100% water" beside "Frozen surface: water", and Europa's liquid is famously UNDER the ice; **five of Sol's seven hydrosphere bodies are frozen** (Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Enceladus, Triton). The label now follows the tag — surface liquid / surface ice / surface volatile, marked boiled off or supercritical — reading a published derived value, so no physics moved. (b) **Radiation band vs range: a real but INVISIBLE inconsistency, recorded as B8, not fixed.** The mean is composed from the per-star spectral components while the endpoints are rebuilt from a flat photon/particle fraction times the range total, so the mean can land marginally outside its own range — measured on Sol, 3 of 34 bodies (Neptune, Triton, Neptune's Rings), worst excess ~0.4%, which rounds away at the block's 1 d.p. Physics, and out of scope here. (c) **Day length vs "tidally locked" is the same class and is already B7** — an authored spin against a derived lock. Cross-referenced there. (d) **Type vs Surface temp is the same class and is already B6** — the classifier keys on `Teq_K` for 26 fingerprints. (e) **Ruled out, with the reason:** Orbit distance / Orbital period (the period is derived FROM `a_AU`, or for a binary member from the `n_rad_per_s` both members share, which comes from the same separation); Mass / Radius / Gravity / Density / Ascent Δv (one source pair, `massKg` + `radiusKm`); Atmosphere pressure / Air mix (one `body.atmosphere`, and atmospheric escape rewrites both together); Habitability (reads `planet.temperatureK`, the surface figure, and scores its solvent off the phase-aware fluid-layer model, so it agrees with both corrected rows). **Blast radius, and it is wider than the batch brief assumed: `bodyFacts` has FOUR consumers, not two** — the shared `buildGuideDocument` (so `DocPanel` AND `FilteredDocumentView`), the legacy `CatalogueBrowser` Field Guide, the holo HUD info card (`catalogue/+page.svelte:611`) and a direct fact list (`:893`). One line reaches all of them. **Verified on both document consumers, per F7/F9's lesson:** `FilteredDocumentView` (Venus 480 °C / 463–499 °C; Jupiter −114 / −129 to −98; Europa "Surface ice 100% water") and `DocPanel` (Europa identical on all three rows). **One judgement call worth knowing:** on a tidally-heated body the surface range is WIDE, because the profile's upper bound is the tidal-hotspot term — Pandora now reads 13 °C to 1,197 °C and Europa −250 °C to 401 °C. That is honest, it is inside the physics, and it is character-for-character what the GM's own body panel already prints, which is the point of a shared figure. | fixed v2.1.323-beta |

| A6 | **In the DOCUMENT view of a system, the star's page should list its natural satellites — the planets — exactly as a planet lists its moons.** It currently does not, so the only way down into the system from the star is the picker at the top, and that is sometimes ineffective. Every other body in the document gets a satellite list; the star is the one node missing it, and it is the node you land on first (E1 preselects the primary star on entry), so the omission is on the FIRST page a player sees. Treat it as the same list the planets already render — `buildGuideDocument` / `systemTopology` — not a new bespoke block. Fixing this also gives the document a working navigation path that does not depend on the picker at all. **FIXED v2.1.324-beta.** **Root cause: the helper existed and the drill-in section simply never called it.** `guideDocument.ts` built its navigator from `membersOf` / `moonsOf` / `constructsOf` only; `listBodiesOf` — the direct-orbiters-in-orbit-order query the BodyPicker and the legacy `CatalogueBrowser` chip row both already use — was never imported. So this was a missing call, not missing topology. Same block shape as the moons, same `drillItems`, and using `listBodiesOf` rather than `planetsOf` deliberately, so BELTS are listed too instead of being pickable only by tapping the chart. Heading is chosen by content: `Planets`, `Belts`, or `Planets & belts`. **Keyed on `selected.id`, NOT `subject.id`**, because `subject` has already been resolved from a barycentre to its dominant member, and a circumbinary planet hangs off the barycentre. **The de-duplication filter is load-bearing twice, and both cases are real rather than defensive:** (1) `orbiters()` excludes only moons, and **Pluto is `roleHint: 'planet'` parented to the Pluto-Charon barycentre**, so that page would have offered Pluto as its own satellite; (2) `membersOf` matches on `n.parentId === bary.id` as well as `memberIds`, so a circumbinary planet is ALREADY claimed as a barycentre "member" and would have been listed twice. **Verified numerically over the whole campaign, not on the reported body: all 60 stars in 42 systems, every list length compared against the ground truth read straight from the data — 33 stars list 92 bodies between them, 0 mismatches, and the 27 stars with no orbiters correctly render no block.** Also swept all 210 body pages for a page offering ITSELF as a drill target: none. **Verified live** on `FilteredDocumentView`: Sol lists Mercury→Kuiper Belt in orbit order with belts carrying the `⋯` glyph, and Sol → Jupiter → Europa drills all the way down without touching the picker. In the Alpha Centauri triple: Rigil Kentaurus → Polyphemus, Proxima → its two planets, Toliman correctly empty. **Honestly NOT verified on live data: the circumbinary (P-type) path, because the bundled campaign contains no such body** — 20 barycentres, none with a non-member planet child. Proved on a synthetic fixture instead, where both circumbinary planets appear exactly once. **Three things found while doing it, all recorded rather than fixed:** duplicate node IDs in two bundled systems ([[D3]]), the "Moons" heading being used for companion STARS on a barycentre page ([[A25]]), and a ringed planet's ring appearing in no drill list at all ([[A26]]). | fixed v2.1.324-beta |

## F — Player Views: preset editor (one batch, 2026-07-30)

All from a single pass over the preset editor. Several may share a root — F4/F5 are both "the preview
re-frames when it should not", F2/F3 are both "true-scale mode breaks proportion".

| # | Observation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | **Body graphics were being drawn on the SYSTEM MAP itself. They must NEVER be.** Body graphics (photo / disc / sphere) are for the INFO BLOCK only; the map always uses the 2D or 3D render. This was stated once before during the D5/E2 work and fixed for the 3D list — so this is either a regression or the fix never covered 2D. **Highest priority in this bucket: it is a rule, not a preference.** Cause of the recurrence: the earlier fix (f947826) forced sphere for `holo3d` only and deliberately LEFT the control on the 2D map, because a flat body sprite was then considered a legitimate 2D-map look. Fixed at the source instead — `bodyGfx` is gone from `HoloStyle` and from the scene entirely (type, setter, render branch, `buildBodyDisc`), so no map style can carry one. | fixed v2.1.286-beta |
| F2 | At TRUE scale, the "glow" points are far too large and do not stay in proportion to the orbit lines — an oversaturated field of giant blobs. One root with F3: everything the scene draws at a FIXED size (minimum body radius, wireframe glow vertices, belt rubble, ring particles) was sized for the READABLE end of the dial and then applied at every setting. `markerScale()` now shrinks all of them with the dial, floored at 2% of readable. 2D and 3D are the same engine, so both. | fixed v2.1.288-beta |
| F3 | Same at true scale for RINGS and BELTS — they lose proportion when zoomed to actual sizes rather than readable sizes. The diagnosis was right: same root as F2, same fix. **Residual, see A9:** a body can be VISIBLE at true scale or in PROPORTION at true scale, not both — Earth's true radius is about 0.05 px at whole-system framing. The floor survives at 2%, so bodies are still over-sized against their orbits at the extreme end; the belt no longer buries them. | fixed v2.1.288-beta |
| F4 | Changing a general setting (e.g. belt type) re-zooms the preview to the star. Appearance settings should never move the camera. `setFraming` was the one setter in the scene that did not bail when handed the values it already held — it re-armed its 48-frame ease on every call, and `applyStyle` calls it for every style object, which the editor rebuilds on every keystroke. | fixed v2.1.290-beta |
| F5 | "Frame whole system (never zoom to a body)" did not show the whole system in the preview. The distance was a fixed `GRID_RADIUS * 1.5` with no reference to the lens: at fov 45 that fits a half-extent of about 7.5 of the 12 units a system occupies, so the outer third was always off the edge. Now the same fov/aspect maths `frameDistance` already used for a single body — then fitted to the BOUNDING SPHERE rather than a flat extent, so a tilted shot does not clip either (v2.1.298). | fixed v2.1.291-beta, v2.1.298-beta |
| F6 | 2D low-poly / wireframe render styles apply to the STAR but not to the bodies. Same root as F1: those styles only exist on the sphere path, and the 2D map's bodies were flat sprites. The star is never a sprite, which is why it alone obeyed. | fixed v2.1.286-beta |
| F7 | Body Graphics → photo: nothing appears in the preview until you leave the tab and come back. The loader was keyed on the selected body alone, and the line that clears the image for every non-photo mode stamped that same key — so switching TO photo without changing body looked, to the loader, like nothing had happened. Keyed on subject AND mode now, in `DocPanel` and `FilteredDocumentView` alike (both carried the same pair of lines). | fixed v2.1.292-beta |
| F8 | **VERIFIED, no re-unification needed.** One info-block component: the catalogue renders a single `inspectorAside` snippet for the holo AND the 2D-map tiers, containing exactly one `<DocPanel>`. `DocPanel` and `FilteredDocumentView` import the same builder (`buildGuideDocument`), the same theme resolver (`makeDocTheme`) and the same renderer (`renderDocument`). The settings DID reach both — but two arrived wrong, which is what the 2D-only testing hid: F7 and F9 were both found by this check, and both were faults in the SHARED layer rather than in one surface. One cosmetic gap left, not worth changing: `DocPanel` does not pass `navStyle` to `makeDocTheme`, harmless because panel mode builds no navigator block. | verified v2.1.296-beta |
| F9 | The selected font COLOUR should carry through to the headings in the info box, **including Rainbow**. Two faults in one line of `makeDocTheme`. (1) It flattened the `rainbow` sentinel to a hex before passing the theme on, and the rainbow-heading path in `renderDocument` tests for exactly that sentinel — so those headings had never rendered in ANY surface since v2.1.266, not merely failed to reach `DocPanel`. (2) The preset accent was not part of the colour seeding at all, so choosing a colour moved the chrome and left headings on the document style default. The accent now outranks the style seed for the accent + heading slots; an explicitly tweaked slot still outranks both. A follow-up found the live player view passing the pre-flattened accent to the engine while the editor passed the raw one — the exact preview-vs-live drift the shared resolver exists to prevent. | fixed v2.1.293-beta, v2.1.296-beta |
| F10 | The info-panel WIDTH slider should show its effect live as you drag, and should read as a percentage of the screen rather than a raw pixel count. Now a stored FRACTION of the viewport (`inspectorWidthPct`), converted to the pixels of whatever display it lands on when a preset is applied — a proportion travels from the GM's screen to a player's, a pixel count does not. The preview drew the raw pixel figure capped at 340, so the top half of the slider's travel moved nothing; it is a percentage of the stage now. | fixed v2.1.294-beta |
| F11 | **FEATURE, not a bug.** Pin the info panel to top / bottom / left / right to change the look and feel, with the view sliding to re-frame around it the way it already does when the panel appears. | captured, feature |

## G — Features (deliberately not bugs — do not hand these to a bug batch)

| # | Observation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| G29 | **RENUMBERED 2026-08-17 from G24 — that id was claimed twice on 2026-08-16 by two sessions; the coordinator's numbering keeps G24, this row moves.** **COLOUR AS A TAG VALUE TYPE — owner, 2026-08-16: *"Should we add colour as a valid data type for a tag? Its still a single (hex) value with a different type of picker."*** **The observation is right and the change is small, but it belongs to the TAGGING workstream and the schema change is on the CATEGORY, not on the tag** — a tag value is already a string and a hex is a string, so nothing is blocked today; what is missing is a `valueType` on the category so the editor knows to offer a swatch instead of a text box, and so a bad value can be rejected. `tagDefaults` is where categories are declared and [[B52]] records that tag storage is that workstream's live territory. **ONE CAUTION FROM THE BIOSPHERE WORK, because it is the case that looks most like a colour tag and deliberately is not one:** an authored layer colour is an INPUT — nothing re-derives it — and [[B52]]'s own test says an input is DATA, so it lives on `BiosphereLayer.colorHex` rather than in a tag. A colour TAG earns its place where the colour is a label a GM is applying to things (a faction's livery, a route, a region), not where it is a property of the thing itself. Worth saying in the spec, or the first user of the new type will be the wrong one. Related: [[B52]], TAG-4. | **ROUTED 2026-08-18 to "SSE2 Tagging Rewrite 2" on the owner's instruction ("the tagging workstream has done a load of work — add it to that to get tags done") — the one exception to "assign it nothing through this board", made by the owner. Category-level `valueType`, not a tag change** |
| G2 | **Document navigation links flow side by side and wrap, and that is now the DEFAULT.** Requested directly 2026-08-01 while the A25/A26 work was being verified: "sometimes it is many rows — side by side buttons is the default". The drill-in lists drew one full-width row per item, so Sol's thirteen planets turned the end of a page into a column of links; A26 had just added a Rings row on top. **Built as a third `NavStyle`, `chips`**, alongside the existing `plain` and `boxed` — laid out inside `drawList` rather than as a new block kind, because it is the same list with a different arrangement, so every drill-in list (planets, moons, rings, companions, constructs, the parent row) got it at once without any of them knowing. **The one real risk was hit-testing**, since side-by-side chips share a y band where rows never did: each chip pushes an X-BOUNDED region, which the document's hit test already prefers when present (the schematic's boxes work the same way). Verified by clicking Jupiter out of thirteen chips on one line and landing on Jupiter. An over-long name ellipsises to a full-width chip rather than running off the edge — the one way a flowing layout can break where rows cannot. **Default changed to `chips` for new presets**, per the request; `boxed` and `plain` remain selectable and are relabelled "Buttons — one per row" and "Plain text". A preset already stored keeps whatever it has. **FOLLOW-UP v2.1.331: in rainbow mode each button carries the hue of that body's MARKER on the schematic above.** Asked for as "can each of those buttons be a different colour?", then refined to "make those colours match the planet colour on the diagram above". **Built by SHARING the index rather than re-deriving it:** `systemSchematic` now exports `rainbowHue` and `rainbowHueIndex`, and its own drawer consumes the exported builder instead of an inline copy — so there is one map, and a chip and its dot cannot drift apart by construction. The builder attaches `ListItem.color`; the renderer only paints what it is handed, which keeps the look in the data layer rather than in the drawer. **Off-chart items are handled honestly:** moons and constructs are not drawn on the schematic and have no index, so they fall back to their position in their own list — varied, but not pretending to match a marker that is not there. Monochrome ignores the colour entirely, the same exemption the rainbow headings take. **The `hsl()` colour forced one change:** `hexA` only parses `#rrggbb` and silently returns its input, which would have painted a fully opaque chip — the tint goes through `globalAlpha` instead, which works whatever the format. **Verified across BOTH bundled maps: 490 navigator buttons that point at a charted body, ZERO whose colour differs from `rainbowHue(rainbowHueIndex(system).get(id))` — the exact expression the schematic's `markerCol` paints the dot with.** A pixel check of the drawn markers agreed on 7 of 12 and was INCONCLUSIVE on the rest, which is worth recording rather than hiding: each disagreement sampled a NEIGHBOUR's hue (Earth read Venus's, Pluto and the Kuiper Belt read Neptune's) because the schematic's hit boxes overlap on a crowded row, so it is a limitation of the sampler and not a colour fault. The parent-nav row was found uncoloured by that sweep and fixed in the same pass. | shipped v2.1.330-331-beta |

| # | Observation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| G1 | **More ARRANGEMENTS for the starmap textual view — a form, pickable boxes, star/planet icons.** Requested 2026-07-31. Today `buildStarmapDocument` (`catalogue/document/starmapDocument.ts:30`) emits exactly ONE shape: heading, optional italic description, `rule`, and a single `list` block of one row per system with a "1 star · 8 planets · 12 moons" sub-line. **The engine is far more capable than that view uses** — `blocks.ts` defines twelve block kinds (`heading, text, keyValue, tags, list, image, bodyDisc, rule, spacer, columnStart, columnEnd, schematic`) and `ListStyle` alone already offers six (`plain, illustrated-bullets, numbered-dossier, terminal-log, ledger, manifest`). The starmap document uses four blocks, no list style and no `keyValue` at all. So most of this is arranging capability that already exists. **Four candidates, cheapest first.** (1) DOSSIER/FORM — per system a level-2 heading then a stack of `keyValue` rows (Primary / Companions / Planets / Moons / Depth / Distance) then a `rule`. Literally a form, ZERO new block kinds, and the most different from what is there. Build this one first. (2) STAR-GLYPH CATALOGUE — a row of real coloured discs per system, primary large, companions smaller, planets a trailing run. `bodyDisc` already draws "from the body's true colour" and `systemVisualStars` already returns the star list, so the colours are DERIVED. **Hard rule: do not add a class-to-colour lookup table for this** — that is precisely the renderer shortcut that was reverted before. Needs one small addition: a glyph ROW of several small discs inline, rather than the current one-disc-per-block. (3) PICKABLE BOXES — **note the trap:** `columnStart`/`columnEnd` is NOT a general grid, it is image-specific (a left image strip with text flowing right), so a true 2-3 column card grid needs new layout capability in the renderer and is a real job. The cheap 80% is a new `ListStyle: 'cards'` — each item a bordered full-width box that highlights when selected. One enum value, no layout engine. Ship that and see whether the grid is still wanted. (4) SCHEMATIC PER SYSTEM — `SchematicBlock` already exists and takes a whole `System`, and `systemSchematic.ts` already draws them; a small schematic per system would be the standout look and reuses machinery already paid for. Most work of the four. **THE DESIGN STEER THAT MATTERS MORE THAN ANY OF THEM:** make this ONE new `layout` option on `StarmapDocOpts` and the preset, composing WITH the existing `documentStyle`, `listStyle` and colouration — a matrix (layout x style), not four bespoke views. That is a lot of distinct looks for very little code and it preserves the one-builder-one-renderer property F8 verified and that caught F7 and F9. **Follow-on, not part of this:** the SYSTEM-level document (`guideDocument`) has the same single-shape limitation, so whatever lands here should extend to it later. **RAINBOW — an open design question per arrangement, to be answered while building rather than up front.** When the preset accent is `rainbow`, what does the rainbow colour here? Either each ROW or BOX takes a different part of the spectrum walking down the list — the system document already does something like this, giving each drill-in item a hue (`guideDocument.ts:64-71`, `rainbowHue()`) — or it applies to the LABELS and headings only, leaving rows in the document's normal colours. It may well differ by arrangement: a stack of cards can carry a hue each without shouting, where a dense form probably wants it on the field labels alone. Set the colour in the BUILDER, not the renderer (`blocks.ts:105`). **One landmine:** never flatten the `'rainbow'` sentinel before `renderDocument` sees it — doing so is what broke the Guide's rainbow headings from v2.1.266 until F9 found it (`documentStyles.ts:85-86`). Check every arrangement in Rainbow as well as the plain styles. | captured, feature |

| G25 | **A PLANET AND A CONSTRUCT CAN BOTH BE GIVEN A CUSTOM PICTURE; A STAR CANNOT — owner, 2026-08-15: "we have the ability to customise the image of a planet and a construct but NOT stars — we need to unify."** **THE SURFACE IS ABSENT, NOT HIDDEN.** The upload block is F2, and it lives on the Composition tab (`BodyBasicsTab.svelte:578-602` handlers, `:947-970` markup). `BodySidePanel.svelte` offers that tab on the belt/ring branch (`:60`) and on the ordinary-body branch, but a STAR takes the `{:else}` at `:66` and is given Details / Orbit / System Info only — so there is no route to the block at all. | B63 | **LUNA'S NOON IS 209°C AND SHOULD BE ABOUT 120°C — AND THE CAUSE IS NOT EXTRA ENERGY, IT IS THAT THE DAY/NIGHT SWING IS SYMMETRIC WHEN RADIATIVE EQUILIBRIUM IS NOT.** Owner, 2026-08-16, reporting Luna at mean **-3°C** with **total -214°C to 209°C** and a **day↔night term of -205 to +200**, and suspecting *"we have worked stellar radiation hard — so we may have added a bit of energy that needs detuning."* **THE ARITHMETIC REPRODUCES EXACTLY, so the model is doing what it says.** `physics/surfaceTemperature.ts:84-88`: Luna is airless so `damp` is 0 and `diurnalSpread` is 1; it is planet-locked so `effRotHours` is its 655-hour ORBITAL period; `rotFactor = min(2.5, max(0.5, 655/24))` **clamps to 2.5**; `diAmp = 0.30 × Teq × 1 × 2.5` = 0.75 × 270 K ≈ **202 K**, applied as `mean ± diAmp`. That is the reported ±200. **WHY THAT IS WRONG, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A CONSTANT: THE HOT SIDE HAS NO PHYSICAL CEILING.** A sunlit surface cannot exceed its SUBSOLAR EQUILIBRIUM temperature, `T = (S(1-A)/sigma)^(1/4)`. For Luna at 1 AU with a bond albedo near 0.11 that is **382 K, about 109°C** — and the measured peak is about 120°C. **The model has no notion of that bound, so it simply keeps adding.** The night side has the mirror problem in reverse: it asymptotes toward a floor rather than falling linearly, and real equatorial lunar night is about 100 K (-173°C) against our -214°C. **So the true swing about a 270 K mean is roughly +112 / -170 — STRONGLY ASYMMETRIC — and `mean ± diAmp` cannot express that shape at any value of the constant.** **THIS MATTERS FOR THE FIX: DETUNING THE 0.30 WOULD BE WRONG.** Scaling it down to cap the day side would make an already-too-cold night colder still, and it would break every body where the current value is roughly right. **The fix is to BOUND the hot term at subsolar equilibrium and give the cold term a floor, not to shrink the amplitude.** **IT IS NOT A NEW REGRESSION, AND I CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: `surfaceTemperature.ts` has not been touched since v2.1.250-beta**, over four hundred versions ago. **What I did NOT verify is whether Luna's `Teq` has MOVED under the recent stellar work — and it would matter, because `diAmp` is directly proportional to it, so a rise in Teq widens the swing by 0.75 of it.** That is the first measurement to take, and it is the half of the owner's hypothesis that could still be right. **MEASURED 2026-08-16 AND IT SHARPENS THE WHOLE ITEM: Luna's `equilibriumTempK` IS 270.28 K, AND THAT NUMBER IS CORRECT.** For a body at 1 AU with a bond albedo near 0.11, `(S(1-A)/4sigma)^(1/4)` = **270.3 K**. **The engine's ENERGY BALANCE is right; the fault is entirely in what the model does with it.** **AND THE TWO SYMPTOMS I HAD FILED AS SEPARATE ARE ONE FAULT, WHICH IS THE REAL FINDING.** `equilibriumTempK` is a POWER balance — the single temperature at which a sphere radiates away exactly what it receives. **It is NOT the mean surface temperature, and for a body with a large day/night swing it is well above it, because radiated power goes as T^4.** A surface that is 390 K at noon and 95 K at midnight radiates the same total as a uniform 270 K body, but its AVERAGE TEMPERATURE is far lower — real Luna sits around 215-250 K depending how you average, against our 270. **So "the mean is 20 K high" and "the swing is symmetric" are not two bugs. They are the same T^4 nonlinearity seen from two ends: the model takes an energy-balance figure, calls it the mean, and hangs a symmetric swing off it.** **THAT INVERTS THE FIX AND MAKES IT MORE PRINCIPLED THAN "bound the hot side": derive the DAY and NIGHT temperatures from energy balance, and let the MEAN fall out of them — rather than deriving both from a mean that was never a mean.** One change fixes all three symptoms at once: day too hot, night too cold, mean too high. **Note the corollary for the anchors: on Venus the swing is tiny, so mean and Teq nearly coincide and nothing should move. The bigger the swing, the further the mean must sit below Teq — which is itself the test.** **A SEPARATE, SMALLER DISCREPANCY WORTH NOT CONFLATING: the MEAN is about 20 K high** — -3°C against a real lunar equatorial mean near -20°C. Different question, different term, do not fix it with the same constant. **AND THE `rotFactor` CLAMP AT 2.5 IS DOING A LOT OF UNEXAMINED WORK:** Luna's 27-day solar day gives 27.3 and clamps, so every slowly-rotating body lands on the same multiplier however slow it is. Related: [[B42]] (the seasonal term two lines above this one), [[B34]], and the standing rule that a quantity correct for its purpose can still be published as a lie. **FIXED v2.1.685-beta, and the inverted diagnosis was the right one — one change, all three symptoms.** Day and night are derived from the balance and the mean is what they average to: with `f` the fraction of absorbed energy reaching the night side, the day hemisphere radiates `(2-f)sigma Teq^4`, the night `f sigma Teq^4`, and the sub-stellar point `(4-3f)`, which at f=0 is the local equilibrium `sqrt(2) x Teq` — the ceiling the model never had. **`f` has TWO channels and they compose:** the existing damping term (bulk transport by air and ocean, UNTOUCHED, and Venus does not move by a single kelvin) and heat stored in the ground, expressed as the standard thermal parameter `I sqrt(omega) / (sigma Tss^3)`. **That is where rotation belongs, and it answers the `rotFactor` clamp question the entry raised: the clamp is GONE.** Rotation no longer scales an amplitude; Ganymede and Callisto were identical to the kelvin and now differ, both within 5 K of measurement. **ONE constant, regolith's MEASURED thermal inertia (50), raised where an atmosphere puts gas in the pore spaces to conduct through — which is real physics and is why Mars holds its night far better than the airless Moon.** **MEASURED against every anchor and fitted to none:** Luna noon 111 C (measured ~120, the bond-albedo bound reads ~10 K low by construction), night -165 C (measured -173), mean 214 K where Diviner measures ~215 — **so the entry's separate 'mean is 20 K high, against a real -20 C' is CORRECTED: -20 C is the naive average of the two extremes, and the real equatorial average is ~215 K, which the new mean lands on without being aimed at it.** Mercury 421 C noon at perihelion (measured 427) and -176 C night (measured -173), **and its captured 3:2 resonance now reads as a very slow day/night cycle rather than a permanent face** — the sun does rise on Mercury, and `lockedSpin` already kept its real period. Mars -94 to 13 C, mean 209 K (real ~210). Titan, Pluto and Triton come out very nearly uniform, which is correct and which the old model could not express at all. **THE TOTAL IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLAMPED at the sunlit ceiling:** that bound is on the globally-averaged balance and a real surface beats it locally, so Luna's total lands on 121 C against a measured 120 while its day/night term stays inside 111. Quadrature preserved throughout. **THE TWO TEMPERATURES ARE NOW NAMED, WHICH IS THE HALF THAT COULD HAVE BECOME A LIE:** `temperatureK` is the RADIATING temperature and still feeds the classifier, the tags and the thermal fixed point; `temperatureProfile.meanK` is the mean a reader sees, in the panel, the info block, the catalogue and the trace. **DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: writing the derived mean back into `temperatureK`.** It would move the classifier and the albedo/cloud fixed point for every airless body at once, and that is the owner's call, not a side effect of a display fix — see the OPEN QUESTION below. Tags chased: `activity/sublimating` is the only one that moved (Ganymede, Dione, Rhea, Iapetus lose it) because it buckets off the PEAK, which is now bounded; at their real peak temperatures water ice is effectively static, so losing it is right. `climate/polar-ice`, the `hydrosphere/*` phase tags, `tidal/volcanism` and `tidal/lava-flows` all checked and unmoved. PHY-19. Pinned by `surfaceTemperature.spec.ts` and five anchors in `physics-baseline.test.ts`. | **fixed v2.1.685-beta — session notes: `docs/dev/surface-temperature-notes.md`** |

CHEAPLY here rather than designing the final form). **PRECISION ON "IS EVERYTHING SOL-BASED?" — NO, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE GOOD NEWS.** The **ZONES ARE CORRECTLY DERIVED**: `zones.ts:18-22`'s `getLuminosity` computes L from the star's own radius and temperature by Stefan-Boltzmann, and the silicate line, frost line, formation frost line, CO ice line, goldilocks zone and `systemLimitAu` all follow from it. **It is only the PLACEMENT that is Sol-based — and the zones are used merely as MIN/MAX FILTERS, never as the basis for spacing.** So the engine already computes the right numbers and | B80 | **THE FROST LINE WAS DERIVED FROM STELLAR MASS INSTEAD OF LUMINOSITY, AND FOR MOONS IT WAS ASKED OF THE PLANET — OWNER-DIAGNOSED 2026-08-17, and the diagnosis is exactly right.** Legacy generation computed `frost_line_base_au * sqrt(M_host / M_sun)` at `generation/planet.ts:133` and `generation/placement.ts:9`. **The physics wants LUMINOSITY: `d_frost ~ 2.7 AU * sqrt(L/L_sun)`. Since `L ~ M^3.5` on the main sequence, the correct distance scales as `M^1.75` — so a `sqrt(M)` form is not an approximation of it, it is a different curve, and it is wrong in OPPOSITE directions at the two ends.** **Measured against the luminosity-derived line: M8 dwarf 12.9x TOO FAR OUT (0.809 vs 0.062 AU), L dwarf 42.6x, K5 2.3x, and a hot B2 star 10x TOO CLOSE (8.5 vs 85.4 AU). A moon was therefore almost always 'inside the frost line', so generated moons of cold outer giants were essentially never icy.** Fixed by routing both sites through `zones.ts`, which already derived every zone from luminosity correctly, via a new `stellarContextFor` that walks the parent chain to the STAR and returns the body's distance from IT. **The two lines are NOT interchangeable and the distinction is now load-bearing: `formationFrostLine` (~170 K) decides what a body could form AS; `currentFrostLine` (~125 K) is present-day ice stability. Sol's are 2.26 and 4.97 AU.** Rule: GEN-4. Guard: `generation/frostLine.spec.ts`, whose load-bearing case is two stars of EQUAL MASS and different luminosity — identical under any mass-based form. **ALSO FOUND, NOT ACTED ON: `generation/placement.ts` and its only caller `components/PlacementMenu.svelte` are DEAD — nothing imports the component, and it reads `store.rulePack` off a `Starmap` type that has no such field. | B81 | **THE KILL ZONE AND DANGER ZONE ARE THE ONLY ZONES NOT DERIVED — THEY MULTIPLY IN THE STORED `radiationOutput`, WHICH [[B57]] RECORDS AS DRIFTED BY UP TO 60,000x.** Found while auditing every zone across the full stellar range at the owner's request after [[B80]]. **THE GOOD NEWS FIRST, because it is most of the answer: the six CONDENSATION LINES ARE CORRECT AND SCALE CORRECTLY EVERYWHERE.** All of them come from one function, `getDistanceForTemperature`, which inverts the equilibrium-temperature relation to `a = R_star (T_star/T_eq)^2 / 2` — luminosity-correct by construction, since `R^2 T^4` IS luminosity. **Verified across fifteen classes from an O5V supergiant to a Y1 dwarf, about ten orders of magnitude in luminosity: every line finite and positive, correctly ordered (silicate < soot < formation frost < frost < CO2 < CO) in every case, habitable zone ordered and inside the system limit in every case, and every line scaling as EXACTLY sqrt(L).** So [[B80]] was a fault in the legacy generators' private copy, never in `zones.ts`. **THE EXCEPTION IS `calculateKillZone` (`zones.ts:30-59`), which computes `0.1 * sqrt(uvFactor * radiationOutput * L)` — reading `star.radiationOutput`, a STORED pack value, where every other zone derives.** Measured: giving Sol `radiationOutput: 1000` moves its kill zone 0.100 -> 3.16 AU (31.6x) and its danger zone 0.5 -> 15.8 AU. **This QUALIFIES the claim in [[B58]]'s note that 'the zones are right; | G27 | **V4: LOOK-BACK TIME — SHOW A DISTANT SYSTEM AS THE LIGHT LEFT IT, NOT AS IT IS. Owner, 2026-08-16:** *"one V4 feature which may be cool in intergalaxy games — you can use the dynamic ageing tools to show a galaxy what our solar system looks like at that distance of lightyears."* **IT IS FREE ONCE [[G17]] EXISTS, WHICH IS WHY IT BELONGS WITH IT: the machinery is AGE and DISTANCE, and V3.1 already puts real distances on the map while G17 provides the ageing.** Look-back time is just `distance in light years` subtracted from the system's age — no new model, no new data. **AND IT IS REAL PHYSICS RATHER THAN A GIMMICK: you cannot see a distant object as it is, only as it was.** **BUT SHARPEN IT BEFORE BUILDING IT, BECAUSE THE OBVIOUS VERSION IS INVISIBLE.** At a thousand light years the look-back is a thousand years, and **a Sun-like star changes by nothing measurable in that time** — even Andromeda at 2.5 million light years leaves a G dwarf essentially unmoved. **Ageing a Sol-like system by the light-travel time and showing the result would produce an identical picture and read as a broken feature.** **WHERE IT ACTUALLY BITES IS THE INTERESTING PART AND IS WORTH BUILDING TOWARD DELIBERATELY: short-lived stars.** An O star lives three to ten million years, so **at intergalactic range you are routinely looking at stars that have already died** — the light is still arriving from something that is now a remnant. **"That star your navigator is steering by does not exist any more" is a GM hook, and it falls straight out of the existing ageing model** the moment distance is subtracted. Same for a supernova whose remnant is already spread, and for anything the ageing slider moves fast. **SO THE FEATURE IS NOT "age the system by the travel time" — IT IS "tell me which of the things I can see are already gone", which is the same computation with a far better output.** Related: [[G17]], [[G20]], [[G26]], `docs/dev/v4-scope.md`. | **captured 2026-08-16 — V4, rides with [[G17]]; build it as "what is already gone", not as "age it slightly"** |

Decks, haze and a giant's cloud chemistry now take the top-of-atmosphere spectrum; ground and ocean take what got through. **A SECOND FAULT WAS UNDERNEATH IT:** even with cream cloud, a quarter of Venus's rock still showed, because the deck veils by `cloudOpacity x coverage-bucket` and 0.8 x 0.92 leaves 26% — nobody has ever seen Venus's surface from orbit. **The quantity that settles it was already derived and unused: TRANSMISSION.** If a sky passes 2% of the light down it is no more transparent coming back up, so the surface stack now fades toward what is above it as transmission falls. **SCOPED TO transmission < 0.12 DELIBERATELY, and the reason is a real double-count:** the transmission figure INCLUDES the cloud deck, which has already veiled a few lines earlier, so applying it everywhere counts the same weather twice — Earth lost its blue to a second helping of its own cloud (#97a2a8 to #bbc1cb) before the threshold went in. **Untangling that properly means the deck's own optical depth reaching the renderer, which it does not: `deriveCloudDecks` computes tau and then throws it away, and only a five-way coverage BUCKET survives on the tag.** That is the real root cause and it is a tag-format change. It was NOT the same issue as the disc; it was a new one, in the eye model rather than in the renderer.** Plain von Kries divides by the illuminant's own cone response, which assumes the eye can discount any light however little of it there is. Measured: Venus's sky leaves the S cones **0.48% of their home share**, and the maths asked for a **134-fold gain**. Checked while fixing B1: **not downstream of it.** Adrian's greenhouse is +336.8 K before AND after — B1 moved the Teq underneath it (246 → 304 K), not the greenhouse term. The ratio is the model's own shape: forcing goes as `log(1 + sqrt(100·pp))`, then the response is `log` again, so partial pressure enters twice-logarithmically and saturates hard (Adrian pp 7.3 → 3.33, Venus pp 88.8 → 4.56, a ratio of 0.73 on 8.7% of the pressure). `broadening = min(1, sqrt(P))` is also pinned at 1 for anything over 1 bar, so it distinguishes nothing above that. Then CHECKED against every anchor the Solar System offers, not just Venus: Mars 0.006 bar +5.8 K (measured 6), Earth 1.013 bar +32.8 (33), Titan 1.45 bar +14.1 (12), Venus 92 bar +523.6 (505). Note POLAR does not exist in `Grid.svelte` today (typed `'grid' | 'hex' | 'traveller-hex' | 'none'`), so it is either a new type or lives in a different renderer — establish which before scoping. (3) **Traveller Map specifically wants thicker SUBSECTOR EDGES and HEX NUMBERING**, both of which are conventions of the real Traveller map and are what makes it read as one. `travellerMetadata.importedSubsectors` already exists on the starmap type, so the subsector boundaries may already be derivable rather than needing authoring — check before designing. Thicker subsector edges are drawn as RIBBONS with real world-space width - THREE ignores line thickness on nearly every platform, so heavier has to be geometry rather than a parameter - and the numbering gate was lowered from 0.5 scene units to 0.22, which is why the numbers had never appeared on a normal map. **`travellerMetadata.importedSubsectors` was checked as the entry suggested and is NOT the source**: it is per-import metadata for hover titles, whereas the boundary is a property of the LATTICE (every 8th column, every 10th row), so it is derived, and the geometry now comes from the same shared generator as the hexes. The boundary is a continuous line including the bridge between columns - see the note at the foot of [[A37]]. **(1) EVERY GRID TYPE NOW TAKES THE SAME TREATMENT, and that meant moving POLAR onto the shared path rather than adding options to it.** The dimensional quality the request liked is the depth curtain under each line; polar was raw `LineLoop`s with a per-ring dim baked in, so it could take neither the depth nor the falloff. Rings and spokes are now edges through `addLattice` like every lattice, which gives both for free. The spokes are SEGMENTED for the same reason the squares had to be - a per-vertex fade judges a full-length spoke by its far end and drops it whole. **(2) BRIGHTNESS FALLOFF IS A DIAL: "Grid falloff", 0 to 100%, on every overlay type including polar.** 0 is even brightness across the field; 100% is bright near cells gone by the edge. One function maps the dial to the fade window, so the numbers sit in ONE place instead of being sprinkled through the renderer, and the dial itself is preset data (`starmapGridFalloff`) as the entry requires. **RULED OUT, since the entry asked it to be established: POLAR is not missing.** It does not exist in `Grid.svelte` because that is the GM's 2D SNAP-grid, a different renderer with a different job; the 3D starmap has had `plain` and `scaled` polar all along, and the shared `MapOverlay` vocabulary already carries both. No new type was needed. **ALIGNMENT AND SCALE VERIFIED against the GM's own grid, not assumed.** `Starmap.svelte` mounts `Grid.svelte` with `originX={0} originY={0}` and `gridSize = 50`, which is `DEFAULT_MAP_CELL`, so both lattices start at map (0,0) at the same cell size; the scene hands the generator `cfg.size * mapK`, the map-to-scene fit, so a GM cell is exactly one player cell. Pinned by two tests that reproduce Grid.svelte's centre formula VERBATIM and compare it against `hexCentres` to nine decimal places over a hundred hexes, plus a linear-scaling check. A system the GM snapped to a hex lands dead-centre in the player's. **COMPLETED v2.1.376-beta - the falloff dial now reaches EVERY view that draws a grid, not only the starmap.** The system stage has its own grid picker and therefore needed its own dial. It has one: a second, separate preset field (`gridFalloff`), **defaulted to 0 so the system view is unchanged unless a GM asks for it** - that view has always been evenly lit and a silent change to the most-used surface in the app is not a feature. Deliberately NOT sharing `starmapGridFalloff`: the grid TYPE already shares one field across both stages, which is a recorded fault, and repeating it here would have been repeating a known mistake. **Making the system view able to fade at all needed a different mechanism from the starmap's, and this is the part worth recording.** `holo/scene.ts` draws its grid through `addGridLines`, which keeps every vertex's ABSOLUTE position for the floating-origin rebase. The fade is computed from those absolute positions, once, at build time - so it stays anchored to the system while rebasing moves the drawn coordinates. A fade computed from the drawn coordinates would have slid with the camera focus, which is the trap `project_sse_v2_floating_origin` exists to warn about. **Found on the way and NOT unified, recorded unnumbered: the system view has a THIRD copy of the lattice geometry**, and it has already drifted - its hexes are POINTY-topped (axial q/r, `60k-30` corners) where the GM grid and both starmaps are FLAT-topped. The four numbers the dial interpolates between are the SHAPE of the response curve, not tuning. Adding it put the "is this a hex overlay?" test in five places, so it now has a NAME (`isHexFamily`, `hasSubsectors`) - that is [[A34]]'s failure in miniature and it was one edit from happening. A test asserts all three hex overlays produce the IDENTICAL lattice, so the difference stays what is drawn ON it. **(c) GRID DEPTH IS A SLIDER, not a switch** - how far the curtain hangs is the whole of the effect. Reads a boolean from presets saved before this rather than migrating them. | G6 | **BANKED FOR LATER: a minimum-mass filter on the printed reports, to cut asteroids and other small bodies out.** Requested 2026-08-01 and explicitly banked rather than queued. A slider setting a minimum mass, with bodies below it omitted from the report, and **the slider showing how many bodies are included and excluded** as you move it — that read-out is the part that makes it usable, because a bare mass figure means nothing to a GM but "42 of 156 bodies" does. Worth considering whether the same filter belongs on the guide document and the info surfaces, since the underlying complaint — "there are too many trivial bodies in the way" — is not unique to paper; but the request was specifically about reports and should not be widened without asking. **REFINED 2026-08-02, and the refinement is the good part.** (1) **The user sets the gate; the app does not guess.** Explicitly framed as "doing a mass gate slider you can set rather than try and tell you what you are not interested in" — so no heuristic, no clever inference about which bodies matter. A slider and a number. (2) **Show the MOST MASSIVE BODY EXCLUDED, not merely a count.** "42 of 156 included" tells a GM nothing about whether the gate is set right; "the largest thing you are hiding is Ceres" tells them instantly. That single read-out is what makes the control usable, and it should update live as the slider moves, before the report is generated. **Show BOTH — the count is wanted too, confirmed 2026-08-02: "we can still have the numbers so they know how many have been excluded."** So the read-out carries how many are in, how many are out, AND the largest one out. They answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other: the count tells a GM the SCALE of what the gate is doing ("you are hiding 114 of 156 things"), while the named body tells them whether the gate is in the RIGHT PLACE ("...and the biggest is Ceres"). A worker should treat neither as optional. **THE PATTERN ALREADY EXISTS AND IS TESTED — REUSE IT RATHER THAN REINVENTING.** The ubox importer solves the identical problem: `import/ubox/convert.ts:57` takes `options.minBodyMassKg` defaulting to `RECOMMENDED_MIN_MASS_KG`, counts what falls below at `:76`, and reports it as a skip reason (`types.ts:104`, `'below-mass-threshold'`); `import/ubox/index.ts:28` computes the live "N bodies included" count WITHOUT a full conversion, which is exactly the responsiveness a slider needs; and `ubox.spec.ts:188` pins the default against real bodies — "keeps Pluto, drops the 4e20 TinyRock". **So the threshold constant is already calibrated and already means something**, and the report filter should share it rather than inventing a second number that disagrees. If the two genuinely need different defaults, say why. | captured, feature — banked |

| G11 | **DESIGN INVESTIGATION ONLY: spec the Traveller importer properly.** Requested 2026-08-03 after [[D6]] — the importer will be improved at some point, and now is a good moment to specify it rather than patch it. **DELIVERABLE IS A DESIGN DOCUMENT** (`docs/dev/traveller-import-design.md`) plus an updated G11 entry. Do not build the feature. **START FROM THE EVIDENCE, WHICH IS ALREADY IN HAND.** [[D6]] found that a Traveller-imported Earth freezes at -16 C with a 70% ice surface, because `Traveller-6 (Standard - Earth-like)` carries no water vapour while the pack's own `Nitrogen-Oxygen (Earth-like)` does — one concept defined twice, drifted. That is a symptom; the question this doc answers is how many more of the same kind there are and what the importer SHOULD do. **QUESTIONS TO ANSWER.** (1) **AUDIT the Traveller atmosphere table against the pack's native equivalents.** Where a Traveller entry names the same physical thing as a native one, do their compositions agree? Every disagreement is a D6 waiting to happen. Deliver the table, including the entries that match. (2) **Are declared constraints ENFORCED?** Traveller-6 states `temp_range_K: [280, 310]` and was applied to a 257 K world. Does the selection honour the ranges the data declares, and if not, are the ranges meaningful or decoration? A constraint the data states and the code ignores is worth more than any single bug. (3) **WHAT DOES TRAVELLER ACTUALLY GIVE US, and what must be inferred?** A UWP is a handful of digits — size, atmosphere, hydrographics, population, government, law, tech. Everything else this engine needs (mass, radius, orbital distance, temperature, composition) is inferred. Map that boundary explicitly: which fields come from the import, which are inferred, and — following [[B10]]'s precedent — WHICH CARRY AN "INFERRED" TAG so a GM can tell an imported fact from a guessed one. That distinction is a promise to the reader and it should be designed in, not retrofitted. (4) **HOW SHOULD HYDROGRAPHICS DRIVE THE ATMOSPHERE?** Traveller states a world's water coverage directly. D6's underlying gap is that surface water does not reach the greenhouse; an importer that knows hydrographics is exactly where that could be honoured, or where it should defer to a derived-vapour model. Say which, and note the physics half is its own item. (5) **WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN WHEN TRAVELLER AND THE PHYSICS DISAGREE?** A UWP may assert a breathable atmosphere on a world this engine would freeze. Options are to trust the UWP and let the physics contradict it, to let the physics win and flag the divergence, or to nudge the inferred inputs (orbital distance, albedo) until the stated outcome is reachable. This is the central design question and the doc should recommend one with reasons. **SCOPE WIDENED 2026-08-03 — THE IMPORTER IS PRODUCING PHYSICALLY INVALID BODIES, AND THAT IS NOW THE HEADLINE.** Reported symptoms: **about half of imported gas giants come out TOROIDAL**, and planets land **implausibly close to their star**. **(6) THE TOROID CAUSE IS FOUND AND IT IS A KNOWN FAULT CLASS IN AN UNCOVERED PATH.** `src/lib/traveller/importer.ts` NEVER SETS `rotation_period_hours` — a grep across it finds no assignment. `physics/rotation.ts` computes `spinFraction(rotationHours, densityGcc)`, so an absent or zero period reads as INFINITELY FAST ROTATION, which lands past `NEAR_BREAKUP_AT` (0.8) or `BREAKUP_AT` (1.0) and yields `near-breakup` / `unstable` — the toroidal-tending shapes. This is exactly [[B9]]a's finding, **"a placeholder zero is a CLAIM, not an absence"**, in a route that fix never reached: [[B10]] pushed spin provenance through "all three body-creation routes" and the importer appears to be a FOURTH nobody counted. Confirm that, and if so `docs/dev/generation-duplication-map.md` is understating the problem and should be corrected. **(7) THE DEEPER PATTERN, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS SURFACED NOW.** The importer's inferences were tolerable when the engine derived little. The engine now derives rotational deformation, thermal state, classification, radiation and geology, so a guessed or missing input no longer sits quietly — it becomes a visible absurdity. **Every field the importer leaves absent or guesses is a candidate for the same failure**, so enumerate them all rather than fixing the two that were noticed: what does the importer set, what does it leave to a default, and what does that default MEAN to a physics model that now reads it? The orbital distances are the second known case; find the rest before they are reported one at a time. **(8) COMPARE THE GENERATION SYSTEMS AND RECOMMEND A SIMPLIFICATION.** There are already two live system generators and three body-creation routes (`docs/dev/generation-duplication-map.md`), and the importer is another. Set them side by side: what each one sets, what each infers, where they disagree, and what a single shared "make a plausible body" path would have to provide to replace the lot. **The tidy-up is scoped for V2.3+ and is NOT this session's job to build** — but this audit is the right place to say what it should look like, because nobody has yet had all four paths in view at once. **METHOD:** verify claims against the code and the rule-pack data, say plainly where you are reasoning rather than measuring, give a RECOMMENDATION rather than a survey, phase it, and include a "not worth doing" section. Flag anything needing an owner decision instead of deciding it. **DO NOT** implement, change the rule pack, or touch `src/lib/traveller/**` beyond reading it — but DO say which of the faults you find are one-line data fixes worth doing immediately and which need the redesign. Related: [[D6]], [[B9]], [[B10]], [[D2]]. | captured, design only |
| G10 | **The system map should offer the same grid options and falloff sliders as the starmaps — minus hexes, with a 1 AU fixed grid and polar.** Requested 2026-08-03. **MOST OF THIS ALREADY SHIPPED IN [[G4]] — check before building.** `lib/map/mapOverlay.ts` is now THE overlay vocabulary shared by all four spatial views (2D orrery, 3D holo system, 2D starmap, 3D starmap), `lib/map/latticeGeometry.ts` is the one generator behind them, `MAP_OVERLAY_OPTIONS` is described as "the one dropdown list — every view's overlay picker renders THIS, so they can never drift apart", polar is already in the set (`plain` = rings and spokes, `scaled` = rings labelled with real distances), and the falloff dial was reported as reaching every view that draws a grid. **THREE THINGS ARE GENUINELY LEFT, and the middle one is the valuable one.** **(1) "EXCEPT THE HEXES" IS CURRENTLY SILENT RATHER THAN HONEST.** `forSystemScale` folds hex to square before the system view can draw one, so hexes already do not appear — but because every view renders the SAME dropdown, the system map still OFFERS "Hex", "Subsector hex" and "Traveller hex", and a user picking one silently gets squares. Filter the options per view so a view only offers what it can draw. Do this WITHOUT splitting the list into two — the whole point of `MAP_OVERLAY_OPTIONS` is that it cannot drift, so filter it, do not copy it. **(2) THE SYSTEM GRID IS NOT A DISTANCE AT ALL — MAKE IT 1 AU.** `holo/scene.ts:1005` sets the cell to `GRID_RADIUS / 7`, a fraction of the scene radius, so it scales with the view and means nothing physical. A 1 AU cell turns a decorative plate into a SCALE REFERENCE a GM can read at a glance, which is much the more useful thing. **Handle the extremes deliberately rather than discovering them:** a 40 AU system gives about 40 cells across, which is fine; a compact system half an AU wide would show no lines at all, and a map out to the Kuiper belt would show a hundred. Either step by decade (0.1 / 1 / 10 AU, picked from the framed extent) or clamp the count and SAY which — a fixed 1 AU that vanishes on a tight system is worse than a labelled decade. Note `scaled` already labels polar rings with real distances, so there is a precedent for a physically meaningful overlay to follow. **(3) CONFIRM THE SLIDERS ARE EXPOSED** on the system map's own settings, not merely reaching it in code — [[A32]] and [[A40]] were both cases of a control whose range never arrived at the view. **REFINED 2026-08-03, AND THE TWO REFINEMENTS ARE ONE FUNCTION — build it once.** **(a) THE GRID STEPS BY DECADE WITH A CROSSFADE.** The 1 AU cell should BRIGHTEN and subdivide into ten as you zoom in, and do the reverse on the way out so you see 10 AU and then 100 AU squares. That is the honest answer to the extremes problem raised above — a fixed 1 AU vanishes on a compact system and draws a hundred lines on a Kuiper-belt view — and the crossfade is what makes it read as one continuous grid rather than a jump: as the finer level approaches usefulness it fades UP while the coarser fades DOWN, so at any zoom you see one dominant level and a ghost of the next. Standard map and CAD behaviour, and worth doing properly because a grid that jumps is more distracting than one that does not adapt at all. **(b) THE SCALED POLAR RINGS SHOW UNTIDY DISTANCES** on BOTH the starmap and the system map — they should land on round numbers ending in 0 or 5 rather than whatever the current ring spacing produces. Almost certainly the same cause as the grid: the ring radius derives from a fraction of the scene extent (the system grid uses `GRID_RADIUS / 7`) rather than from a chosen interval, so the LABEL is honest about a distance nobody would choose. **(c) THE SHARED PIECE: one "nice interval" utility serves all of it.** Pick the step from the 1 / 2 / 5 x 10^n sequence so that a framed extent yields a sensible number of divisions — the classic nice-number algorithm — and let the square grid, the polar rings and their labels all call it. It must be UNIT-AGNOSTIC, taking a raw extent and returning a step, because the starmap works in light years or parsecs and the system map in AU; the same logic serves both and a second copy per unit is exactly the duplication the standing rule warns about. | G8 | **"Next eclipse, and how big" — a derivable, evocative fact the engine already has every input for.** Proposed 2026-08-02: can a body always say when its next eclipse is, and its size? **Yes. So "next eclipse" is a forward search over the propagator for an alignment, and "how big" is the ratio of angular diameters, each just `radius / distance`. **THAT RATIO IS THE GOOD PART, because it decides the KIND of eclipse and it is pure arithmetic.** Ratio near 1 gives a total eclipse; occulter smaller than the star gives an annular one; much smaller and it is only a transit — a dot crossing a disc. **Three calibration anchors sit in the bundled Sol and all three are famous, so this can be validated rather than trusted:** Luna and the Sun subtend almost exactly the same angle from Earth, which is WHY totality is possible and why it only just covers; **Phobos is far too small ever to give totality and its real transits are annular**; Deimos is barely more than a moving speck. If the model reproduces those three it is behaving. **DESIGN QUESTIONS TO ANSWER RATHER THAN ASSUME.** (1) **Observed from WHERE?** An eclipse happens somewhere. The natural readings are a satellite crossing the star as seen from its primary, and the primary eclipsing the star as seen from a moon — both are interesting and they are different events. Choose, and say which. (2) **COST: a forward search over a propagator is not free, so it must be ON DEMAND and never inside a derivation pass.** [[B13]] is the cautionary tale — a per-pass cost that also broke idempotence. Compute when a reader asks, cache against the clock, and keep it out of `process()`. (3) **HONESTY ABOUT WHAT IS PREDICTED.** Real eclipse seasons arise from NODAL PRECESSION, which this engine almost certainly does not model — so the answer is "when these elements next align", not an ephemeris. That is perfectly good for a game and it should say so rather than implying observatory precision. **Sequence AFTER [[C5]]**: inclination and reference frame are the whole game here, and predicting eclipses on a frame that is about to change means doing it twice. **BUILT v2.1.383-beta - `src/lib/system/eclipses.ts`, validated against all three anchors and shipped into the shared body block.** **THE THREE DESIGN QUESTIONS, ANSWERED.** **(1) OBSERVED FROM WHERE: you are standing on the body whose data is open, at the point where the shadow falls.** That one viewpoint covers BOTH readings the entry asked about - a satellite crossing the star as seen from its primary, and the primary covering the star as seen from a moon - because both are "the star gets hidden from where I stand", and the number it yields is something an observer actually experiences. A THIRD reading turned up that the entry did not list and it is not a footnote: **barycentre PARTNERS**. Pluto and Charon eclipsed each other every few days through the late eighties and that is how Charon's radius was measured; a member's parent is the BARYCENTRE, so the partner is a sibling rather than a parent or a child, and a rule written for parents and children misses it entirely. **Standing on the SURFACE rather than at the centre is not a refinement either, and getting the surface point wrong was the one real modelling error made here.** The obvious choice is the sub-OCCULTER point, directly under the moon. It is wrong: it pins the observer to whatever latitude the occulter is over, and for a moon in its primary's equatorial plane that is the equator - so Phobos appeared to transit only at the martian equinoxes, when in reality its shadow tracks a wide band of latitudes and rovers see transits through most of the year. The observer stands where the SHADOW falls, on the axis star-occulter-here. The displacement matters at all because it is a whole body radius, which for Luna is 1.7% of the distance - and 1.7% is the difference between an eclipse that just covers the Sun and one that just fails to. **Totality lives in that margin.** **(2) COST: two free pre-filters, a season gate, and a reduced system - and never a derivation pass.** Nothing here is reachable from `process()`; it is called by `bodyFacts` when a reader asks, and `nextEclipseCached` holds the answer until the date it predicted has gone by, which is the whole caching rule and comes straight from how it is read. **Pre-filter one is the 25% floor** - how dark it could EVER get is arithmetic on orbital radii, so a speck is dismissed without a single propagation, which is what stops Deimos at 1%. **Pre-filter two answers "does the shadow ever MISS?"**, and it exists because searching for a date is worst exactly where a date is least meaningful: Io passes into Jupiter's shadow on essentially every one of its 1.77-day orbits, so the honest answer is "every 1.8 d" and the search is skipped entirely. **The test is geometry, NOT "is it a moon of a giant", and Callisto is why:** its miss distance reaches 109,000 km against Jupiter's 69,911, so it escapes the shadow for part of the cycle - exactly what the real Callisto does, alone among the Galileans. **A POLAR orbit falls out of the same arithmetic**: the plane-to-plane angle is near 90 degrees there, the miss distance is the whole orbital radius, and such a moon gets fierce SEASONS instead of a cycle. **The season gate is that same geometry taken per moment** - over one orbit the closest the shadow axis comes to the observing body is `a * sin(beta)`, beta being the star's angular distance from the orbit plane, so a whole non-season is skipped at a coarse stride. An earlier version used a loose margin instead and was useless: it never closed for Phobos at all. **And the biggest win was not an algorithm.** The propagator places EVERY node on every call, so the search is handed a system reduced to the three bodies involved plus their ancestors - the same propagator on a smaller input. **Saturn went from 8.2 s to 243 ms, a 34x cut**; every body in Sol now answers in under 250 ms cold and 0.1 ms cached, 584 ms for all 24 at once, and in practice only the SELECTED body is ever computed. **(3) HONESTY: `approximate` is on every prediction and the wording never implies otherwise.** Elements are held fixed - there is no nodal precession here - so what is answered is "when these elements next line up", not an ephemeris. **THE THREE ANCHORS ALL LAND, and they are asserted as physics rather than pinned to whatever the code printed.** Luna and the Sun come out at a ratio of 1.06 from Earth's surface, which is why the eclipse found is a near-thing 60% partial; **Phobos comes out at 0.607, giving a 37% ANNULAR transit and never a total one** - the real figure is about a third of the disc; Deimos comes out at 0.10, about 1%, below the floor and never propagated. Earth from Luna is 3.7x the Sun, so Luna gets totality. All 23 tests in `eclipses.spec.ts` read the bundled Sol directly rather than a fixture. **PRESENTATION: a date and a percentage, in the SHARED body block** (`bodyFacts`), so it reaches the GM inspector, the printed player report and the 2D/3D info panels from one place - `describeEclipse` builds the string so three surfaces cannot word it three ways. It reads "in 107 d - 37% annular (Phobos)", or "every 1.8 d - total (Jupiter)" for a cycle, or an absolute date when the caller supplies its campaign calendar's formatter. **The row is OMITTED when no clock is passed**, rather than guessed: a caller with no clock has not asked for one. The document surfaces redraw a canvas, so they get the clock at 1 Hz of WALL time rather than per frame - a date only needs to be right to the second, whatever the time scale. **WHAT WAS NOT DONE: no visual check.** The Browser pane does not composite here, so the row was verified by driving `bodyFacts` and `buildGuideDocument` live in the page and reading the strings back, not by looking at it. Someone should open Mars in the GM inspector and in a printed player report and confirm the row sits sensibly among the orbital rows in both. **TWO FINDINGS APPENDED BELOW**, one of them the reason this could not simply reuse the propagator as written: **`computeWorldPositions3D` does NOT apply C3's satellite frame.** Related: [[C3]], [[C5]], [[B13]]. **THE GM PANEL HAS THE ROW TOO, from v2.1.413-beta — owner's request, and it closes the gap this entry's own design left.** `describeEclipse` was written so "the same string reaches the GM panel, the printed player report and the info panels", but only the player-facing surfaces were ever wired; the GM's read-only body block (`BodyTechnicalDetails`) had every other orbital row and not this one. It now sits at the END of the orbital group, after Resonance, which is where it belongs because that is what it is made of. Sampling on wall time is the rule this feature already landed on for the document surfaces - a date only needs to be right to the second, whatever the time scale - so it is the same rule, not a new one.
