The two are never reconciled. For a locked body the sidereal day EQUALS the orbital period (here 72 h), and the solar day with respect to its primary is infinite. Decide which wins and make it one number: physics-drives says the derived lock should set the rotation period (and say it did), the alternative is that an authored rotation suppresses the lock — but showing both is not an option. Applies to every locked body with an authored spin, not just Pandora. **Re-confirmed from the display side by the A5 sweep (v2.1.323):** these two rows are the same class of fault as A5 — two figures that look like one quantity, arriving from different stages — but unlike A5 the display cannot pick a winner honestly, because both values are genuinely present on the body and only physics knows which is real. Left here deliberately rather than papered over in `bodyFacts`. Shares its shape with [[A5]] and [[B6]]. **FIXED v2.1.333-beta.** **Root cause: two stages answering one question, and the temperature model had already picked a side.** `surfaceTemperature.ts:83` reads `effRotHours = tidallyLocked ? (orbitalPeriodHours || ...) : rotationHours` — so the thermal model has ALWAYS used the orbital period for a locked body and ignored the stored spin. The stat block, `rotationFactor()` in the dynamo and `rotationalDeform()` all read the stored number. The lock now sets it, which unifies them rather than adding a third opinion. **MERCURY IS THE ANCHOR AND IT NEARLY BROKE.** A blanket 1:1 rule would have overwritten Mercury's **measured 1407.6 h day** with its 2110.9 h year. Mercury is despun but NOT synchronous: at e = 0.206 it is captured in a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance (Goldreich & Peale 1966). So `lockedSpin()` keeps a spin sitting on a half-integer ratio of the orbit when the orbit is eccentric enough to hold it (e >= 0.1, ratio >= 1.5, within 2% of p:2, order <= 4:1), publishes `orbit/spin-orbit-resonance` = "3:2", and the stat block prints the resonance instead of "tidally locked". Everything else takes its orbital period. Pinned in the baseline as a value that must NOT move. **What the thresholds RULE OUT, checked body by body rather than assumed:** Chazon (ratio 1.523, within 1.5% of 3:2) is excluded by e = 0.029 — too circular to hold it; Conquestor (ratio 0.508, e = 0.126) by the sub-synchronous floor, since despinning passes THROUGH 1:2 toward 1:1 and does not stop there; Fames (e = 0.29), Adonis, Bellum and Fuller by not being near any half-integer. Across all 561 bundled bodies the exception fires on exactly one body — Mercury, four times, because Sol appears in four maps. **The numbers, measured against a worktree at the parent commit.** 23 locked bodies had a spin contradicting their own orbit; **23 -> 4, and all 4 are Mercury**. 117 locked bodies had NO spin at all and now have one. In Sol 20 rotation periods moved and **every one by under 1.2%** — their authored day already WAS their orbital period, so the shift is only our Kepler solution against the real one: Pluto/Charon 1.12%, Deimos/Ariel 0.72%, Luna 655.7 -> 659.03 h (0.51%), Io 0.02%. Pluto's retrograde sign survives. In the fictional maps the moves are large because the numbers were flavour: **Pandora 41.8 -> 74.76 h** (the reported body), LV-426 50 -> 80.6, Adonis 15 -> 2630.8, Bellum 9.05 -> 2152.3. **No temperature, no habitability and NO CLASSIFICATION moved anywhere** — expected, since the thermal model was already using the orbital period. **The one consequence worth arguing about, stated plainly: 53 bodies lost `magnetic/dynamo`** (41 to unshielded, 12 to tenuous), including Proxima b, Ross 128 b, Luyten b and the outer TRAPPIST-1 worlds. **40 of them had no rotation at all**, so `rotationFactor`'s "unknown -> 0.6" default had been handing every rotation-less planet an Earth-like field — a magnetosphere derived from not knowing, the same fault class as [[B9]]. Given their real 9-49 day spin the model says what it has always said about a slow rotator. **The threshold was NOT retuned to soften this** — see [[B12]]: it has no anchor between Venus and Earth and is now load-bearing for ~40 bundled planets. One body also lost `shape/oblate`, correctly: a world forced to a 200 h day is not flattened. Also found while measuring: [[B13]]. | fixed v2.1.333-beta |
| B5 | Mars's surface albedo is 0.154 from rock + metal makeup alone; the measured Bond albedo is 0.25, because Mars is bright with ferric dust and polar caps. Exposed by B1: the bogus CO2 deck had been carrying Mars to 0.236, right for the wrong reason. Costs Mars its real 210 ppm water-ice wisp (it survives to Teq ≈ 214.5 K; Mars now sits at 216.7). Same class: Io 0.153 vs measured 0.63 (SO2 frost), Luna 0.15 vs 0.11, Mercury 0.169 vs 0.088. `deriveOxidation()` already grades the rust but reads `geoActivity.surfaceAgeGyr`, derived AFTER the thermal solve — so this needs the geology derivation moved too, or it reintroduces the one-pass lag v2.1.282 removed. **Plan when it gets a session:** it is a surface-albedo model, not a Mars patch — the measurements point three different ways at once. Bare rock wants to be DARKER than the current flat 0.15 (Mercury 0.088, Luna 0.11 — the model is too bright for both), while bodies with surface DEPOSITS want to be brighter (Mars 0.25 from ferric dust, Io 0.63 from SO2 frost). So: lower the bare-rock constant, then add brightening from the deposits the engine already derives — `surface/oxidised` for rust, frost/cap coverage for the rest. The blocker is ordering: everything that grades those deposits (`deriveOxidation`, `deriveGeoActivity`) runs after the thermal solve, and `deriveGeoActivity` itself takes `teqK`, so it cannot simply move — either the non-thermal part of geology splits out ahead of the solve, or surface deposits join the fixed point. Expect real classification movement; needs the same before/after diff B1 used. **DECIDED 2026-08-02: ATTEMPT IT, KEEPING THE GATE.** The ordering hazard has not changed and the gate stands exactly as written — if geology cannot be separated from `teqK` without creating a new circular read, STOP and write up rather than reintroducing the one-pass lag v2.1.282 removed. **What HAS changed is that the pattern is now proven:** [[B13]] moved a derivation across a pass boundary and pinned it with an idempotence test, which is precisely what this needs; note B13's own caveat that its move was DOWN across the boundary and this one is UP across the thermal solve, which is the harder direction. Take B13's idempotence test as the model and ship one with the fix. **A CONCRETE, QUANTIFIED ACCEPTANCE TEST, added 2026-08-01 after "Mars once had CO2 wisps of cloud and they are not visible now".** Confirmed in `tests/output/solar-system-derived.json`: Mars carries `teqK = 216.7116` and **no `structure/cloud-deck` tag at all**, while Venus (sulfuric-acid veil), Earth (water overcast) and Titan (methane overcast) each carry one. The threshold recorded above is Teq 214.5 K, so **the deck is missing by 2.2 K** — and the missing deck is the WATER-ice wisp at 210 ppm (`H2O: 0.00021` in the campaign data), not a CO2 one; Mars has real CO2 clouds but they were never what the engine modelled. Since `Teq` goes as `(1 - A)^(1/4)`, the arithmetic is direct: at the model's A = 0.154 Mars sits at 216.7 K, and at the measured Bond albedo A = 0.25 it would sit at **210.2 K**, i.e. 4.3 K BELOW the survival threshold, so the deck returns with margin rather than marginally. **That is the acceptance test for this item: fix the albedo model and Mars regains its wisp WITHOUT a single line of cloud code or any Mars-specific branch.** If the wisp does not come back, the albedo change has not moved far enough; if it comes back on a body that should not have one, the deposit brightening is too generous. **Note the history, because it explains why this looked like a regression:** the wisp used to appear, propped up by the bogus CO2 deck B1 deleted, which had been carrying Mars to A = 0.236 — very close to the real 0.25, but right for the wrong reason. Nothing broke; the fault was always there and B1 removed what was concealing it. **NOT BUILT. STOPPED AT THE HARD GATE, deliberately, with the evidence below. B5 STAYS OPEN.** **The clean split does not exist, and the triage above undercounts the problem by three.** It says `deriveGeoActivity` "itself takes `teqK`, so it cannot simply move". True, but `teqK` is one of **four** inputs that are downstream of the thermal solve, and it is the least of them: 1. `teqK` — direct, but used in exactly ONE branch (`geoActivity.ts:141`, the Triton solar-seasonal geyser, `teqK < 60`). On its own this one WOULD be carvable. 2. `hasSurfaceWater` — from `deriveFluidLayers` at `SystemProcessor.ts:657`, pass THREE. The solve is at `:416-433`, pass two. 3. `hasSubsurfaceOcean` — same `fluidLayers` call, same pass. 4. `icyShell` at `:684` — from `surfacePhase` and `makeupIceIsSolid`, and **[[B4]] added that temperature gate deliberately at v2.1.283** ("ice-rich interior and icy shell are different claims"). So carving out the single `teqK` branch would not free geology: the water-PHASE inputs would have to come with it, and those are the thermal solve's downstream products by design. Undoing that to make albedo work would undo B4. **What "deposits join the fixed point" would actually mean, since that is the remaining route.** Every iteration of `solveThermalState` would have to run fluid layers -> icy shell -> subsurface ocean -> `deriveGeoActivity` -> `deriveSurfaceAgeGyr` -> `deriveOxidation` -> surface albedo. The solve is deliberately NON-MUTATING — evaluated against a probe so the answer never depends on what a previous `process()` left on the body — and all seven of those derivations mutate the body today. That is a rewrite of most of pass 3, not an ordering tweak, and getting it wrong reintroduces exactly the one-pass lag v2.1.282 removed. Which is not hypothetical: [[B13]] is that lag, alive right now, in surface radiation. **THE OBVIOUS SHORTCUT IS THE TRAP, and it is worth writing down before someone reaches for it.** "Do the frost half and leave the rust" looks free — frost and cap coverage need no geology. It is the single most dangerous version: **a BRIGHT condensate makes the solve BISTABLE**, and frost is the canonical case (ice-albedo feedback is genuinely bistable in nature — that is what snowball Earth IS). The rule from the albedo session applies at full strength. **And the bare-rock half ALONE would make Mars worse.** Current anchors, read from the derived output: Mercury 0.169 (measured 0.088), Luna 0.150 (0.11), **Mars 0.154 (0.25)**, Io 0.153 (0.63). Lowering the bare-rock constant toward Luna and Mercury takes Mars to about 0.11 — further from its measurement, warmer, with knock-on into its cloud decks and every rocky body in every map. Fixing two anchors by breaking a third is what [[B2]]'s rule exists to prevent. The two halves have to land together, exactly as the plan says. **Two things established that make the next attempt cheaper.** (a) **Mars ALREADY carries `surface/oxidised=moderate`** — the rust signal exists and is graded; nothing needs deriving, it is purely a question of when. Venus, TRAPPIST-1 c/d, Adrian, Chazon and 11 others carry it too: **17 bodies of 561**, and `climate/polar-ice` covers 10. Io carries no frost tag at all, so its 0.63 needs a NEW SO2-frost derivation rather than a wire-up — the Io case is not "read the tag". (b) **`SURF_ALBEDO = { metal: 0.18, rock: 0.15, carbon: 0.05, ice: 0.62, gas: 0.30 }` is hardcoded at `albedo.ts:22`**, and B5's own plan requires those in rule-pack DATA per the architecture rule. **RECOMMENDED FIRST STEP for whoever picks this up, and it is safe on its own:** migrate `SURF_ALBEDO` and `OCEAN_ALBEDO` into the rule pack as a pure no-op (same numbers, read from data, empty derived diff). That is independent of the ordering problem, satisfies the constants-in-data rule, and leaves B5 with only the ordering question. NOT done here because the session that builds the model should choose the schema — it will need per-deposit brightening coefficients too, not just the three base numbers, and guessing that shape now means redoing it. **Also weigh the sequencing:** the whole rust half moves 17 bodies, and the price is restructuring the processor's central solve. [[B13]] is the same ordering fault in a cheaper place and is probably the right thing to fix first — it would establish the pattern for moving a derivation across the solve boundary, with an idempotence test, on a subsystem where getting it wrong costs far less. **MEASURED 2026-08-03 (stage 1 of the second attempt), and the measurement CLEARS THE GATE — by contradicting two of the three things the stop above was based on.** **(1) `teqK` IS EFFECTIVELY INERT: perturbing it ±10 K moves `surfaceAgeGyr` on TWO bodies out of 366.** The stop says "`deriveGeoActivity` itself takes `teqK`, so it cannot simply move", and the gate is written around dragging `teqK` backwards. It is the Triton solar-seasonal geyser branch (`teqK < 60`) and nothing else, exactly as the earlier note guessed — but the magnitude was never measured, and it is two bodies. **The hazard the gate names is not the hazard that exists.** **(2) THE REAL COUPLING IS `hasSurfaceWater`, ALONE, AND IT IS TOTAL: flipping it moves `surfaceAgeGyr` on 136 bodies and changes the OXIDATION GRADE on all 136 of them.** (`hasSubsurfaceOcean` 16, `icyShell` 20.) The mechanism is the plate-tectonics branch: surface water → mobile lid → 0.2 Gyr resurfacing → under `deriveOxidation`'s 0.3 Gyr floor → no rust. Earth is the clean case and it is CORRECT: Earth's surface is too young to rust. So the ordering problem is real, but it is one input, not four. **(3) AND THAT ONE INPUT IS ALREADY COMPUTED INSIDE THE SOLVE.** `deriveAlbedo` (`albedo.ts`, the hydrosphere branch) already calls `phaseAtP(hydroComp, surfT, pressure)` on the probe every iteration to decide whether the surface liquid is dark ocean or bright frost. "Is there liquid water standing on the surface" is that same question. The solve is not missing the information; nothing is currently passing it to geology. **(4) THE "REWRITE OF MOST OF PASS 3" IS NOT REQUIRED, because the claim that "all seven of those derivations mutate the body" is wrong for the three that matter.** `deriveFluidLayers(body, pack)` returns `FluidLayer[]`; `deriveGeoActivity(i: GeoInputs)` returns a `GeoActivity`; `deriveOxidation(body)` returns a string. **All three are pure functions** — the PROCESSOR assigns their results, the functions do not mutate. `solveThermalState`'s `evaluate()` already calls two pure derivations (`deriveCloudDecks`, `deriveAlbedo`) against a shallow `probe` for precisely this reason, and its own comment says so: "Neither writes, so a shallow copy is enough." Adding three more pure calls to that probe is the same pattern, not a new one. **Nothing moves backwards: geology is still COMMITTED in pass 3 from the converged temperature, and gets the same answer because it is the same pure function on the same converged inputs — which is what makes it idempotent rather than lagged.** **(5) THE BISTABILITY THE STOP WARNS ABOUT IS REAL BUT IS ONE BODY.** The feedback is genuine — colder → water freezes → not "surface water" → stagnant lid → older surface → more rust → brighter → colder — and it is the snowball-Earth loop, so it must be bounded, not dismissed. Measured: 34 bundled bodies are rust-eligible (iron ≥ 0.05 and an oxidiser), and exactly **ONE** of those sits within 8 K of the water freezing point with a hydrosphere — Testion's "forest" (T 268.9 K, coverage 0.4, metal 0.19, oxidiser 0.63). That is a containable, nameable risk with a convergence assertion, not an unbounded one. **CURRENT ANCHORS, re-read rather than trusted:** Mercury surf/bond 0.169 (measured 0.088), Luna 0.150 (0.11), **Mars 0.154 (0.25), teq 216.7 K, `surface/oxidised=moderate`, `surfaceAgeGyr` 3.85, regime inactive, NO cloud deck**, Io 0.153 (0.63), teq 117.2, no frost tag of any kind. All four cloud-deck-free, so the anchors are pure surface albedo with nothing overhead confusing them. **BUILT v2.1.372-beta. ALL FOUR ANCHORS LAND FROM ONE MODEL WITH NO PER-WORLD BRANCH — Mercury 0.169→0.088 (measured 0.088), Luna 0.150→0.110 (0.11), Mars 0.154→0.256 (0.25), Io 0.153→0.569 (0.63)** — and **the acceptance test passes on its own predicted number: Mars goes to teq 209.8 K against the 210.2 this entry forecast, and its 210 ppm WATER-ice wisp condenses again** (`structure/cloud-deck=water wisps` plus its virga), with no cloud code touched and no Mars-specific branch anywhere. **THE MODEL.** Bare ground is darker than the flat 0.15, and **metal is darker than rock** — a space-weathered iron regolith is about the darkest natural surface there is, which is why Mercury at 62% metal is the darkest rocky body in the Solar System. Brightness is then ADDED by two deposits the engine already derives: oxide dust from `surface/oxidised`, and **volatile frost wherever the atmosphere's dominant gas is below ITS OWN freezing point**. The second is deliberately general rather than an Io rule, and generality is what makes the split come out right on its own: Io's SO2 freezes at 198 K and Io sits near 100, so Io is FROST; Mars at 210 K is above CO2's 195 K, so Mars is DUST and not frost — exactly the two different mechanisms this entry said the measurements were pointing at. **HOW THE GATE WAS HONOURED.** Nothing moved backwards across the solve. The rust is EVALUATED INSIDE the fixed point against the same non-mutating probe `deriveCloudDecks` and `deriveAlbedo` already use; the processor still COMMITS geology in its own pass from the converged temperature and gets the same answer back, which is what makes it idempotent rather than one pass behind. [[B13]]'s idempotence test — Sol, imported Sol, both starmaps, every example — passes unchanged, and that is the proof. The system age is threaded into `solveThermalState` rather than defaulted, because it must be the same figure the processor uses when it commits geology or the albedo would be computed against a different surface age than the body ends up carrying. **THE BISTABILITY WAS BOUNDED, NOT DISMISSED: 0 of 366 bodies fail to converge, before or after, and the acceptance test asserts it.** **EVERY MOVER JUDGED.** Albedo moves on 254 of 366, mean 0.036. **Class changes: ONE distinct body** — Proxima Centauri d sub-earth→hot-eyeball, because a darker surface takes it 317.1→322.7 K and over the 320 floor: **BETTER**, its real equilibrium temperature is nearer 360 and it is tidally locked, hot and dry. **THE ONE THING THAT GOT WORSE, reported rather than buried: PLUTO LOSES its methane wisps.** Its nitrogen frosts out, taking it 0.299→0.579 against a measured ~0.72 — a large gain — and the resulting 36 K surface then drops the methane deck. Real Pluto does have methane haze, so **the cloud-deck model may want a look at very low temperatures**; not fixed here. LV-426's ammonia deck thins from overcast to veil. Everything else holds: Earth 0.308→0.303, Venus 0.757 unmoved, Titan 0.285→0.278, Europa 0.62 unmoved, Triton 0.618 unmoved and keeps its deck. **Derived diff: ZERO class changes in Sol and exactly TWO tag changes** — Mars gains the wisp pair, Pluto loses the methane pair; the rest of the 950 lines is albedo and the temperatures that follow it. **Constants are rule-pack DATA** (`planets.json` `surface_albedo`), per this entry's own recommended first step — including the per-grade dust coverage and the frost ramp, not only the three base numbers, so the schema question it flagged is answered. **Three corrections to this entry, all from stage 1's measurement:** `teqK` is not the blocker (±10 K moves TWO bodies); `hasSurfaceWater` is the entire coupling (136 bodies, all changing oxidation grade); and "all seven of those derivations mutate the body" is wrong for the three that matter — `deriveFluidLayers`, `deriveGeoActivity` and `deriveOxidation` are pure, which is what made the whole thing a three-line addition to `evaluate()` rather than the rewrite of pass 3 this entry feared. | fixed v2.1.372-beta |

| B8 | **The surface-radiation mean can sit marginally OUTSIDE its own min/max, because the three figures are composed two different ways.** Found by the A5 sweep (v2.1.323) while checking every paired figure in the stat block for A5's fault; recorded rather than fixed, because it is physics and because it is currently invisible. `calculateSurfaceRadiation` (`physics/radiation.ts`) builds `surfaceRadiation` from the PER-STAR spectral components (`components.photon` / `components.particle`, each already shielded), while `fluxToDose` at `:198-202` rebuilds the endpoints from a single flat `rawPhotonFrac`/`rawParticleFrac` applied to `calculateTotalStellarRadiationRange`'s totals. The comment at `:194` says the endpoints are kept "consistent with the same component model used above" — they are consistent in SHAPE but not identical in composition, so the two can disagree in the last fraction of a percent. **Measured on the bundled Sol map: 3 of 34 bodies land outside** — Neptune (2.28 vs a 2.26–2.28 range), Triton (2.57 vs 2.54–2.56), Neptune's Rings (0.57 vs 0.54–0.56). **Worst excess ~0.4%, and the stat block prints the range at one decimal place, so nothing contradictory reaches a reader today** — which is exactly why it is here and not fixed: the display is honest, the model is very slightly not. **Why it is worth a line anyway:** the same fault at a larger amplitude is what A5 was, and a multi-star system (where the spectral mix genuinely differs between the near and far ends of an orbit) is where this would grow rather than stay at 0.4%. Whoever takes it should check a binary before deciding it is negligible. Related: [[A5]]. **FIXED v2.1.334-beta — and BOTH halves of the triage above were wrong, which is the finding.** **The recorded cause is impossible.** The mean is `(photonFlux + particleFlux) * DOSE + bg`, and expanding it gives **exactly** `fluxToDose(components.total)` — the shielded mix cancels algebraically, because `rawPhotonFrac` is defined as `components.photon / total`. `fluxToDose` is linear and monotonic in flux. So the spectral composition CANNOT push the mean outside its own endpoints; the excursion had to be in the flux, one level down. **Real root cause: a missing TERM, not a rounding difference.** `calculateStellarRadiationComponents` adds an episodic flare dose to the particle channel (`star.flareActivity * FLARE_PARTICLE_WEIGHT`); `calculateTotalStellarRadiationRange` was a SECOND sum of the same quantity with no flare term in it at all. The mean therefore carried a dose the endpoints did not, by exactly `(1 + flare/2)` — which is why the excess is systematically ABOVE the maximum and never below the minimum. **The measurement, over all 420 ranged bodies in every bundled system rather than Sol alone: 105 land outside, not 3, and the worst is 19.75% of the mean, not 0.4%.** Wolf 359's Graveyard reads 4.46 against a 3.30-3.58 range — Wolf 359 being a famously active flare star, which is the entire mechanism visible in one row. Epsilon Eridani's belts 14.5%, Lacaille 9352 e 5.9%. Sol was simply the benign case: a quiet G star has little flare activity, so its worst body was 0.4%. **THE BINARY TEST THE ITEM ASKED FOR REFUTES ITS OWN HYPOTHESIS.** Multi-star systems are the MILDER case — 34 offenders, worst 5.71% — and single-star systems the worse, 71 offenders, worst 19.75%. What drives this is stellar ACTIVITY, not the spectral mix differing between the near and far ends of an orbit. Had it only been checked on a binary it would have been closed as negligible on the wrong evidence. **Fix: delete the second sum.** `calculateStellarRadiationComponents` takes a distance selector, and mean / min / max are all it, evaluated at the current, far and near distances. Every star's split and flare weight are constants of the star and flux falls monotonically with distance, so **min <= mean <= max now holds by construction**, not by luck. 105 -> 0. Pinned by a test whose subject is a flaring star on an eccentric orbit. **Derived diff touches exactly four fields on 68 bodies** — `stellarRadiationMin/Max`, `surfaceRadiationMin/Max`. No mean, no temperature, no habitability, no class moved, which is the expected shape: the mean was always right and the endpoints were short. Sol's three named offenders now bracket — Neptune 2.277 in 2.271-2.284, Triton 2.566 in 2.553-2.579, Neptune's Rings 0.566 in 0.553-0.579. | fixed v2.1.334-beta |

| C1 | `condensateTint` (cloudDecks.ts ~165) pulls every deck to within 60/255 of white. The physics is that a clean SCATTERER goes white however dark the liquid (water) while an ABSORBING suspension keeps its colour however finely divided (Jupiter's brown hydrosulphide, martian dust). | C5 | **Which plane does a moon actually orbit in? The Laplace plane, and we approximate it with a flag.** Raised by the C3 audit. C3 rotates a satellite's orbit into its parent's equator, which is right for regular satellites and wrong for distant ones: beyond roughly fifty host radii solar perturbation wins over the parent's oblateness and the orbit follows the SYSTEM plane instead. The real answer is the Laplace plane, which transitions smoothly between the two with distance. C3 approximates it with a per-orbit `frame: 'ecliptic'` declaration, set on Luna (60 Earth radii) and Phoebe (222 Saturn radii). **The case that shows the limit is Iapetus:** at 61 Saturn radii it is squarely in the transition, its orbit genuinely precesses about the Laplace plane, and its quoted 15.47 deg is conventionally referenced to Saturn's equator — so it is currently treated as equatorial and drawn 15.47 deg off the ring plane, which is defensible but not exactly right. **What a proper fix looks like:** compute the Laplace plane from the host's J2, mass ratio and the moon's semi-major axis, and orient the orbit to it — a physics change, in the propagator or a derivation feeding it, needing a before/after across the bundled maps. Until then the flag is the honest lever, and PROC GEN should set it for anything it generates beyond the transition. Related: C3 (c), also open. **MEASURED 2026-08-02, NOT BUILT — and the measurement says do not build it. VERDICT: the flag is not merely a good enough approximation for the bundled data, it is EXACT, and exactly one body is anywhere near the transition.** **Method:** classical Laplace radius `r_L^5 = 2 J2 R_p^2 a_p^3 (M_p/M_star)` and local Laplace-plane inclination to the host's equator `tan(2 i_L) = sin(2 eps) / ((r_L/a)^5 + cos(2 eps))` (Tremaine, Touma & Namouni 2009), computed for all 19 moons in both maps. J2 came from literature — the map carries no J2 field, which is itself worth knowing if this is ever built. **The transition population, by `a/r_L`:** Iapetus **1.44**, then Callisto 0.82, Deimos 0.53, Titan 0.49, Ganymede 0.46, Oberon 0.43, and everything else at or under 0.32. Above the line: Luna 6.25 and Phoebe 5.23, both already flagged. **So the distribution is not a spectrum with several awkward cases — it is a tight equatorial cluster, two bodies out in the ecliptic regime, and Iapetus on its own in the middle.** And the near-misses do not matter even where they are close: Callisto is at 0.82 but Jupiter's obliquity is 3.13 deg, so the ENTIRE equator-to-ecliptic gap it could be wrong by is 3.13 deg and its Laplace plane sits at 0.84; Deimos at 0.53 gives 0.87 deg. Nothing between Iapetus and the cluster is wrong by as much as a degree. **THE METRIC IN THE ORIGINAL ENTRY IS THE WRONG ONE, and getting this right reverses the conclusion about Iapetus.** The Laplace-plane offset is not the rendering error, because a moon's quoted `i_deg` is not referenced to its Laplace plane — it is referenced to the parent's equator (regular satellites) or the ecliptic (Luna, Phoebe). The only question the flag has to answer is WHICH OF THOSE TWO the catalogue number was quoted in, and on that test all 19 are right, including Iapetus: its 15.47 deg is equator-referenced, so equatorial renders it where the real Iapetus is. **C3 left Iapetus alone and calling it "defensible but not exactly right" undersold it — leaving it alone was correct, and setting the flag would have moved it about 7 deg WRONG.** **What the Laplace plane genuinely buys for Iapetus, stated so nobody has to re-derive it:** its orbit precesses about a plane 23.3 deg from Saturn's equator with a free inclination of about 7.9 deg, so its inclination to the equator swings roughly 15.5-31 deg over a precession cycle — order 5,000 years on a rough J2-plus-solar estimate (published figures are nearer 3,000). A static plane is a snapshot that is correct now and drifts over millennia, which is below the resolution of any campaign. **RECOMMENDATION: do not build a continuous Laplace model on the strength of the bundled data — zero bodies would move today.** Its value is entirely in **C3 part (c), PROC GEN**, where there is no catalogue to quote and the generator must CHOOSE a plane rather than record one; there, `a/r_L` is the right switch and the formula above is the whole model. That makes this item a dependency of the generation work, not of the map data. **The renderer was re-verified after the [[D4d]] data changes** by reproducing `scene.ts`'s `toParentEquator` exactly and measuring each moon's orbit normal against the ring-plane normal: Saturn's inner six sit 0.01-1.57 deg from the ring plane, Iapetus is the odd one out at 15.47, Luna 23.97 and Triton 22.70 (= 180 - 157.3, the acute angle for a retrograde orbit). Identical to C3's own figures, so nothing drifted. **What was NOT done: the visual check.** The Browser pane is not displayed in this environment and screenshots time out, so the numbers above are a faithful reproduction of the renderer's transform rather than a look at the screen. Someone should still eyeball Saturn once. **No data changed, so the D4d kit test stays green trivially.** | measured, recommend not building |

Altair IV, the one host I could reach in the automated sweep, also has no spin, so nothing there could turn regardless. Feature positions come from a seeded PRNG per body id (`seeded(9001)` craters, `seeded(9002)`, and so on) under the stated intent that "every feature seeds its own positions so the look is stable" — stability was the goal, and staticness is the same thing seen from another angle. **THE TRAP, and the reason this is not a one-liner:** rotating the disc's features about its centre is not a spinning sphere, it is a spinning record. A real spin carries features ACROSS the face and compresses them into the limbs, so an honest fix needs feature positions treated as sphere longitude/latitude and projected per frame, or at minimum a horizontal traverse with limb foreshortening. A naive `rotate()` will look worse than the current stillness and should not be accepted as a fix. Inputs needed: `rotation_period_hours` and the current time — both already available, and both now trustworthy after [[B7]] and [[B9]]. **Note also this only shows when zoomed in:** `DISC_OVERLAY_MIN_R = 11` px gates the overlay, so nothing is promoted at whole-system framing (see [[A10]]). **DITCHED 2026-08-03.** The lighting is correct, which is the part carrying the physics — a reader sees the body lit from its star, and the terminator tracks the orbit. Only the seeded surface features are static, and the honest fix is a spherical projection (features carried across the face with limb foreshortening) rather than the flat rotation that would be reached for first, which looks worse than stillness. (b) `membersOf` tests `ids.includes(n.id)` against the barycentre's `memberIds`, so the PLANET matches the star's id and is listed as a barycentre member: the Struve 2398 barycentre page shows "Moons: ★ Struve 2398 B | ● Struve 2398 A b" — two rows, one id. The planet's id is referenced by nothing. On failure the test does not print a 300 KB string mismatch — it names the values that moved, keyed by node id rather than array index so a re-ordering reads as a move instead of four hundred changes, and says which side is likely wrong. **Proven in both directions, which is the only way to trust a guard:** reverted Phoebe's frame flag and the Hail Mary's sign-off in the kit and it failed naming exactly those two, one as "dropped by the build"; re-indented the shipped SciFi map to 2-space with no content change and it failed with the separate "same values, different bytes" message; restored both, green; then bumped the version and confirmed it stays green, which is the appVersion normalisation doing its job. **Full suite: 914 passed, the same 4 pre-existing `src/routes/page.spec.ts` failures as on a clean tree (a `starmapStorage` mock missing `loadPreUpgradeStarmap`, nothing to do with this).** **One erratum in the history:** the fix 4 commit message says the Astrophage tanks are "a two-thousandth" of the antimatter stand-in's; they are not — Hail Mary 4000/900 to 2000/450, Blip-A 9000/3000 to 3000/1100. The numbers in the data are right. **NOT amended, and that is worth knowing about this repo:** `git commit --amend` was run while the concurrent session had committed on top, and it rewrote THEIR commit's message onto their tree. Recovered intact with `git reset --soft` to their sha (identical tree and parent, so nothing was lost), but the rule now is: **while a second session is committing, never amend and never rewrite history — make a new commit.** **Two things left deliberately unfolded, both appended unnumbered below:** the standalone `Sol_Expanse-System.json` has the same missing Luna flag ([[C3]] audited the bundled starmaps, not the standalone examples), and the real map's RV super-Earths carry the archive's own inflated radii — the population-wide version of the fault that fix 6 pinned on Adrian. The fault is upstream. **VERIFIED, IT IS THE RULE-PACK DATA:** `static/rulepacks/starter-sf/atmospheres.json` gives Traveller-6 a composition of N2 0.78-0.79, O2 0.20-0.21, Ar 0.009-0.01 and CO2 0.0004-0.0006 — **and no H2O at all**. The bundled Earth carries `H2O: 0.00398`. Water vapour is the DOMINANT greenhouse gas on Earth, roughly half to two-thirds of the +33 K, so without it the world gets only the trace CO2 term and settles near its equilibrium temperature — about -8 C at 0.919 AU. It reads -16 C because it is colder still: the resulting ice raises the albedo, which cools it further. A snowball, arrived at honestly. **A SECOND SIGNAL IN THE SAME BLOCK, worth checking either way:** that atmosphere declares `temp_range_K: [280, 310]` — the rule pack says it belongs on a 280-310 K world, and Terra is at 257 K. So either the importer selects an atmosphere without honouring its own declared range, or the range is aspirational and unenforced. Find out which; a constraint the data states and the code ignores is worth more than this one bug. **TWO WAYS TO FIX IT, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME SIZE.** (1) **DATA, cheap:** add H2O to Traveller-6 (and audit the other Traveller atmospheres for the same omission), matching how the bundled Earth is authored. Fixes the symptom and is consistent with constants living in rule-pack data. (2) **PHYSICS, right:** water vapour should be DERIVED from surface temperature and available water rather than authored, because its abundance is set by Clausius-Clapeyron and authoring a fixed fraction ASSUMES THE ANSWER — 0.4% is Earth's equilibrium at 288 K, and stating it on a world that would be cold begs the question. That is the same circularity [[B1]] solved for albedo/temperature/cloud with a bounded fixed point, and the existing `solveThermalState` is where it would belong. **Recommend doing (1) now and raising (2) as its own item** — but note that (1) alone will make every authored Earth-like world warm regardless of where it orbits, which is wrong in the other direction, so whoever does it should say so plainly rather than declare the class fixed. **SHARPENED 2026-08-03, and the real diagnosis is the DUPLICATION RULE, not a tight boundary.** Asked whether the importer is missing a calculation or the physics boundaries are too tight: neither. **The same rule pack defines "Earth-like atmosphere" TWICE and the two disagree.** `Nitrogen-Oxygen (Earth-like)` carries `H2O`; `Traveller-6 (Standard - Earth-like)` does not. One concept, two entries, drifted — which is exactly the test the standing rule sets ("could these two answer the same question differently"), and the importer happens to select the one that is wrong. **UNDERNEATH IT IS A GENUINE MODEL GAP, and this is the part worth fixing properly:** Terra has 70% surface water and ZERO vapour above it, which is impossible at any temperature above absolute zero. The engine KNOWS there is an ocean — it renders the coverage and tags the frozen surface — but the greenhouse never asks, because vapour is only ever AUTHORED and never DERIVED from available water. So this is another instance of the recurring shape: a fact the engine holds does not reach the calculation that needs it. The boundaries are not too tight; the wiring is missing. Related: [[B1]], [[B4]], [[B5]], [[D2]], [[G11]]. | **FIXED v2.1.880-beta, and the diagnosis in this row is now HALF STALE - read this instead.** The pack-data half was NOT done and should not be: the wiring the row says is missing had since been built (`atmosphere.ts`, an ocean-vapour term), and what was actually wrong with it was a GATE - `surfaceTemp > 273 && < 373`. That put a ~10 K STEP into a loop that feeds itself, so a world a hair below freezing lost its whole vapour greenhouse and the loss is what kept it frozen. MEASURED on the reported configuration (Traveller-6 mix, 0.95 bar, 70% hydrographics, real Sun): greenhouse 35.3 K -> 24.7 K across ONE 0.1 AU step, world +16.9 C -> -2.4 C and frozen. AFTER: 32.1 -> 30.4, world +13.6 C -> +0.5 C, not frozen; at the reported 0.919 AU it now reads **+26.7 C**. The fix is the saturation curve (Clausius-Clapeyron via the pack's own `saturationPressureBar`), scaled by coverage and by a column-mean humidity calibrated on Earth alone, `tanh`-limited so a boiling ocean cannot run away. **IT IS NOT WATER-SPECIFIC** - the solvent is whatever the hydrosphere says and the gas is whichever condenses to it, so a methane sea warms its world with methane. **DUPLICATION FOUND AND UNIFIED:** `cloudDecks.evaporationFraction` was computing the same sea-vapour quantity from a different curve and a different humidity law (its comment claimed Earth lands on ~1% vapour; Earth's column mean is 0.4%); both now share `liquids.ts surfaceVapourSource` and keep only their own humidity factors, which are genuinely different quantities (surface vs column mean). **SOL DID NOT MOVE** - both generated fixtures are byte-identical, because every hand-authored H2O is treated as a FLOOR. Engine map PHY-21. **TWO FINDINGS RAISED, NEITHER FIXED HERE:** (a) the pack's saturation curve reads ~24% low at 288 K and ~37% low at 323 K (three log-interpolated anchors) - the calibration constant absorbs it at Earth but the SHAPE is wrong away from Earth, and `liquids.json`'s water anchors are where that lives; (b) the Universe Sandbox fixture's Earth carries 300 ppm CO2 against the pack's 448, worth 5 K on the same world - two Earths in one codebase that disagree, and the old over-wet vapour law was silently paying for it. **THE SECOND SIGNAL IS ANSWERED: `temp_range_K` IS UNENFORCED on this path and that is correct** - `importer.ts` maps the UWP atmosphere digit straight to a mix name, because in Traveller the UWP is the authority on what the air is; the range is advisory for the generator's own draw. |

Process repeatedly and Juventas's `a_AU` goes **2.5e-6 -> 2.91 -> 4.55 -> 5.46 -> 5.97 -> 6.26 -> 6.42 -> 6.51 AU**, converging near 6.5. **A blatant PHY-1 non-idempotence, and `idempotence.test.ts` does not catch it because no fixture there has a co-orbital at all (`grep -c coOrbital` = 0).** **THE MECHANISM, and the number is the giveaway: the 60-degree L4 OFFSET IS BEING READ AS THE PAIR'S SEPARATION.** The chord across 60 degrees at 5.204 AU is 2*a*sin(30) = **exactly 5.2040 AU**, which is the barycentre's own semi-major axis, and that is the value the runaway climbs toward before overshooting. **TWO PASSES BOTH CLAIM `parentId` AND `orbit` FOR THE SAME NODE AND NEITHER KNOWS ABOUT THE OTHER:** `reconcileBarycenters` (`SystemProcessor:179`) sees two comparable masses, promotes them to a `Pomona-Juventas Barycentre` and re-homes both onto it; then `deriveCoOrbitalOrbits` (`:189`) runs, and `lagrange.ts:398` `node.parentId = secondary.parentId` RIPS Pomona back out to the Sun while leaving the barycentre standing with Juventas as its only real child. Next pass, reconcile measures the wreckage - Pomona at L4, the barycentre 60 degrees away - and rebuilds Juventas's orbit from that separation. Round and round. **ROOT CAUSE IS THE SCHEMA, NOT A SPOT FIX GONE WRONG: `coOrbital` exists only on `CelestialBody`, never on `Barycenter` (`types.ts:513`), so "a PAIR whose barycentre rides L4" is INEXPRESSIBLE.** The GM is trying to say something the data model has no words for, so each pass interprets the half-expressed thing its own way. **THIS IS A REAL CONFIGURATION, not an exotic one: (617) Patroclus-Menoetius is a genuine binary Jupiter trojan - two ~110 km bodies about 680 km apart librating about L4 together - and (624) Hektor, which this very map contains, has a moonlet.** **WORST PART: NO WARNING.** `assessCoOrbitalStability` only speaks for nodes carrying `coOrbital`, and Juventas loses its link, so the whole runaway is silent - no `stability/*`, no `fate/*`, nothing. Silent corruption of authored data is the one outcome the steer-don't-stop rule cannot live with: steering requires SAYING something. **FIX SHAPE, and it is the flexible-systems move rather than another patch — roughly a day: (1) allow `coOrbital` on `Barycenter` (one schema line); (2) `deriveCoOrbitalOrbits` derives the BARYCENTRE's orbit from the secondary and leaves the members' mutual orbit about it alone; (3) ONE OWNERSHIP RULE, written into the engine map: if a node OR its barycentre carries `coOrbital`, the L-point derivation owns its orbit and parentage and reconcile must not re-home it; reconcile owns only the members' orbits about the barycentre. No overlap, so no fight. (4) The stability verdicts then come almost free from machinery that already exists: Gascheau via `maxTrojanMassKg` on the pair's COMBINED mass, and a new and genuinely useful criterion - the pair's own separation must stay well inside the Hill radius at L4, which `hillFactor`/`coOrbitalScale` already compute. A binary trojan that is too wide for its own L-point is exactly the "very unstable" the owner expects to see.** INTERIM, IF NOT FIXED NOW: the honest cheap half is to make the collision LOUD rather than silent — when reconcile is about to promote a pair in which either member carries `coOrbital`, refuse the promotion and tag it, so the GM is told the engine cannot model this yet instead of watching a number drift. **FIXED PROPERLY, owner's call: "a more robust underlying system trumps spot fixes and this will likely fix a number of other barycentre issues. It is because they entered the program late in the day and were likely not implemented properly then."** THE FIX IS THE OWNERSHIP RULE, now engine-map PHY-32: whatever carries `coOrbital` is the thing AT the point, and `deriveCoOrbitalOrbits` owns its `orbit` and `parentId` alone. The converse was the missing half - a node that is a MEMBER of a barycentre never rides a point, the PAIR does - so `promoteMassiveCompanion` now hands the marker UP to the new barycentre (which has already taken the primary's orbit and host) and strips it off both members, and the derivation strips it off any member it still finds one on. `Barycenter.coOrbital` is the one schema line that makes it expressible. The members then just orbit the barycentre and nothing touches them. **A SECOND, OLDER BUG FELL OUT OF THE SAME TEST AND IS FIXED TOO: a correct Patroclus-scale binary trojan read `stability/very-unstable` for "External orbit overlap with Jupiter".** A co-orbital pair has its secondary's semi-major axis BY DEFINITION, and `assessBinaryPairStability`'s sibling crossing test read that as a catastrophic overlap with a body 760 million times its mass. [[G43]] P2 exempted exactly this for a SINGLE trojan (`coOrbitalExempt`); the pair assessor never got the equivalent. This one predates B98 and would have mis-flagged any binary trojan anyone ever built. **AND THE SILENCE IS GONE - `assessCoOrbitalPairStability` asks the two questions a pair asks that a single body does not:** Gascheau on the pair's COMBINED mass (a pair is heavier than either member, so a trio one body would survive can fail once doubled), and the criterion only a pair has - its own separation against the Hill radius it has AT the point, on the same 0.3/0.4/0.5 sep/Hill bands the binary-tightness test upstream uses, so there is one idea of "too wide" and not two. The fate is deliberately NOT directional, and that is a real contrast with [[B19]]: when a point stops holding a pair BOTH members leave, and there is no lighter one being thrown by a heavier one. **MEASURED, `physics/coOrbitalPair.spec.ts` (8 specs):** the marker lands on the barycentre; the pair sits at 5.2040 AU; the members keep their real 673 km mutual orbit; **the companion's `a_AU` is now BYTE-IDENTICAL from pass 1 to pass 8 where it used to reach 6.5 AU**; the whole system is byte-identical reprocessed (PHY-1); a Patroclus-scale pair is CLEAN with no tags at all; and a pair at 75,000 km (sep/Hill 1.35) reads Very Unstable + `fate/eject` on BOTH members with the reason naming the mechanism and the numbers. Full suite 3121 green. NOTE ON THE FLAKE: `broadcastContract.spec.ts` (VTT/PeerJS, a 5 s timeout) fails intermittently under full-suite load and passes 29/29 in isolation; nothing in the changed files touches that machinery. Not related, but worth someone's time separately. **FOUR SURFACES DONE:** engine-map PHY-32, `/physics#resonance` gains the pair-at-a-point paragraph with Patroclus, and `docs/tags-guide.md` gains the pair rules. `physicsTrace` needs nothing new - it reads `orbitalStabilityDetails`, which now carries the pair reasons. **UNSEEN: nobody has looked at a binary trojan in the running app; the specs are the evidence.** | **FIXED v3.0.108-beta — ownership rule PHY-32, plus an older mis-flag of every binary trojan; owner reloads and a binary trojan should sit still and read clean** |

THREE FAULTS, LOCATED: **(1) THE RETRY LOOP.** `broadcast.ts:159-168`: on `unavailable-id` the service destroys the peer, sets `this.peer = null`, fires `onHostIdUnavailable` — but leaves `hostRequested = true`. `initSender(sessionId)` at `:279-289` re-hosts whenever `hostRequested && !peer`, and `SystemView.svelte:1507` calls `broadcastService.initSender(broadcastSessionId)` on every system entry, so each click into a system re-attempts the SAME id, collides, and asks again. DECIDING TEST for the owner: reload twice within 10 s → prompt both times; close, wait 90 s, load once → no prompt.** **Owner, later the same evening: "tried a refresh and that bug does not come up again" — consistent with (4): the holder was time-bound (a ghost, or a dev preview since closed), not a live second GM. The fixes stand: release on pagehide, retry before prompting, dev-origin guard, notice on OK.** **OWNER'S CONSOLE, 2026-08-19, on a FRESH load of the bundled SciFi map after "OK a few times then Cancel":** `wss://0.peerjs.com/peerjs?…&id=local_neighbourhood_scie-hydra-spica-309` — the stack is `_handleMessage → _abort → emitError → (our handler) → destroy → close`, i.e. the broker answered ID-TAKEN for that id and our handler tore the socket down before it opened. **The bundled files carry NO `broadcastId` (checked both example dirs) and the mint is crypto-random (`broadcastId.ts:143`, rejection-sampled), so a fresh mint CANNOT have a real holder** — a dev preview of the same map holds a DIFFERENT random id. Therefore the holder of `hydra-spica-309` was THIS machine's own registration of it (a re-register while the first socket was still alive on the broker, or an id persisted from an earlier session that the previous page had just hosted). Self-collision, exact re-register path not pinned from the log. **(5) THEREFORE: RECORD IT — every host attempt (id, caller, outcome, PeerJS error type, timestamp) goes into the always-on `__ssePerf` event ring (`perfEvent`, the P2 machinery), so the next occurrence answers itself with one `__ssePerf.events(60,'peer')` dump instead of a theory. So it is the auto-host-on-load (v2.1.753) meeting the broker's hold on a just-dropped id — any quick reload prompts anyone. Owner confirms the id scheme is as designed (map slug + space-term words + digits, unique by construction); the collision is always with oneself. PROMPTED to the VTT session as its next item, ahead of testers.** **FIXED v2.1.814-beta (VTT session), all five in the order asked: (1) RECORDED â every host attempt/outcome is a `perfEvent('peer', {phase, id, caller, attempt, errType, outcome})` in the always-on ring, phases host-attempt/host-open/host-collide/host-skip/host-error/rehost-id-changed/pagehide; `__ssePerf.events(60,'peer')` is the one action. (2) `peer.destroy()` on `pagehide`. (3) `unavailable-id` retries the SAME id 1.5 s / 3 s / 5 s (~10 s) before prompting; the prompt fires ONCE per id (`promptedIds`). (5) OK shows `remoteNotice` "New session id minted â existing player links and QR codes have stopped working." (6) no AUTO-host from localhost/127.0.0.1/[::1]/*.local (`isDevOrigin`), explicit enable unaffected â guard chosen over namespacing (wire + stored id unchanged). TESTS: `broadcastContract.spec.ts` gains a fake broker (`FakePeer` with a taken-id registry) and four A57 cases â free id hosts once; transient ghost is retried and hosts with NO prompt; persistent holder prompts exactly once and three subsequent `initSender` calls make ZERO new registrations; OK's new id hosts and only explicit enable re-hosts the old one â AND the E12 flakiness is fixed at the root: expectations now `waitFor` the delivery instead of counting ticks, and both services are built before anything is sent. NOT verified in a browser here (shared tree mid `npm install`; another session's dev server on this folder) â ACCEPTANCE HANDED BACK: reload beta 3x inside 10 s -> no prompt; same saved map in a second browser -> prompts once only; OK -> notice + new id hosts (broker probe: ID-TAKEN); Cancel then 3 system entries -> no re-prompt; localhost dev tab with the same map -> id not stolen. Expected: scrubbing while playing seeks and playback resumes from the new time. | **FIXED v2.1.863-beta.** **The cause is one line, and it is NOT the lead in this row:** `handleScrubInput` opened with `if (isPlaying) setPlaying(false)` - the jog stopped the clock on purpose and nothing on the release path ever started it again. A paused transport stays paused. **VERIFIED IN THE RUNNING APP by driving `requestAnimationFrame` BY HAND** - the pane does not composite and BOTH the jog and playback are rAF loops, so nothing about this is observable otherwise (same technique as the headless starmap checks; worth knowing for any future time bug): playing at +1h/s from 05:05:48, the transport stayed on Pause through the jog, the clock seeked to 07:37:44, the shuttle sprang back to 0, and playback carried on to 07:38:42 and 07:39:40. **Seven tests in a new `TimeControls.spec.ts`, which states what it can and cannot prove: the regression guard is the DISPATCH (no `playbackRunning: false` reaches the campaign) and it was checked against the old code, while the play/pause LABEL cannot tell old from new in a harness that does not echo the prop back - the component re-syncs `isPlaying` from `temporal.playbackRunning` and undoes the pause. Two earlier drafts of those tests passed for exactly that wrong reason.** |

An INTERMITTENT stretch therefore means a path where the canvas's CSS size changes without the observer firing or before the controller exists (a hidden tab reflowed then shown; the preset/layer switch swapping views; the CRT filter overlay scaling by CSS). Reproduce with `?perf=1` and log `resize` calls against `window.innerWidth/Height` while changing aspect; find which surface (holo canvas, 2D SVG, document) is the one stretching first. Route: "Starmap stars as stars" F71 knows the render surfaces, or the mop-up session. | **CLOSED — fix v2.1.899-beta, owner eyeballed the cover-page resize and SIGNED OFF 2026-08-21** | **FIX SHIPPED v2.1.899-beta, NOT VERIFIED ON THE LIVE SURFACE — leave this row OPEN until someone eyeballs it.** Reaching the player catalogue view needs a broadcast session between two windows, which a worker session cannot create, so what follows is the row's own fix shape implemented and unit-tested rather than a confirmed cure. **WHAT WAS CHECKED IN THE CODE, and it narrows the lead:** the stage is NOT unmounted while the cover is up - `.preset-cover` is `position: absolute; inset: 0` over a `.preset-stage` that stays laid out - so the ResizeObserver *ought* to fire, and "ought to" is exactly what makes an intermittent fault. **TWO GUARDS, both in `Starmap3DView` and `HoloView`:** (1) a content rect below 1 px is DROPPED - a momentarily unlaid-out container reports 0x0, and taking that as a size sets a 2x2 backing store which the next real frame draws stretched across the viewport, which is the reported symptom reached from the other direction; (2) `revalidate()` re-reads `getBoundingClientRect()` rather than trusting the last observation, and runs on window resize and on `visibilitychange`. **THE REVEAL IS WIRED WITHOUT THE PAGE KNOWING WHICH VIEWS EXIST:** `dismissCover` fires a window resize on the next frame, so any renderer that listens re-measures and one that does not is unaffected. `starmap/revealResize.spec.ts` pins the guards (5 tests). Engine map RENDER-S22. **THE THIRTY-SECOND CHECK OWED: open a player link with a cover page, resize the window to a clearly different aspect (tall to wide) WHILE the cover is up, then tap through — the starmap should fill the new shape with round stars and an undistorted grid, not letterboxed or smeared. | A63 | **REMOTE PLAY: A COMPLEX MAP (Sol) TAKES A WHILE TO ARRIVE AND THE PLAYER SCREEN FREEZES WITH NO FEEDBACK — "you are not sure what's up and are tempted to hit reload"; the GM screen may also time out (or the redial retries make it worse). Owner asks: a loading bar players see after the transition? Owner, 2026-08-21.** TWO SEPARATE COSTS, and the fix has a cheap half and a real half. (1) THE FREEZE is the receive side: a multi-MB `SYNC_STARMAP` arrives as ONE message and the parse + campaign re-clone runs on the main thread ([[P2]]'s meters measured 33 s of stringify on the SEND side of the same payloads; `rx.*` counters exist since 746). No bar can draw DURING a blocked main thread — so a progress bar for the parse itself is not possible without chunking. (2) THE WAIT is transport: PeerJS chunks internally but exposes NO progress events. **CHEAP HALF (do first): a tiny `SYNC_INCOMING { type, approxBytes, systems }` pre-announce sent before the big payload; the player shows a holding state ("Receiving the starmap — 27 systems, ~5 MB…", indeterminate spinner) the moment the transition lands, cleared on arrival — kills the reload temptation for half a day's work. REAL HALF (V3.1): app-level chunking of SYNC_STARMAP with sequence numbers — a TRUE progress bar, incremental parse off the main thread where possible, and it is the same 16 KB-frame lesson Mappadux already paid for (`project_dmr_datachannel_frame_limit`). Also check the GM-side timeout suspicion: the redial timer + a long transfer may indeed collide — the A57 host-attempt ring (perfEvent 'peer') now records enough to see it.** | cheap half **fixed v3.0.0-rc.18-beta**; real half (transition-themed chunked progress) is V3.1 — row stays open for it | **CHEAP HALF DONE v3.0.0-rc.21, RESHAPED AFTER THE OWNER SAW IT, AND MEASURED. Real half (chunked bar) is V3.1 — spec written up as `docs/dev/loading-screen-design.md`; this row stays open for it.** **THE FIRST CUT WAS INVISIBLE AND THE REASON IS THE INTERESTING PART.** Owner: "not seeing it at all... sure it is showing and not being interfered with by the transition itself". It was not the transition. Sniffed off the real channel during a real join: `REQUEST_STARMAP` t=59932, `SYNC_INCOMING` t=59932, `SYNC_STARMAP` t=59933 — **one millisecond apart** — and the holding state measured **9 ms alive**, never getting a frame to paint. Correct behaviour, badly expressed: on a local 45 KB map there is nothing to wait for. **FIX: A GRACE TIMER, NOT A SIZE THRESHOLD** (400 ms). If the payload beats it the screen never exists — the owner's own *"if local (cached) it just does a single transition"*. A size threshold would have been a guess about the transport; the clock already knows. **SHAPE, per the owner: the same flow as V3.1, spinner instead of bar** — transition IN, loading screen, transition OUT. The corner pill is gone; **the interstitial IS the loading screen** ("probably the default - message down low"), which is where `QuoteInterstitial` already renders `statusText`. The loading screen is a STAGE (`'loading'`), so the existing transition machinery plays OUT of it for free and the cached case is '' -> 'map:…' as it always was. **MESSAGE IS PACK DATA:** `playerStrings.incoming`, default "Incoming Transmission…", with our own plain detail line under it ("27 systems, ~5.0 MB"). **VERIFIED LIVE, three cases:** slow → screen appears at 650 ms with the message and a live spinner, clears to the map on arrival; inside the grace (250 ms) → still "Reaching the host", no flash; cached (announce and payload back to back) → `loadingScreenEverAppeared: false`. **ONE GAP STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN:** no transition INTO the loading screen on a COLD join, because the preset that names the transition arrives WITH the starmap — you cannot play a themed transition before you know the theme. Already-connected players get both. Closing it means the preset id in the announce; it is in the V3.1 doc. |
| A64 | **NEW, BUILT: per-link transfer figures and a live count of who is watching — owner, 2026-08-21, asked alongside [[A63]] to tell over-transmission from slowness.** DONE v3.0.0-rc.22, all three surfaces verified in a live GM+player pair. **(1) A COUNTER ON THE PLAYER VIEWS RAIL ICON:** local in green, remote in orange, e.g. "1-2" — and per the owner, **on the icon only (not the label) and never a zero**: a lone local window reads "1", nobody connected shows nothing at all. Nothing is stringified to print a number about it, because that is the very cost this feature exists to expose. **A same-machine link therefore has NO bytes** — a BroadcastChannel hands over a structured clone — so it reports messages and says so, rather than a 0 that reads like a measurement. **THREE TRAPS, each of which produced a plausible wrong answer silently, all in engine map NET-1:** presence must key on a WINDOW id (a receiver's `sessionId` is the id it is LISTENING TO, and a bare `/catalogue` link has none — the first cut counted nothing and raised no error); the meter must sit at `sendMessage` alone (metering `sendIfChanged` too double-counts, metering only it made a player report zero sends); and a GM has no meter for a LOCAL window, so that row's figures come from what the player REPORTS — the only source, not a fallback. New protocol message `PLAYER_PRESENT`, a few bytes once per GM heartbeat. 13 formatter tests + 7 contract tests. | built 2026-08-21 — owner-requested, shipped with A63 |

| G46 | **LOCAL TRANSFERS AND HOW A JOURNEY IS DRAWN — the owner's own "too hard, 3 models ago" item, reopened with the causes MEASURED.** Owner 2026-08-26: *"a good time to actually properly tidy up local transfers - orbit changes and transits to moons... That code IS a bit broken... the maths kinda works but the visualisation is a bit rubbish - the ship along the path is a bit haphazard."* Plus a user: *"could burns be visualised, like having your orbit change during it... ship paths should be visible, and it starts glitching out when you speed up time."* DESIGN NOTE WRITTEN: `docs/dev/local-transfer-visualisation-design.md`, with Q1-Q5 and recommendations. THE CAUSES, measured on the Sol Expanse fixture through the real solver, not guessed: **(a)** the solver generates ONE uniform path (one sample per 2 days) and SLICES it into Accel/Coast/Brake by time, so a sub-hour burn inside a 3-year transfer catches no samples and a fallback stuffs the last two COAST samples into it — the drawn burn then implies **1,371 km/s** (Most Efficient accel: 3,356,198 km in 0.68 h), 603 km/s and 1,215 km/s on the other phases, for a ship that does ~10 km/s in an hour. That is the "haphazard" motion, and it is worst exactly where the eye goes. **(b)** `samplePlanPathAtTime` assumes samples are uniform in TIME (`fraction x (n-1)`) and interpolates straight lines between them — one point per **48 hours** on the coast with gaps up to **4.1 million km**, which is precisely what "glitches when you speed up time" looks like. **(c)** there is NO orbit-change picture: a transfer between two orbits of one body draws a path to the body's CENTRE and then pops the ship into a parking orbit ([[B92]], 90,884 km of step). The Hohmann figure the owner sent (initial/transfer/final + two burns) is the model users arrive with and the app draws none of it. **(d)** the aerobrake dip (v3.0.78) is real in the numbers — passes, altitude, circularisation — but has no geometry, so the requested PURPLE LINE has nothing to follow. FIX SHAPE, one principle: a segment owns its own path, at its own resolution, in its own frame — per-phase generation, TIME-STAMPED samples, local frames for local transfers, manoeuvres as first-class drawable geometry (the dip then costs a few points, not a special case). **WARNING FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: the transit specs pin Delta-v and TIMING, not path GEOMETRY, so they will not catch a regression here** — the new gates have to ship with the change ('drawn speed between consecutive points never exceeds what the ship can do' is the cheap one). Wants its own session WITH THE BROWSER, since every fault is visual; the numbers above are the before-figures to beat. | captured 2026-08-26 by the G43 session — design-first, no code; provisional id, both forms checked free **PASS 1 SHIPPED v3.0.82 (2026-08-26).** Per-phase paths + time-stamped samples, in all THREE plan builders (Lambert, Fast, assist). Measured before -> after on the same fixture: Most Efficient accel **1,365.8 -> 19.4 km/s**, its brake **1,223.1 -> 10.9 km/s**, Efficient Now accel **602.6 -> 18.8**, brake **496.7 -> 11.0**; assist arrival brake **109.6 -> 13.9**. Interplanetary coasts UNCHANGED (608 vs 607 points, same max gap to 0.004%) - checked, not assumed. Resolution now follows GEOMETRY not the clock: a Jupiter-local coast turned **56.84 deg** between drawn points and now turns **3.90**. Two more faults surfaced the moment the drawing became honest and are FIXED here: the display integrator marched at a flat two-day step and fell off any eccentric conic near periapsis (a valid e=0.9986 Lambert leg drew as a 53 AU excursion at 313 km/s; the step is now capped by swept ANGLE), and the assist drew leg 2 from a point that was never on its own trajectory. NEW GATES SHIPPED WITH IT, not after: `transit/pathGeometry.spec.ts` - 12 assertions over real plans from the real solver, covering speed, spacing and stamps. **The speed gate was PROVEN, not merely watched to pass**: reinstating the borrowed-sample fallback fails it at 1,366 km/s against a ceiling of 68, and 11 of the 12 go red. B92's tripwire still pins what it pinned. **PASS 2 NOT STARTED** - the orbit-change (Hohmann) picture and the aerobrake dip line, Q3/Q4/Q5 still unanswered. Structural notes for [[G47]] collected in `docs/dev/local-transfer-visualisation-design.md` section 6. New finding raised: [[B93]]. **v3.0.83 - THE DRIVE VECTORS, raised by the owner mid-session** (*"always make sure the ship is pointing in the right direction... rockets firing really is the best direction check as that is the only time it is needed - pointing in direction of desired vector"*, and *"3D model has made it a thing - before then it was just not done"*). Segments now PUBLISH `deltaV_ms` and `thrustDir`; nothing infers either. Two measured faults fixed: **(1) the plume's thrust was inferred by differencing segment start/end state velocities, and most builders leave `endState.v` a literal zero** - against a commanded 0.3 g that read 2.4x on the Hohmann departure, 2.8x on its brake and **0.03x on a 57-hour torch burn**, i.e. the drive looked OFF through the longest burn in the game; now 1.0x across all four families at 0.3/1/3 g. **(2) the hull was aimed down its COURSE and flipped for a brake** - fine for a torch (0.1 deg and 177.4 deg, within 2.6 of prograde/retrograde, which is why nobody saw it) and badly wrong otherwise: **the Most Efficient arrival burn would have been drawn 107.3 deg off and the gravity assist's 153.2 deg off, very nearly backwards**. An efficient arrival burn is frequently PROGRADE despite the `Brake` label - at the top of a transfer ellipse you are slower than the orbit you are joining. Also fixed: **the acceleration ARROW showed net gravity only**, ~4 orders of magnitude too small during a burn and pointing at the star (the published-as-a-lie rule); it now includes the drive. The VELOCITY arrow was fixed by pass 1 itself - it reads the sampler, so during a burn it had been reporting 1,366 km/s. Gate: `transit/burnVectors.spec.ts`, 7 assertions incl. the pre-G46 fallback path. Engine map RENDER-S34. New structural notes S8 (transit is entirely 2D - 38 inclined nodes in the fixture, up to 0.4689 AU of out-of-plane offset the solver never sees; route lines already read a `z` that is always 0) and S9. **v3.0.84 - TRANSITS GO 3D, at the owner's request** (*"we had better do the distances for 3d transfers too"*). S8 is now FIXED rather than merely recorded: `getGlobalState` called `propagateState`, the FLAT projection, so every transit ever planned ran between the SHADOWS of two bodies on the reference plane - while `propagateState3D` with the full 3-1-3 rotation had existed all along for the holo view. Owner called it exactly: *"the maths should be no different"* - only TWO places in the solver were ever dimensional, the transfer ANGLE in `solveLambert` (a difference of `atan2(y,x)` bearings) and the final velocity assembly. | B95 | **JUPITER'S BANDS VANISH ON THE FIRST ATMOSPHERE EDIT AFTER OPENING, AND COME BACK ON THE NEXT ONE — user report relayed by the owner 2026-08-26, with his composition screenshot.** The user's own words, and his last observation is the diagnostic one: *"I'll edit NH3 from 0.129 to 0.128 and it'll get rid of the planet's bands, and then I'll move NH3 from 0.128 to 0.127 and it'll come back again... it doesn't just happen with NH3, this happens with like everything **if you edit it for the first time after opening up SSE**. But I think only after the first time? This effect doesn't show up even when I actually am significantly changing atmospheric species presence."* **THE OWNER SUGGESTED THIS WAS 'JUST PHYSICS' AND THE USER PUSHED BACK. BOTH ARE HALF RIGHT, AND THE SPLIT IS THE WHOLE ITEM.** There IS a hard physical cliff: `bandCount` (`rendering/apparentColor.ts:143`) returns **0 bands when `gasFrac < 0.3`**, binary, no hysteresis — so bands really are all-or-nothing and a threshold really is involved. **But `gasFrac` cannot legitimately move when you edit the atmosphere at all**, which is why the user is right that it is a glitch: it comes from `makeupFractions(body)` (`physics/makeup.ts:144`), which returns the body's STORED `body.makeup` when present (:145) and otherwise INFERS one from mass and density (a giant short-circuits to `{gas: 0.8, ice: 0.2}` at :153). **Neither path reads the atmosphere, and `BodyAtmosphereTab.svelte` never touches `makeup` — grep returns nothing.** So a 0.001 NH3 change flipping the bands means the MAKEUP is changing underneath, and THAT is the bug; the banding is only where it becomes visible. LEADING HYPOTHESIS, matching 'only the first time after opening': the loaded save carries a stored `makeup` so :145 returns it, and the first edit strips or recomputes it onto the inferred path, whose answer differs and lands the other side of 0.3; every later edit is already on the recomputed path, hence stable. The alternation on successive 0.001 steps may be a second sub-case rather than the same one — MEASURE, do not assume. **PROBE FIRST, and the probe IS the deliverable of pass one:** load his map, dump `body.makeup`, the resolved `gasFrac` and `body.apparentColor.banding` BEFORE any edit, after the first edit, and after the second. The diff is the fault. **WHY THE SUITE DID NOT CATCH IT, and this is a real coverage finding:** `system/idempotence.test.ts` walks every key on every node (so `apparentColor.banding` IS compared) and even checks 1v2 AND 2v3 specifically because *"a quantity can oscillate with period 2"* — but it tests `process(process(process(x)))` with **NO EDIT between passes**. The user's fault lives in **load → edit → process**, a sequence nothing pins. A regression gate for that sequence should ship with the fix. RELATED: `apparentColor` is already slated for retirement pre-V4 ([[B54]]/[[B66]]/[[B76]]/[[B77]]) and this is more evidence for it, but do NOT fold this into that — a user is hitting it now. ASK THE OWNER FOR THE USER'S MAP: it goes in `../user-test-files/` per the standing rule, never the repo. **CORRECTION, same day, and it matters for how the fix is scoped: THE CLAIM ABOVE THAT AN ATMOSPHERE EDIT 'CANNOT' MOVE `gasFrac` IS TOO STRONG.** `body.makeup` is NOT inert — `reconcileGiantMakeup(body)` REWRITES it during `process()`, at BOTH `SystemProcessor.ts:681` (early) and `:1255` (composition round 2), and `process()` runs on every edit. The atmosphere is still not a documented input to it, so the coupling to an NH3 nudge remains UNEXPLAINED rather than disproved — which is exactly what the probe must settle. **AND THE SMOKING GUN IS THE COMMENT ABOVE THE EARLY CALL, which describes this precise bug class already having happened once in this very function:** *"Only classification used to make the correction, one pass too late: the first process() ran the temperature model against the authored makeup and the second against the corrected one, **so the same file gave two different temperatures depending on how many times it had been loaded**."* That is the user's 'only the first time after opening' signature verbatim, in the one function that writes the field `bandCount` ultimately reads. The early call was added to fix it FOR TEMPERATURE; **anything reading `makeup` at a different point in the pass order could still be reading the pre-correction value once, and `apparentColor` is a strong candidate.** IMPLICATION FOR THE FIX, and it is the reason this correction is worth writing down: **the owner's instinct to smooth the cliff is good UX and worth doing on its own merits — but if a second instance of the pass-order fault is live, smoothing MASKS it.** Bands would fade in and out gently instead of popping, and the underlying value would still be unstable across a load. New `perfProvider` registry — the holo scene registers `renderer.info.memory` (geometries/textures/programs), so **GPU-side resource counts sit beside the JS heap in one line: the leak detector for the rebuild-per-snapshot path**.
