Plus a **load guard**: a `localStorage['sse-load-guard']` stage stamp armed before the auto-load, advanced through each stage, cleared only when the load completes. If it is still set at startup the previous load never finished, so the app **does not auto-load**; it offers *Try loading again* / *Start without loading it* / **Download a copy (.json)** — the emergency export runs straight from storage and renders nothing, so a map that cannot load can still be rescued. **The guard can never brick the app itself, by construction:** it clears on a PAINTED frame (double-rAF) **OR** on a 15-second timer, whichever comes first. **The timer is not belt-and-braces, it is a fix for a false positive found live:** a tab that is hidden or not compositing paints no frames at all, so a load that completed in a background tab tripped the guard on the next visit. A timer only fires if the main thread is alive; a genuinely hung render blocks both paths, which is the case the guard is for. **(c) MEMORY VISIBILITY.** `memoryWatch.ts` reads `performance.memory` (Chromium only — Firefox/Safari expose nothing and it says so rather than guessing). Settings → System → **Memory** shows used / the browser's **allocation limit** with a bar; a banner warns once at **80%** and again at **90%**, re-arming only below **65%** so a session sitting at the line is not nagged. **MEASURED, not asserted:** full cold load of the 44-system bundled map, `load.storageRead` 3 ms, **31-47 ms per system**, `load.complete(painted)` reached with the guard cleared; heap 19-22 MB against a 4.0 GB limit. Warning ladder exercised by overriding `performance.memory` live — 88% gives the amber "good moment to save", 95% the red "save NOW", and the banner sits above the load overlay (z-index 5000) so it survives any screen. **AND THE INSTRUMENTS IMMEDIATELY EARNED THEIR KEEP — the 30 ms repaint yield in `recalcAllSystems` costs 1000 ms PER SYSTEM in a HIDDEN tab**, because background tabs clamp timers to 1 Hz: measured 47 ms/system foreground against 1000 ms/system hidden, i.e. **44 s versus 2 s for the bundled map, and unbounded on a big one**. Now yielded only while `!document.hidden` — nothing paints and nobody can click Stop in a hidden tab, so there is nothing to yield for. That is a real (if partial) contributor to "loading takes far too long" and it was found by reading the stage stamps, not by reasoning. **NOT MEASURED YET, and it is the whole point of the next session — none of this is a performance FIX:** baselines on (a) GM view, (b) player view idle, (c) player view with a ship in transit, (d) the phone, (e) a locally built 85 kly map, each with `[sse-perf]` + a DevTools profile + heap snapshots start and end. Then the ranked findings report — what is hot, what leaks, what is heavy on the wire — before anything changes behaviour. **The affected user's device and browser are still unknown beyond "a low-end mobile", and the 85 kly reproduction has not been built.** Related: RENDER-S19 (no bundled example carries a construct with a journey, so transit paths cannot render in tests or a bare preview). **(d) THE DIAGNOSTIC BUNDLE, v2.1.489-beta — `io/diagnosticBundle.ts`, offered after Stop load, on the safe-mode screen, and ON DEMAND from Settings → System → "Reporting a problem".** A load hang is the one fault a user CANNOT usefully report: the app is frozen, a phone has no console, and the only visible evidence is a stopped bar that may read 100%. So the app packages the evidence itself — a zip with `README.txt` (what it is, which file to load, and to post it to FrunkQ on the Discord), `report.json` (reason, guard stage, which systems were re-derived and which one it stalled on, every load stage with timings, memory against the limit, device incl. `deviceMemory`/`hardwareConcurrency`/DPR, storage against quota, what was on screen, map extent, a shape summary per system, and every perf counter) and the map itself. **BOTH MAP COPIES SHIP WHEN THEY DIFFER, which is the design point:** `recalcAllSystems` rewrites `node.system` IN PLACE, so mid-load the live map is a half re-derived mixture that never existed on disk. `starmap.json` is ALWAYS the loadable one (the stored INPUT — test-load it, and if it loads elsewhere the fault is the device or the scale, not the data); `starmap-in-memory.json` carries the half-derived state (how far the engine got and what it produced). The owner's framing: "for a halfway-through-load issue we will need both; an on-demand one will only have currently loaded." **CONSENT PROPERTIES, all pinned by the spec (engine map UI-L5):** built only on request, downloaded to the user's own device, nothing uploaded, README states the contents, and the campaign is confined to named files the user may delete while still sending a useful report. **AND OPENING A REAL BUNDLE IMMEDIATELY FOUND A BUG IN THE BUNDLE — the method working on itself.** The extent block read `system.x`, but a saved map stores coordinates under `position: {x,y,z}` IN PIXELS, so **it reported an extent of ZERO across a real 42-system map** — silently, and it would have read zero on the 85 kly file this whole item is about, destroying the one measurement it exists to carry. Fixed with the flat spelling kept as a fixture fallback, plus the pixels→units conversion (`scale.pixelsPerUnit`) so a bundle can be matched to a report phrased in light years, and the spec fixture rebuilt to the PRODUCER's shape rather than the type's — RENDER-S17's rule in another family. Verified end to end from the running app: 42 systems, 78.96 ly across, matching an independent computation over the same file. **NOTE FOR THE NEXT SESSION: the owner will send bundles from live faults, so `report.json` is the first thing to read on any new report.** Docs: `docs/dev/debug-tools.md` indexes every instrument (this, `[sse-perf]`, `[sse-load]`, `__camDebug`/`__shipDebug`/`__routeDebug`/`__ringDebug`, the memory gauge) with the question each answers; the engine map now points at it from the top. **(e) THE REPORTED FAULT IS FOUND, REPRODUCED AND FIXED — v2.1.490-beta. IT IS THE SNAP-GRID OVERLAY, AND IT IS NEITHER A PHYSICS COST NOR A DATA VOLUME PROBLEM.** Built the reproduction locally rather than waiting for the user's file: two systems 85,103 ly apart written into storage, then the ordinary auto-load. **It loaded fine — until the grid overlay was switched on, which is the variable nobody had.** `components/Grid.svelte` draws by walking the map ONE CELL AT A TIME in MAP units (`view / zoom / cell`), and zoom is fitted to the map's own extent, so **the loop count is set by the distance between the two furthest systems and nothing bounds it.** Measured live at the fitted zoom of 2.6e-4: square grid **61,422 x 46,066** lines, which really did build a **4.95 MB path string**; hex grid **81,896 x 53,193 = 4.36 BILLION iterations**. Timed the real loop in the browser at **663,647 hexes/second on a fast desktop** → **1.8 hours** of blocked main thread while growing a **~670 GB** string. It cannot finish anywhere; it dies of memory, on every device, every time. **That is the whole report — "takes too long to load", "it basically crashed", scales with how far apart the objects are — and it explains the screenshot exactly, because this runs AFTER the physics pass, so the bar reads 100% while the app is already gone.** **THE FIX IS A LEGIBILITY GATE, NOT A MAGIC CAP:** at that zoom a 50-unit cell is **0.013 SCREEN pixels**, so those billions of hexes were drawing nothing a human could see. Below 3 px the grid does not draw, which is the rule `starmapScene.renderMapGrid` has always used for the 3D starmap ("too dense to be useful") — **that is why the 3D view never had this fault**, and the fix brings the 2D map into line rather than inventing anything. **MEASURED BEFORE AND AFTER on the reproduction:** unloadable (hex) → **loads in ~140 ms, heap 34 MB, `load.complete(painted)`**. **REGRESSION CHECKED, because a grid that stops drawing is a visible change:** on the bundled 42-system map the fitted zoom is 0.397 (a **19.9 px** cell, nowhere near the 3 px gate) and the hex grid draws **2,072 hexes** exactly as before, confirmed by screenshot. **A CAP SITS UNDER THE GATE AS A BACKSTOP, and getting the pair right needed the test:** the first attempt (3 px / 40,000 cells) would have **silently truncated a legitimate grid**, because the densest legible hex view genuinely wants **82,112** cells — the spec caught it by asserting the two constants against each other rather than in isolation, and the cap is now 250,000. **STILL OPEN AND UNCHANGED BY THIS:** the 2 fps player-view rebuild storm and the whole baseline programme — this fault has nothing to do with `holo.setSystem`. **NOTE `Starmap.svelte` passes Grid a HARDCODED `viewWidth={800} viewHeight={600}`** rather than the real viewport, so the loop bound is not even the true visible area; a separate latent bug, deliberately left alone. Engine map: **UI-L7**. **OWNER'S DECISION 2026-08-07, AND IT CLOSES THIS ITEM RATHER THAN LEAVING IT OPEN: THE PLAYER-VIEW REBUILD RATE IS NOT A PROBLEM YET.** His framing, and it is the right one: this was something an agent NOTICED in a trace, not something a user reported, and it "may not be a problem". **So the deliverable changes from a FIX to a set of INSTRUMENTS.** Put metering in place that can be switched on from the console, make sure it carries everything anyone would need to debug this problem class in future, **and — his specific ask — make it DISCOVERABLE FROM THE ENGINE DOC, so an agent working anywhere near this area knows what tools already exist.** Then P1 is **DONE**, and the rebuild question is revisited only if performance problems are actually SEEN, or in a dedicated performance-tuning pass. **DO NOT build a same-system patch path speculatively.** **WHAT WAS DONE TO SATISFY THAT (v2.1.502-beta): `engine-map.md` RENDER-S22**, which names every meter that answers this area and the question each one actually answers — `holo.setSystem.same` as the wasted-work count and therefore the go/no-go number, `.ms` for average rebuild cost, `renderer.info.memory` through the `perfProvider` registry as the leak detector for the rebuild path, the `bc.*` payload counters, and `holo.ringRefineFrame` — plus how to switch them on and a pointer to `debug-tools.md` for the full index. **AND THE ONE GENUINE GAP IS NAMED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER, in both documents: NOTHING RECORDS WHY A REBUILD FIRED.** The counters prove four rebuilds happened in five seconds; nothing says which upstream change caused each, which is exactly what a future investigation would need first. **The camera work already paid for this lesson — `__camDebug` only became useful once it recorded WHICH INPUT caused each change, and that is what settled RENDER-S15.** A reason label on the `setSystem` counter is therefore the first thing to add if this area is ever chased, and it is written down as such. The baselines are parked WITH this, not abandoned: they belong to a tuning pass, not a bug hunt. | **CLOSED v2.1.502-beta.** Load crash fixed v2.1.490; instruments/brake/bundle v2.1.488-489; rebuild rate parked by owner decision as not-a-problem-yet, with metering + engine-map RENDER-S22 in place to diagnose it instantly if it ever is |
| B19 | **Mars is tagged "Stability · Fated: flung out". It is not going anywhere.** Sanity check 2026-08-01. Mars's orbit is stable on any timescale a game cares about; the inner Solar System shows only mild chaos over billions of years. A prediction of ejection points at the test, not at Mars. **Where it comes from:** `physics/stability.ts:146` — `if (delta < 5.5 && !isResonanceProtected(inner) && !isResonanceProtected(outer)) out.fate = 'eject'` — a MUTUAL HILL SEPARATION test, with other eject paths at `:126` (mass-ratio dependent) and `:362`. The 5.5 threshold is itself defensible: the literature puts long-term instability below roughly ten mutual Hill radii for comparable masses, so 5.5 is conservative rather than aggressive, and the constant is probably not the fault. **HYPOTHESIS, NOT VERIFIED — CHECK IT FIRST:** Mars against Earth is about 26 mutual Hill radii and could not trip this. But Mars's outward NEIGHBOUR IN ORBIT ORDER IS THE ASTEROID BELT, and [[B11]] has just established that belts return early from the third derivation pass. If a belt node carries a mass and is included in the neighbour pairing, then the mutual Hill radius is being computed between a planet and a diffuse belt, which is not a two-body problem and will produce nonsense. Confirm what Mars is actually being paired with before touching any constant — print the pair and the delta. **If that is it, the fix is about which nodes are ELIGIBLE for a pairwise stability test, not about the threshold**, and it will affect every system with a belt between planets rather than Mars alone. Do not "fix" this by raising 5.5 until the pairing is proven sound. Related: [[B11]]. **FIXED v2.1.338-beta. THE HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED AND THE THRESHOLD IS INNOCENT — both checked before anything changed.** **Belts were already excluded.** `annotateGravitationalStability` filters `roleHint` 'belt' and 'ring' out of `orbitalNodes` before any pairing, with a comment naming this exact hazard ("their massKg is a debris-density proxy, not a point mass"), and `stability.spec.ts` already had a test for it. No planet is being paired against a diffuse belt. **The 5.5 threshold never fires here.** Printed the pair and the delta first, as the entry demanded: Mars's inward neighbour in the starmap Sol is **433 EROS**, a 16 km near-Earth asteroid carried as `roleHint: 'planet'` at a = 1.458, and the pair sits at **DELTA = 9.28** — well outside 5.5. The constant is untouched. **The real cause is the ORBIT-OVERLAP branch (`stability.ts:95-126`), and it is one line below where anyone was looking.** Eros's eccentric orbit genuinely does cross Mars's, so the crossing test fires correctly; with a mass ratio of ~1e-8 it correctly returns `eject` rather than `collision`. Then `mergeAssessment` copied that fate onto **BOTH** members of the pair. **The code's own comments already stated the intent** — "a lightweight crosser is scattered out", "packed systems shed their lighter member" — so the model always knew which body it meant and simply never recorded it. **Fix: `StabilityAssessment` gains `fateNodeId`**, set to the lighter body on both eject paths (crossing and Hill spacing) and left unset for a `collision`, which between comparable masses genuinely IS mutual. Severity and reasons still merge onto both, because both bodies really are in a risky pair — only the FATE is directional. **Measured over every bundled system: 29 bodies tagged `fate/eject` -> 22, and all seven that dropped it were the heavier half of their pair.** Mars keeps its metastable severity and loses the verdict; Eros keeps it, which is right. GJ 876 is the clean demonstration — b at 4.32e27 kg drops it while c at 1.36e27 and e at 8.72e25 keep it. **`tests/output/solar-system-derived.json` is UNCHANGED, correctly:** the baseline is built from `static/examples/Sol_2030-System.json`, which contains no Eros — the reported body lives in the starmap Sol. The sweep above is the measurement. Pinned by three tests, one of which asserts the delta is outside 5.5 so nobody re-blames the threshold. **Two things noticed and NOT fixed:** several bodies carry a reason reading "...so it stays stable" beside "Predicted outcome: flung out", because the fate came from a different driver than the reason that is printed next to it ([[B24]]); and for two nearly equal masses on the Hill path "lighter" is close to arbitrary, though naming one is still more honest than naming both. | fixed v2.1.338-beta |
| B18 | **Uranus scores 50% habitability — above Mars at 8% and Enceladus at 35%.** Sanity check 2026-08-01. Uranus is an ice giant with no solid surface, crushing pressures at depth, violent winds and extreme cold at the cloud decks. Even on the most generous atmospheric-envelope reading it should not outrank a rocky world with a real surface or a moon with a subsurface ocean. The RANKING is the evidence here, more than the absolute number: whatever the score means, Mars and Enceladus should sit above Uranus on it, and they do not. **Suspect a weighting artefact rather than a wrong input** — something over-rewarding atmospheric mass, volatile presence or air mix, which a gas giant trivially maximises while a thin-aired rocky world scores near zero on all three. **Where to start:** `SystemProcessor.ts:1170` clamps `habitabilityScore` to 0-130, with a subsurface-niche floor at `:1179-1180` (`SUBSURFACE_NICHE_SCORE`) and an alien-habitable gate at `:1188` requiring score > 40 and `factors.solvent > 0`. The factor weights feeding that score are the thing to audit — I have not read them, so treat the artefact diagnosis as a starting hypothesis rather than a finding. **Check whether a body with NO SOLID SURFACE should be scoring on this axis at all**: the subsurface-niche floor shows the model already accepts that habitability can mean something other than "stand on it", so the question is whether a giant's envelope is a niche the model means to score, or an accident of factors designed for surfaces. Answer that before adjusting weights, or the weights will be tuned to hide a category error. Sanity anchors to hold the result against once changed: Earth top, Mars low but non-zero, Enceladus and Europa meaningful via the subsurface niche, Venus low, the giants below all of them. **FIXED v2.1.339-beta. IT IS A CATEGORY ERROR, NOT A WEIGHTING ARTEFACT — the category question is answered first, and answering it made the weights irrelevant.** **The axis is a SURFACE model and says so throughout:** the running total is literally named `surfaceScore`, every factor is a surface condition, and `isEarthLike` / `isHumanHabitable` all test what it is like to stand there. **The proof that the model MEANS surface is the subsurface niche itself** — non-surface habitability is handled by ADDING an explicitly named niche with its own floor and its own tier, precisely because these factors cannot express it. So the model had already answered the question: a niche that is not a surface gets named and scored separately, rather than being left to surface factors. A giant's envelope is therefore outside what this axis measures. **Which factor does a giant trivially maximise? All three that survive, and the arithmetic is exact.** Uranus scores **temp 0, solvent 0** — the two worth 50 of the 100 points, and the two that actually decide the question — then **pressure 18 + radiation 17 + gravity 15 = 50**. Neptune is identical, Saturn 49.9, Jupiter 30 (it loses gravity at 2.64 g). **And all three are evaluated at a level that is not a surface:** a giant's `atmosphere.pressure_bar` is pinned to the 1-bar cloud-top reference (a deliberate simplification, ARCHITECTURE.md), and its "surface" radiation and "surface" gravity are computed at that same notional radius. The three factors are not over-weighted — they are being asked about a place that does not exist. Tuning them would have buried that. **Gated on `makeupFractions(planet).gas <= 0.5`, the same test the geology model already uses**, so the two agree on what a surface is. A caught body scores 0 and its Bio tab reads "No solid surface — surface habitability does not apply" instead of a blank panel or a silent 50. **Every anchor the entry set now holds:** Earth 100 (earth-like) > Titan 47 (alien — it has a real surface and real liquid methane) > Europa 35 = Enceladus 35 (subsurface niche) > Mars 8 > Venus 7 > **all four giants 0**. **Swept all 366 bundled planets and moons: 59 caught, every one a giant / neptune / puffy class, and ZERO of them have a surface liquid** — which is the check that would have exposed a false positive. `planet/hycean` is NOT caught, so an ocean under a thick H2 envelope keeps its score. 52 of the 59 were previously scoring over 10 from the surfaceless factors alone. **Derived diff is four bodies and only the giants: 30/50/50/50 -> 0. Their TIER does not change** — it was already `habitability/none`, because `isAlienHabitable` requires `factors.solvent > 0` and they never had any. **Only the NUMBER ever lied**, which is why this survived so long: the tag was right the whole time. **Deliberately NOT done:** whether a giant's ENVELOPE deserves an aerial niche of its own, the way the subsurface ocean has one. That is a design decision rather than a bug fix, and inventing one unasked would repeat the same mistake in the other direction. Also raised: [[B25]]. | fixed v2.1.339-beta |
| B17 | **Io's radiation is far too low — nothing models radiation from a NON-STELLAR source.** Sanity check 2026-08-01. Io shows `moderate (19.2-2... mSv/y)` and tags `Irradiation: low`. In reality Io sits deep inside Jupiter's inner magnetosphere and its energetic particle belt: unshielded surface dose is of order 36 Sv per DAY, around 13,000 Sv/year, making it one of the most violently irradiated surfaces in the Solar System. The engine is out by something like six orders of magnitude, and it is out because the source does not exist in the model rather than because a number is mistuned. **The engine computes radiation from STARS only** — `calculateSurfaceRadiation` and `calculateTotalStellarRadiationRange` are stellar by construction (see [[B8]], which fixed a missing flare term in that same stellar path). **The interesting part, and the reason this is not simply "a missing feature":** the engine ALREADY KNOWS a body can sit inside a giant's magnetosphere. `SystemProcessor.ts:765-768` computes `insideHostMagnetosphere` from the host's mass, gas fraction and field strength, and feeds it to `deriveMagnetism` — but it is used only to influence the MOON'S OWN magnetism, never as a radiation source. So the concept is present and pointed the wrong way: being inside a magnetosphere is currently treated purely as context for a dynamo, when for a close-in moon of a strong-field giant it is the dominant HAZARD. That existing flag is the natural hook. **Scope honestly before building:** a real magnetospheric dose model needs the host's field strength, the moon's orbital distance in host radii, and some belt profile — and it should degrade gracefully to zero for the many hosts with no meaningful field. It will change Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto (in that steep order) and essentially nothing else in the bundled maps, which makes it easy to validate and hard to get accidentally wrong elsewhere. Anchors exist for all four Galileans, so this is a model that can be CALIBRATED rather than guessed — the same standard [[B2]] was held to. **THE INPUTS ALREADY EXIST AND ARE ALREADY ACCURATE — checked in `tests/output/solar-system-derived.json`, so this is far cheaper than "a new physics model" sounds.** A magnetosphere is powered by FIELD x SPIN, and the engine already derives both for every giant: Jupiter `strengthGauss` **4.32** against a measured ~4.3 and rotation 9.925 h; Earth 0.5014 against ~0.5; Saturn 0.2396 (~0.21) at 10.656 h; Uranus 0.2088 (~0.23) at **-17.24 h, retrograde with the correct sign**; Neptune 0.2235 (~0.14) at 16.11 h. Nothing new needs authoring or placeholding — `deriveMagnetism` is already producing the numbers and the radiation path simply never asks for them. **The clean diagnostic, worth using as the before/after test:** Io's `surfaceRadiation` is 20.9397 and Europa's is 20.9276 — near-identical, because solar distance is the only term in the model, while in reality Io takes roughly SEVEN TIMES Europa's dose. Two moons agreeing to four significant figures is the fingerprint of the missing source, and separating them is the headline result. Io's own `strengthGauss` is 0, correctly — it has no dynamo, so all of its dose is external. **Shape of the model:** dose as a function of (host field, host spin) x a steep falloff in orbital distance measured in HOST RADII — the Galilean anchors imply something like an inverse sixth-to-eighth power between 5.9 and 26 R_J. Saturn is the second system and the real test of the field term, since its structure is the same and its field is roughly eighteen times weaker, so Enceladus and Titan must come out far lower than the Galileans rather than merely proportionally lower. Must degrade to zero for hosts with no meaningful field, which is most of them. **DO NOT BUILD THIS AS "A PLANET EMITS RADIATION" — that was proposed 2026-08-01 and it is the wrong mechanism, for a reason that is decisive rather than stylistic.** Three things are easily conflated here and only one is missing. **(a) Self-luminous bodies are ALREADY DONE.** `physics/substellar.ts` models them from mass, system age and radius, exposes `luminositySolar` commented "for irradiating moons", and `isLuminousSource` (`:51-52`) is `roleHint === 'star' || isSelfLuminous` — so a substellar object already joins the same `radiationOutput / d^2` sum as the stars in `calculateTotalStellarRadiation`. The flag is set by the processor's substellar pass (`SystemProcessor.ts:336/347`) and the model's table starts at **13 M_jup**, the deuterium-burning limit. Brown dwarfs are covered; the sum was always a predicate over emitters rather than a hardcoded star check. **(b) Jupiter is correctly EXCLUDED and must stay so.** At ~1 M_jup it is an order of magnitude under that floor, and its real excess output (about 1.67x absorbed sunlight, from Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction) is INFRARED and non-ionising. It is a heat source, not a dose source. **(c) THE ARITHMETIC THAT SETTLES IT.** An emitter-plus-distance model is inverse-square, `r^-2`. The Galilean anchors demand a falloff between **`r^-4`** (Io to Europa: 1.59x the distance, 6.7x less dose) and **`r^-8.6`** (Io to Callisto: 4.4x the distance, 360,000x less dose). No inverse-square source can fit those: calibrate at Io and Callisto is wrong by orders of magnitude, calibrate at Callisto and Io is. That is because the dose is not radiation FROM Jupiter but charged particles TRAPPED BY its field and accelerated by its rotation — a peaked belt profile in planetary radii, which is a different law and needs its own TERM rather than a new entry in the luminous-source sum. **CORRECTED AND SHARPENED 2026-08-01 — "surely we can work out its likely radiation output, magnetic field driven, all procedural and reusable" is RIGHT, and the objection above applies only to the DISTANCE LAW, not to the idea of a derived planetary source.** The intended chain — rotation and composition give a field, the field drives a source strength, that source is summed at the receiving body — is exactly correct and is what this item should build. **And the sum it needs ALREADY EXISTS.** `calculateStellarRadiationComponents` (`radiation.ts:55-82`) splits every source into a PHOTON and a PARTICLE channel, and the particle channel is already attenuated by the receiver's magnetosphere and atmosphere: "Goes in the particle channel so a magnetosphere + atmosphere shield against it (an unshielded close world bears the brunt)." Trapped belt radiation is a PURE particle-channel source with no photon component, so it drops straight into existing, already-shielded machinery. `insideHostMagnetosphere` (`SystemProcessor.ts:765-768`) is already computed and is the natural gate. **So the whole delta is ONE TERM: a belt strength derived from host field x spin, delivered into the particle channel with a falloff in HOST RADII rather than `1/d^2`.** Nothing about the architecture needs changing and no body needs a special case. **CALIBRATION HAZARD, and it is the same shape as the Mars albedo trap in [[B5]]:** Ganymede is the only moon in the Solar System with its own dynamo (~0.0072 G measured) and that shield is part of why its dose sits where it does — but the engine currently gives it `strengthGauss: 0`. Calibrate the belt profile against Ganymede's measured dose without modelling its shield and the shielding gets baked into the belt law, giving a fit that is right for the wrong reason. **Calibrate on Io and Callisto, neither of which has a field, then treat Ganymede's shield as a PREDICTION to check.** Related: [[B8]], [[B12]], [[B5]]. **FIXED v2.1.340-beta.** **Root cause in a sentence: the engine only ever summed LUMINOUS sources, so the dominant hazard for a close-in moon of a strong-field giant had no representation at all** — not a mistuned number but an absent mechanism, and the fingerprint was Io 20.9397 against Europa 20.9276, two moons agreeing to four significant figures because solar distance was the only term either had. **THE SUBSTELLAR PATH WAS VERIFIED END TO END FIRST, as the brief demanded, rather than trusted from the predicate.** Measured on a synthetic host: at 1 M_jup the moon sees 2.01 mSv/yr; at 13 M_jup `isSelfLuminous` flips and it sees **104.4**, then 351 at 20 M_jup and 2626 at 40. The path works, Jupiter at ~1 M_jup is correctly excluded, and the new term sits beside it without touching it. **THE LAW, and its shape is forced by the anchors rather than chosen:** `dose(r) = D0 · (B/B_ref)² · (Ω/Ω_ref) · exp(−r/λ)` with `λ = λ_ref · (B/B_ref)^(1/3)`, r in HOST RADII, delivered into the particle channel. An emitter at a distance is inverse-square; the Galileans demand r^-4 from Io to Europa and r^-8.6 from Io to Callisto, and no power law fits both — but a belt is not a point source, it is a population confined by a field, and **one exponential fits the entire family**. **The exponents are REASONED, NOT FITTED** — there is only one calibrated system, so fitting them would be overfitting: B² is the magnetic energy density available to trap, Ω is the corotation drive that energises the particles, and a dipole's magnetopause standoff goes as B^(1/3), so a weaker host holds a TIGHTER belt as well as a fainter one. Constants live in `generation_parameters` as rule-pack data. No body is special-cased. **CALIBRATED ON IO AND CALLISTO ONLY** — the two Galileans with no field of their own, so no self-shielding is baked into the law. Two anchors, two free parameters, using the ENGINE's radii rather than textbook ones: **λ = 1.6324 R_J, D0 = 1451.1 Sv/day**. | body | r (R_J) | predicted | measured | ratio | | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Io | 6.03 | 3.600e+1 | 3.600e+1 | 1.00 | fitted | | Europa | 9.59 | 4.086e+0 | 5.400e+0 | **0.76** | PREDICTED | | Ganymede | 15.30 | 1.234e-1 | 8.000e-2 | **1.54** | PREDICTED, held out | | Callisto | 26.92 | 1.000e-4 | 1.000e-4 | 1.00 | fitted | **GANYMEDE, the deliberate hold-out, came in 1.54x HIGH — and high is the right direction**, because it is the only moon in the Solar System with its own dynamo (~0.0072 G) and the law does not model that shield. Its buckets are reference points rather than round numbers, and the boundaries are stated in `radiation.ts`: `background` under 10 mSv/yr (Earth's natural background is ~2.4), `elevated` past the 20 mSv/yr occupational limit, `high` 100-1000 (a real mission dose - Mars 214 from Curiosity RAD), `severe` to 1e5 (a lethal total in weeks to months), `lethal` at 100 Sv/yr and up (days or less). **THE RESULT ON THE TWO BODIES THE ENTRY NAMED:** Io `hazard/radiation=lethal` beside `surface/irradiation=low`, and **Europa the same** - both readings correct, because they answer different questions, and now both visible. Ganymede `severe`, Mercury `severe`, Enceladus `severe`, Mars/Luna/Phobos `high`, Callisto `elevated`, Earth/Venus/Titan/Triton/Pluto `background`. **ONE FUNCTION, NOT TWO.** `bodyFacts.ts` already had its own `radBand` bucketing the SAME quantity three ways (low/moderate/high at 5 and 100) - a second answer to one question, and it put **Mars at 214 mSv/yr in the same bucket as Io at 13 million**, a range of sixty thousand described by one word. The row and the tag now share `radiationHazardBucket`, so the info block reads "lethal - 36 Sv/day" for Io and "high - 214 mSv/y" for Mars. Pinned by a new test that asserts the two do not get the same word. **GATED TO SOLID SURFACES**, deliberately: a giant has no ground, so its figure is a 1-bar reading and a "surface hazard" tag would repeat exactly the category error [[B18]] fixed and [[B22]] labelled around. Giants keep their row and get no tag. **DERIVED DIFF: PURE ADDITION.** 24 bodies gain `hazard/radiation` and **nothing else changed at all** - no dose, no weathering value, no other tag. **NOT DONE, and it is the separate physics question this entry flagged: should the belt ALSO feed the weathering model?** Untouched here, on purpose. Europa's real surface discolouration IS radiolytic - sulphur from Io's torus, processed by the very particles [[B17]] now models - so there is a genuine case that a magnetospheric term belongs in the tholin chain. It is a physics change with visual consequences and needs its own before/after diff; see the unnumbered capture at the bottom. **Also left:** the five-word bucket vocabulary here is new and does not match the low/moderate/high used elsewhere - that is [[B20]]/[[B29]]'s to settle, not a reason to hold this. | fixed v2.1.357-beta |
| B29 | **AUDIT: does every tag report the quantity its name claims? Sweep all 41 tag-emission sites.** Raised 2026-08-01 after [[B28]] — "audit and validate this won't happen more, or improve instructions?" Both; this is the audit half, and the instruction half is already in the standing rules at the foot of this file. **The surface is BOUNDED and countable, so this is one session rather than an open-ended sweep:** 41 `tags.push` sites — 32 in `core/SystemProcessor.ts`, then `physics/stability.ts` (2), `physics/surfaceTemperature.ts` (2), `physics/accrete-adapter.ts` (2), `physics/cloudDecks.ts` (1), `physics/resonance.ts` (1), `physics/reasonsToVisit.ts` (1). **ONE QUESTION PER SITE:** what quantity is this tag bucketed off, and is that the quantity a reader would think the tag describes? Record the answer for every site even where it is fine — a table of "tag / source quantity / what a reader assumes / verdict" is the deliverable, because the value is as much in the sites that are CLEAN as in the ones that are not. The next person should never have to re-derive this. **Precedent for expecting real finds:** the equivalent sweep on paired figures during [[A5]] turned up [[B8]], a genuine physics fault putting 105 of 420 bodies outside their own stated range. Three of this family are already known — [[A33]], [[B27]], [[B28]] — and they were each found by accident rather than by looking. **THE DURABLE HALF, and it is the point of doing this at all:** for every mismatch found, add a CONSISTENCY TEST rather than only fixing the label, because a fixed label drifts again the moment the underlying physics moves. The tests are cheap and concrete — for instance, no body with `surfaceRadiation` above a lethal threshold may carry `surface/irradiation: low`. That form of assertion, one per pair the audit finds, is what stops the whole family recurring. **Do NOT fix physics here.** If a tag is wrong because the quantity behind it is wrong, that is a new B item — write it up unnumbered and carry on. This audit changes labels, buckets and tests, not models. Related: [[B28]], [[A33]], [[B27]], [[A5]], [[B8]]. **DONE v2.1.366-beta. THE TABLE IS `docs/dev/tag-audit.md`** — every emission site, including the clean ones, so nobody re-derives it. **FIVE FINDINGS, four fixed as labels/buckets and one recorded as a model question.** **(1) `aurora/*` published a raw 0..1 float** — [[A35]]'s own named case, "Brilliant aurora: 0.78", a number on a scale nothing states. The tier is ALREADY in the key, so the value adds precision the renderer needs and nothing a reader can use: it is now suppressed for readers and kept in the data. **(2) `thermal/self-luminous` published a bare Kelvin figure** and **(3) `feature/polar-vortex` a bare count** — now `1,500 K` and `6-sided`. **(4) `volatiles/ices` packed a `+`-delimited list into one value** (`carbon-dioxide+nitrogen+water+methane`) — banned by the architecture doc's own idiom, and unreadable as a chip. Now one tag per species, which is the pattern the doc sanctions for a body that has several of a thing. **(5) THREE TAGS WERE EMITTED WITH NO REGISTRY ENTRY AT ALL** — `high-humidity`, `biosignature`, `exotic-biology` — so they reached a reader as bare title-cased words with no description. Worse, the last two fire on the SAME trigger for the SAME gas, so a world showed "Biosignature" beside "Exotic biology" with nothing to say they were one observation seen twice. Registered, and the descriptions now distinguish them. **THE DURABLE HALF — `src/lib/tags/tagConsistency.spec.ts`, five assertions over every bundled body:** no bare unitless number may reach a reader (either the presentation layer gives it a unit or suppresses it — a NEW numeric value with neither fails the suite); no delimited mini-format in a value; the hazard word must match the dose it claims to describe ([[B28]]'s example, generalised); and **every emitted key must be REGISTERED**, which is the assertion that caught finding (5) and would have caught it years ago. **The bodies are PROCESSED before auditing, not read out of the bundled JSON** — a stored starmap is a snapshot that may predate the current engine by many versions, so auditing it as-is audits history. **ONE EXISTING TEST WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED:** `save-roundtrip.test.ts` asserted that a tag KEY never appears twice on a body. The architecture doc explicitly sanctions the opposite ("Multiple tags may share a key where a body legitimately has several of a thing... dedupe by (key, species)"), and `structure/cloud-deck` has always done it — the assertion passed only because no test body had two of anything. Now keyed on (key, value), which is the invariant it meant. **RECORDED, NOT FIXED, because it is a model question and this audit does not change models:** `tidal/volcanism` (a tidal peak TEMPERATURE threshold in `surfaceTemperature.ts`) and `geology/volcanic-tidal` (the `deriveGeoActivity` REGIME) are two independent answers to "is this world tidally volcanic?". They agree today — Io is the only body carrying either and it carries both — but nothing enforces it, and [[B1]] is the precedent for what happens next. Also recorded: `atmosphere/breathable` is written once at generation and never re-derived, while `breathable-human` is a rule-pack trigger re-evaluated every pass, so editing a world's air updates one and not the other. Both are in the table. **NOT AUDITED, deliberately:** the provenance tags a concurrent session is adding on the manual-creation route (a new `spin/*` namespace appeared mid-sweep). Left alone; they should get the same one-question treatment when that lands. | fixed v2.1.366-beta — table at docs/dev/tag-audit.md |
| B30 | **Express the radiation hazard as TIME TO HARM, because that is what a non-technical GM can use.** Requested 2026-08-02, refining [[B28]] which had just landed. **Note first that the tag now EXISTS** — B28 (v2.1.357) added `hazard/radiation`, bucketed off `surfaceRadiation` so it carries the belt, gated to solid surfaces, and unified with `bodyFacts`, which had been bucketing the same quantity differently and calling Mars and Io both "high" sixty thousand times apart. Current values: `background` (<10 mSv/yr) · `elevated` (past the 20 mSv/yr occupational limit) · `high` (100-1000) · `severe` (to 1e5) · `lethal` (100 Sv/yr and up). Boundaries are real reference points, not round numbers. **THE ASK IS THAT THE VOCABULARY MAP ONTO SURVIVAL TIME** — extreme meaning minutes to hours, high meaning days — so a GM who does not read sieverts still knows what happens to a character standing there. **AND IT IS DERIVABLE, NOT A TABLE, which is the whole reason it is worth doing properly.** A median lethal acute dose is about 5 Sv, so time-to-LD50 is simply `5 Sv / dose rate`: Io 36 Sv/day gives about **3 hours**; Europa 3.8 Sv/day about 1.3 days; Ganymede 0.12 Sv/day about 40 days; Mars 214 mSv/yr about 23 years; Earth 2.3 mSv/yr about two thousand. One division on a figure the engine already holds, and the LD50 constant belongs in rule-pack DATA where a campaign can argue with it. **Where it should surface, in the order the request put them:** (1) improve the HOVER TEXT on the value in the data block — cheapest, no vocabulary change, and it can say the sentence outright ("a lethal dose in about three hours"). (2) Consider whether the TAG can carry it too — stated as "hard to bundle in a tag, although that would be ideal". It probably can: the tag value could stay a bucket word while the presentation layer renders the time beside it, or the bucket words themselves could be re-cut on survival-time boundaries rather than on dose boundaries. Decide which, and say why. **CAUTION — do not silently re-cut the buckets and leave the numbers behind.** The existing boundaries are anchored to real references (the occupational limit, Curiosity's Mars measurement); re-cutting on survival time must keep those anchors landing in sensible buckets, or a body's tag will move without its physics moving. Check every bundled body before and after. **Long-exposure honesty:** time-to-LD50 is an ACUTE model and is nonsense at background levels — "2,000 years" is arithmetic, not a prediction, because chronic low dose kills by cancer risk rather than by acute syndrome. Below some rate the phrasing must change to a chronic framing rather than quoting a number nobody will live to test. **PROPOSED VALUE, 2026-08-02: make the tag's value DAYS TO LETHALITY — "about 0.2 for Io" — and bucket anything beyond 50 YEARS as background, on the grounds that "it COULD kill you but so could many other things".** The arithmetic checks: 5 Sv / 36 Sv per day = 0.14 days, and 0.2 falls out of a slightly higher LD50, so the constant is the only thing to settle and it belongs in rule-pack data. The 50-year cut-off is a good boundary for exactly the reason given — it is where the acute model stops meaning anything and chronic risk takes over, which is the honest limit noted above. **ONE TENSION TO RESOLVE RATHER THAN IGNORE:** a raw number as a tag value is the fault [[A35]] flagged, and the architecture doc's own idiom is that continuous physics should be BUCKETED into tag values. **The synthesis that satisfies both: bucket names that are TIME WORDS** — `hours` / `days` / `weeks` / `months` / `background` — with the precise figure carried in the hover text and the data block. That is bucketed per the idiom and time-expressed per the request, and a GM reads "Radiation: days" without parsing anything. If a number really is wanted in the tag itself, say why and note that it makes [[A35]] a wont-fix rather than an oversight. Related: [[B28]], [[B20]], [[A33]], [[B29]], [[A35]]. **FIXED v2.1.359-beta. THE TENSION IS RESOLVED IN FAVOUR OF TIME WORDS, and [[A35]] stands — no raw float went into a tag value.** The bucket names ARE the survival time, derived (`LD50 / dose rate`) rather than tabulated, with the precise figure beside the dose in the data block. A GM reads "Radiation hazard: hours" and needs to parse nothing. **Why not days-to-lethality as the value, as proposed:** it is a continuous quantity, the architecture doc's idiom buckets those, and the number would have had to be read against an invisible scale (is 0.2 bad? is 40?) — which is the very thing this item exists to remove. The word does the work; the number is one line away for anyone who wants it. **THE LADDER, and it has SEVEN rungs rather than five because the honesty limit needs two of them:** `hours` (under a day) · `days` (under a week) · `weeks` (under a month) · `months` (under a year) · `years` (under 50) · `chronic` (past 50 years to an acute LD50, but above the 20 mSv/yr occupational limit — real long-term cancer risk, no acute threat) · `background` (at or below it). **THE ACUTE MODEL IS NOT ALLOWED TO SPEAK PAST 50 YEARS.** It describes radiation sickness, and "Earth: 2,000 years" is arithmetic rather than a prediction. Past that boundary the ladder stops quoting time and changes framing, and the spelled-out sentence in the data block is DROPPED entirely rather than printed — pinned by a test that Earth's row contains no "lethal dose" phrase at all. **BOTH ANCHORS SURVIVE THE RE-CUT, checked rather than assumed.** The 20 mSv/yr occupational limit is now the `chronic`/`background` line itself, so it is more load-bearing than before, not less. **Curiosity's Mars figure lands on `years` (~23)** — which is the honest framing anyway: a Mars surface dose is a mission-planning problem measured in years, not a thing that kills you on arrival. **EVERY BUNDLED BODY DIFFED, and the direction holds throughout:** Io `lethal` -> **`hours`** (~3.4 h), Europa `lethal` -> **`days`** (~1.3 d), Ganymede `severe` -> `months` (~40 d), Mimas `severe` -> `months`, Mercury/Enceladus `severe` -> `years`, Mars/Luna/Phobos/Deimos/Tethys `high` -> `years`, Callisto/Dione `elevated` -> `chronic`, Earth/Venus/Titan/Triton/Pluto unchanged at `background`. **Nothing numeric moved anywhere: 0 changed values across the whole fixture** — this is a vocabulary change and the diff proves it. **The LD50 constant is rule-pack DATA** (`generation_parameters.radiation_ld50_sv`, default 5 Sv), so a campaign can argue with it, and the info block's band and the tag both call one function so they cannot drift apart. **Left:** the ladder's floor is `hours` and does not distinguish Io's 3 hours from Jupiter-orbit's 9 minutes — deliberate, since "minutes to hours" was the requested reading for the extreme end and the figure is printed beside the word. | fixed v2.1.359-beta |
| B31 | **THE INVERSE AUDIT: what does the engine DERIVE that a GM would want, and that carries no tag at all?** Asked 2026-08-02 — "anything else we could add tags to that resides in data but could be in tags". **This is the mirror of [[B29]] and should be run by the same session in the same pass.** B29 asks "does every tag report the quantity its name claims"; this asks "what quantity deserves a tag and has not got one". Both are one sweep over the same ground and the answers inform each other. **The precedent is [[B28]], which was exactly this fault:** the gap was an ABSENCE — nothing anywhere carried the annual dose, so a GM filtering tags on Io saw "Space weathering: low" and no indication its surface takes 36 Sv a day. That fault is invisible to any audit that only inspects tags that exist. **Method:** enumerate the DERIVED fields on a processed body (the generated `tests/output/solar-system-derived.json` is the complete list, and it is regenerated on every vitest run so it cannot go stale), and for each ask two questions — would a GM act on this at the table, and is it reachable as a tag? Deliver a table of field / has-a-tag / should-it / verdict, covering the fields that are FINE as well as the gaps, so nobody re-derives it. **Candidates already visible, offered as a starting list rather than the answer:** `orbitalRadiation` and `beltInnerEdgeRadii` from [[B22]] (parking a ship is a real decision and nothing surfaces it); the ascent delta-v shown in the stat block (it decides whether a party can leave, and is arguably the single most actionable figure on a rocky world); `radiationShieldingAtmo` and `radiationShieldingMag` (they explain WHY a dose is what it is); the surface-radiation min/max range. **The discipline that keeps this from becoming tag soup:** a tag earns its place only if a GM would FILTER or DECIDE on it. Everything else belongs in the data block, and the standing rule about bucketing continuous physics applies to anything that does earn one. Say explicitly which candidates you rejected and why — a short rejected list is as valuable as the additions. Related: [[B29]], [[B28]], [[B22]], [[A35]]. **TABLE DELIVERED AND THE TWO CLEAR WINS BUILT, v2.1.359-beta. The rest is recorded below so nobody re-derives it.** **THE DISCIPLINE APPLIED:** a tag earns its place only if a GM would FILTER or DECIDE on it; an explainer belongs in the data block. **ADDED (2):** **`flight/ascent`** — bucketed `loDeltaVBudget_ms`, `trivial` (<2 km/s, a small craft hops off) · `moderate` (<5) · `hard` (<15) · `extreme`. Anchors: Luna 1.9 trivial, Mars 4.1 moderate, **Earth 10.4 hard**, Venus 29.5 extreme. It decides whether a party can leave, and it had no tag at all. **Emitted in PASS 4, not pass 3** — the budget is written in `processFlightDynamics`, so a tag in classification would have read the previous run's number, which is the whole of [[B13]]. Gated to solid surfaces ([[B18]]: there is nothing to ascend FROM on a giant). **`hazard/orbital-radiation`** — the same survival-time ladder for the space a ship parks in, **and only when it is NEWS**: the tag appears solely when its BUCKET WORD differs from the surface one. That gate matters — a naive "1.5x bigger" test gave Titan a second tag reading `background` beside a first reading `background`. Across all of Sol exactly **two bodies qualify: Earth (`background` on the ground, `days` in orbit — the Van Allen belts) and Venus (`background` / `years`)**, which is precisely the surprise worth surfacing. **REJECTED, with reasons — this list is the deliverable as much as the additions.** `beltInnerEdgeRadii`: a geometry figure in host radii; a GM decides "park high or low", and the thing they decide on is the orbital DOSE, which now has a tag. An input, not a decision. `radiationShieldingAtmo` / `radiationShieldingMag`: they explain WHY a dose is what it is, and the causes are already tagged in their own right (`magnetic/*`, atmospheric pressure). A GM filters on the outcome, not the mechanism. Data block. `surfaceRadiationMin/Max`: a variation, not a decision, and already printed inside the row it belongs to ([[A33]]'s rule). `calculatedGravity_ms2`: a genuine table decision, but "0.38 g" is already legible to anyone — the whole case for the radiation tags is that sieverts are NOT. Adding a tag would be tag soup for no legibility gain. `equilibriumTempK` / `temperatureRangeK` / `temperatureProfile`: tagged already, via the surface-temperature profile tags. `orbitalStability`, `geoActivity`, `volatiles`, `tidallyLocked`, `magnetism`, `habitabilityScore`, `hydrosphere.layers`: all ALREADY have tags (`stability/*`, `geology/*`, `volatiles/*`, `orbit/*`, `magnetic/*`, `habitability/*`, `structure/*`) — recorded as FINE so the next sweep does not re-open them. `albedoBreakdown`, `apparentColor`, `auroraEmitters`, `oblateness`, `classification`, `atmosphere.molarMassKg`, `atmosphere.scaleHeightKm`, `photonRadiation`/`particleRadiation`: appearance drivers and model internals. Not table decisions. **LEFT AS ARGUABLE for a later pass, deliberately not built:** `propulsiveLandBudget_ms` / `aerobrakeLandBudget_ms` (landing cost is as real a decision as ascent, but the two-number aerobrake-vs-propulsive choice does not bucket into one word without deciding which the GM means — that needs a call, not a threshold); and `orbitalBoundaries.minLeoKm` (where the lowest safe orbit sits — decision-shaped, but its units and its relationship to [[B22]]'s belt inner edge want settling together, which is [[B20]]'s job). **DERIVED DIFF: 24 bodies gain `flight/ascent`, 2 gain `hazard/orbital-radiation`, and ZERO numeric values moved.** | fixed v2.1.359-beta — table above, two additions built, rest recorded |
| B32 | **"How deep do I have to dig?" — derive the SHIELDING REQUIRED to bring a body's dose down to background.** Requested 2026-08-02 alongside [[B30]]: how far underground to not be hit, or how much aluminium/titanium hull thickness — **target explicitly stated as reaching BACKGROUND**. This is the most directly playable radiation figure yet proposed: it converts a dose a GM cannot act on into a decision a party makes ("you need two metres of regolith over the habitat"). **THE TARGET IS ALREADY DEFINED, so nothing needs inventing:** [[B28]] set `background` at under 10 mSv/yr. Required attenuation is therefore just `surfaceRadiation / 10 mSv/yr`. **AND THE MATHS IS ALREADY IN THE ENGINE, INVERTED.** `radiation.ts:318` computes `atmoTransmission = Math.exp(-shieldingScore * pressure_bar)` — an exponential attenuation against column depth. This item solves the same expression for the DEPTH instead of the dose, exactly as [[B21]]'s zone radius falls out of [[B17]]'s law. **Work in AREAL DENSITY (g/cm2) internally, present as THICKNESS per material.** Areal density is the physical quantity — it is why Earth is safe under about 1030 g/cm2 of air — and thickness is areal density divided by the material's density. Materials belong in rule-pack DATA (density, and any per-material effectiveness), so a campaign can add its own; note the bundled Sol campaign already writes of "Xenonite hull stock", which is precisely the case data-driven materials serve. Reference densities: regolith about 1.5-2.0, aluminium 2.7, titanium 4.5, water 1.0 g/cm3. **CALIBRATION ANCHOR, and it is a good one because it is independently documented:** Mars at 214 mSv/yr needs roughly a factor of 21, which against a GCR attenuation length of order 100 g/cm2 is about 300 g/cm2, or **roughly two metres of regolith** — which is what real martian habitat studies call for. If the model produces that for Mars it is behaving. Io then wants something like eight metres, and the gulf between those two numbers is the whole value of the feature. **THE PHYSICS TRAP, and a naive implementation WILL get it wrong: denser is not automatically better.** Against the energetic ELECTRONS that dominate a giant's belt, high-Z materials such as titanium or lead generate bremsstrahlung — secondary X-rays — so per unit mass they can shield WORSE than aluminium, and worse again than hydrogen-rich materials like water or polyethylene. Ranking materials by density alone would tell a GM to build Europa's shelter out of the worst available choice. Either carry a per-material effectiveness factor in the rule pack, or restrict the answer to hydrogen-rich and low-Z materials and say why. **Also note the answer differs by SOURCE**, which is an argument for doing this after [[B20]]: the depth needed against a stellar particle flux is not the depth needed against belt electrons, and a single number that averages them is a number for nowhere. **FRAMING, STATED BY THE REQUESTER AND IT SETS THE PRECISION BAR: "just handy guides, as radiation is tough to visualise."** This and [[B30]] are LEGIBILITY AIDS, not engineering calculations. Nobody is designing a real habitat from them; a GM is deciding whether the party can shelter here. So prefer the round and memorable to the precise — "about two metres of rock", "a lethal dose in hours" — and do not chase a second significant figure that costs clarity. **The one thing that precision licence does NOT excuse is being wrong in DIRECTION.** An approximate guide is fine; a backwards one is worse than none, because a GM will act on it. The titanium case above is exactly that: a "handy guide" that ranks materials by density would send a party to build Europa's shelter out of the worst thing available. Approximate freely, invert nothing. Related: [[B28]], [[B30]], [[B20]], [[B21]], [[B17]]. | captured |
| B33 | **A 751 C helium giant is tagged "Life-support resupply", "Water/ice refuelling" and "Water ice". Three tags, one missing gate.** Reported 2026-08-02 on Grolith — 112 Earth masses, 86.6 bar He/H2 envelope, 751 C mean surface, `planet/helium`. **VERIFIED, all three rules live in `physics/reasonsToVisit.ts`.** `frontier/life-support` (`:121`) fires on `hasO2` OR (`hydro === 'water'` AND `hasAtmo`); `frontier/fuel-depot` (`:119`) on `makeup.ice >= 0.2` OR `hydro === 'water'`; `resource/water-ice` (`:98`) on `hydro === 'water'` OR `hydroCover >= 0.1` OR `makeup.ice >= 0.3` OR the icy-shell tag. A giant has an atmosphere by definition and enough ice in its bulk makeup to clear those thresholds, so all three fire. **THE COMMON FAULT: these rules describe SURFACE-ACCESSIBLE resources but test BULK COMPOSITION, with no gate on whether the material is reachable or in a usable phase.** Water in a 751 C, 86.6 bar helium envelope is supercritical vapour mixed through a planet-sized atmosphere; it is not ice, not a lake, and not something a ship scoops on the way past. **THE FIX IS ALREADY HALF-BUILT AND IT IS THE ELEGANT PART: `isGiant` EXISTS AS A RULE FIELD** (`:55`, "Gas/ice giant (or gas fraction >= 0.4)") and is used POSITIVELY by `resource/helium-3` (`:95`) and `frontier/gas-skimming` (`:120`), both of which correctly REQUIRE it. **No rule anywhere EXCLUDES giants**, so every surface-oriented rule fires on one. Adding that exclusion to the surface-resource and surface-frontier rules is a small, uniform change against a field that already exists — and Grolith keeps "Gas-giant refuelling" and "Helium-3", which are right. **A SECOND, MORE GENERAL GATE WORTH CONSIDERING, because it catches cases `isGiant` will not:** a `frontier/*` tag is a claim that somewhere is worth STOPPING AT, and the same panel already prints the counter-argument — Grolith's surface-to-low-orbit budget is **52.3 km/s**. A place you cannot practically land on and leave is not a resupply stop whatever it contains, and that delta-v is already derived. Gating frontier tags on it would also catch dense non-giants that `isGiant` misses. **CHECK THE WHOLE `frontier/*` AND `resource/*` FAMILY, not just these three** — the same bulk-composition-versus-accessibility confusion will be in others. **Note the deliberate history on `resource/water-ice`:** its comment records that it "was wrongly capped to frozen worlds <250K", so a temperature cap was REMOVED on purpose to let liquid-water worlds yield ice. That removal was probably right; do not simply reinstate a cap. The missing test is accessibility and phase, not temperature alone. **THIS IS A LIVE FIND FOR [[B29]]** — `reasonsToVisit.ts` is one of the 41 tag-emission sites that audit covers, and this is precisely the question it asks. Route it there. Related: [[B29]], [[B4]], [[B18]], [[B22]]. **FIXED v2.1.368-beta.** **Swept the whole family as asked, by running the tagger over all 366 bundled bodies and listing what fires on the 59 with no surface.** THREE MORE were wrong for the same reason — `resource/heavy-metals`, `resource/exotic-crystals` and `resource/organics` are mining and farming claims — and `platinum-group`, `rare-earths`, `fissiles` and `diamonds` are the same shape and would fire on the right giant. **All ten are now gated.** What a giant KEEPS was checked rather than assumed: helium-3, gas-skimming, deuterium, aerobraking and gravity-assist are byte-identical before and after. **Before, across the 59 surfaceless bodies: fuel-depot 18, water-ice 15, life-support 1 — 34 false claims. After: zero, with all 159 legitimate water-ice tags on surfaced bodies untouched.** **WHICH GATE — NEITHER OF THE TWO THIS ENTRY PROPOSED, and both were measured before being rejected.** (a) `isGiant` reads well but is "classes include a giant type OR gas ≥ 0.4", and the bundled data holds bodies carrying BOTH a rocky and a giant class — `planet/desert + planet/cloudless-gas-giant` at gas 0.00, `planet/ice + planet/ice-giant` at gas 0.00 — so gating on it would strip surface resources from bodies whose own composition says they have a surface. (b) **The delta-v gate is the better IDEA — accessibility is exactly the concept these rules are missing — but it cannot do THIS job**, because for a body with no surface the figure is derived at the notional 1-bar radius and is as fictional as the surface gravity [[B18]] found there. So every imported or generated system prints the pass-1 figure until something edits it. **This is also why the fixture never saw it: `stripDerivedData` in `physics-baseline.test.ts` does not strip `scaleHeightKm`,** so the fixture's Earth is a world that has already been through the atmosphere pass, and the test's one pass is really a pass 2 for that quantity. **(d) THE FULL READ-BEFORE-WRITE SET, swept rather than assumed.** Four edges, not one: own `magneticField` (pass 2 reads, pass 3 writes); own `atmosphere.scaleHeightKm` (same pass, 58 lines late); the HOST's `magneticField` / `rotation_period_hours` / `scaleHeightKm` via the belt term, which additionally depends on NODE ORDER since a moon can be processed before its host; and `insideHostMagnetosphere` reading the host's derived field inside pass 3 with the same order dependence. **(e) A SECOND, UNRELATED NON-IDEMPOTENCE FOUND IN THE SWEEP, and it never converges at all: `processBarycenters`' binary coupling has a LIMIT CYCLE of period 2 in `omega_deg`.** `SystemProcessor.ts:277-278` assigns `m0.omega = ref.omega` and `m1.omega = ref.omega + 180` — but when `m1` IS the reference (it is heavier, or more recently edited) the reference member flips its OWN argument of periapsis by 180 degrees every pass, forever. It is genuine `process()` non-idempotence and it blocks any idempotence test on the Local Neighbourhood, so it is fixed here rather than deferred. **FIXED v2.1.356-beta.** **SEVEN read-before-write edges, not one, and the entry above named only the smallest of them.** Each is the same shape — a value read in one pass and written in a later one — and they are listed in the order they bite. **(1) RADIATION IS NOW ITS OWN PASS, 2c**, after every body has its field, its spin and its scale height. It used to sit in the middle of pass 2. **(2) FLUID LAYERS AND MAGNETISM ARE NOW PASS 2b**, moved out of `processClassification`, and iterated **PARENT BEFORE CHILD** — a moon's induced field asks its host whether it sits inside a magnetosphere, and the belt term asks the host for its field and spin, so in node order both answers depended on where the host happened to sit in the file. **(3) TIDAL LOCKING MOVES ABOVE THE THERMAL SOLVE.** The solve's temperature profile reads `tidallyLocked` and the rotation period and they were written after it; nothing in the lock assessment is thermal (despinning is mass, radius, distance and age), so this is a stale read removed with no circularity created. **(4) GEOLOGY MOVES ABOVE THE WEATHER.** `deriveWeather`'s lightning term reads `geology/plate-tectonics` and `tidal/volcanism` as its convection driver, and the geology block emitted them *afterwards* — so Earth's sky read "frequent lightning" on a fresh load and "constant" on every pass after. **(5) `estimateInternalHeatK` ASKED `body.classes` FOR THE WORD "ice-giant".** The classifier runs a whole pass later and reads the temperature this figure produces — a class name used as a physics input, which is the architecture rule inverted. It now uses the same mass split the interior model already uses (`GIANT_METALLIC_HYDROGEN_MIN_MASS_ME`, exported from `fluidLayers.ts` so there is one home for it). **(6) BARYCENTRE EFFECTIVE MASSES ARE COMPUTED DEEPEST-FIRST**, in their own pre-pass. Alpha Centauri lists its OUTER barycentre first, so on a fresh load the system barycentre summed Proxima plus a stale AB total — **2.43e29 against the true 4.20e30** — which moved every orbit in the system and flipped both primaries from no stability verdict at all to "Very Unstable" on the second pass. The pre-pass also breaks the genuine circularity in doing it in one loop: an inner barycentre needs its parent's mass for its own orbit while the parent needs the inner one's mass for its total. **(7) THE `omega_deg` LIMIT CYCLE**, above. Plus a `settled()` guard on the barycentre split: separation is the SUM of the members' semi-major axes and each axis is then re-derived from that sum, and in double precision that round trip lands one unit in the last place from where it started on every pass, for ever. Nothing physical moves and the number never settles, which is enough on its own. One duplicate writer was removed rather than guarded: a barycentre that is a MEMBER of another had its mean motion written twice, once from its own semi-major axis and once from the pair's separation, two formulas one ulp apart with whichever ran last winning (Algol). **WHY THIS DOES NOT REINTRODUCE THE v2.1.282 LAG, stated plainly because it was the gate.** Nothing was dragged backwards across the thermal solve. Magnetism moved DOWN the pipeline (pass 3 -> 2b), not up; `teqK` did not move at all; the lock moved up but it is not thermal in either direction. The solve still runs before everything that reads its output. **THE ONE EDGE LEFT, AND WHY IT COULD NOT BE ORDERED AWAY.** `applyAtmosphericEscape` reads `magneticField` for its shielding term, and it runs inside pass 2a — before magnetism is derived in 2b. Magnetism cannot move ahead of it, because `deriveFluidLayers` reads the composed surface temperature and `deriveMagnetism` reads `equilibriumTempK`, both of which the solve produces, and escape rewrites the atmosphere the solve reads. That is a real circle: field -> escape -> atmosphere -> thermal -> temperature -> fluid layers -> field. It is NOT closed here. It is opt-in (`evolveAtmosphere`), no bundled body in Sol, either starmap or any example carries the flag, and the physics baseline's own Mars-aging idempotence check still passes because Mars's field is 0 on both passes. Worth knowing: the field's thermal dependency is only the giant helium-rain factor and the induced-ocean case, so for a rocky world with air to lose the field is a pure function of makeup, mass and spin — but a magnetism that is derived early for some bodies and late for others would be two evaluations of one question, which is precisely what the architecture rule forbids. Left as a single evaluation with the residual documented. **THE TEST: `src/lib/system/idempotence.test.ts`.** Process, process the result, process that — and require that nothing anywhere on any body changed, comparing pass 1 against 2 AND 2 against 3 (one comparison alone would have called the `omega_deg` oscillation stable). Five cases: bundled Sol, **bundled Sol through `fixUpImportedSystem`** (the path the campaign actually took), both bundled starmaps, and every shipped example system. It went in RED, on 231 fields, in its own commit ahead of the fix. **THE ANCHORS, AFTER THE FIX.** Earth **2.29897 mSv/yr** (real background ~2.4) — unmoved to five significant figures; Mars **213.692** (Curiosity RAD ~210) — unmoved exactly; Venus 2.000, Luna 512.38, Titan 2.0002, Triton 2.566 — all unmoved. **Io 13,139 Sv/yr = 36.00 Sv/day against B17's 36 anchor, where it read 34.9 before — the fix put B17's own calibration back on its target.** The 3% was the belt evaluating **Jupiter's AUTHORED 4.28 G** while B17 calibrated against the **DERIVED 4.32**: dose goes as B² and the scale length as B^(1/3), which compounds to +3.05%. **Ganymede 45.05 Sv/yr = 0.1234 Sv/day, exactly the pure-law figure B17 quotes and exactly the 1.54x over-prediction it designed for** — which CLOSES B17's open item (a), "Ganymede's authored 0.007 G is overwritten by `deriveMagnetism`'s 0, yet `radiationShieldingMag` reads 0.0768... Left for B13". Europa 1,403.7 Sv/yr (3.85 Sv/day against a measured 5.4, ratio 0.71 where B17 had 0.76); Callisto 38.81 mSv/yr of belt = 1.06e-4 Sv/day against its 1e-4 anchor, 6% high — the one anchor that moved AWAY, and by the same B_ref correction, so B17's two-point fit should be re-derived at 4.32 if that 6% is ever worth closing. Mercury 3,483.6, Enceladus 2,027.1, Jupiter 11.46 / Saturn 5.086 / Uranus 2.665 / Neptune 2.275 at their 1-bar levels — sane ordering throughout. **THE DERIVED DIFF: 26 bodies in Sol, radiation figures and their habitability knock-ons, plus FOUR tag values. No temperature, no classification, no makeup, no orbit and no magnetic field moved anywhere in Sol.** **TAGS CHASED, as the standing rule requires.** Checked: `surface/irradiation` (buckets `irradiationDose`, which moved on 2 Sol bodies — neither crossed a bucket edge); `aurora/*` (reads the field and the dose — the TIER held on all three giants, only the strength VALUE moved, Saturn 0.25->0.26, Uranus 0.26->0.25, Neptune 0.22->0.26); `magnetic/*` (emitted in 2b now, and nothing after strips it); `habitability/*` (radiation is a habitability factor — Ariel is the only score to move, 0 -> 1.48); `weather/lightning` (Earth frequent -> constant, which is the CORRECTION: Earth has plate tectonics and the driver was simply being read too early). Deliberately left: `geology/*`, `surface/age`, `structure/cloud-deck`, `volatiles/*` in Sol — none moved. **THE ONE PLACE PHYSICS GENUINELY CHANGED, measured against a reverted build rather than reasoned: the ice-giant split moves 12 bodies, ALL of them in `static/examples`, NONE in Sol and none in either bundled starmap.** They are mini-Neptunes, hycean and sub-Neptune worlds between 1.3 and 35.6 Earth masses that were being handed **Jupiter's formation heat** — 52 K against the ice giant's 24 K — because their class string did not happen to contain the characters "ice-giant". Internal heat falls by 54% and surface temperature by 4 to 28 K (TRAPPIST-1 g 230.4 -> 208.4 K, Proxima Centauri c 86.8 -> 59.5 K, Testion's "ice giant" 124.0 -> 103.1 K). **No class moved and exactly one tag moved** — Proxima Centauri c gains nitrogen to its retained ices, correctly, being 27 K colder. **NOT DONE, said plainly.** (a) The `evolveAtmosphere` escape edge above. (b) `processEnvironment` still ends with a dead `retainsAtmosphere` local that reads the field; it is unused so it cannot cause drift, and it was left rather than widen the diff. (c) [[B5]] is still gated — this establishes the pattern it asked for (a derivation moved across a pass boundary with an idempotence test to prove it), but B5's move is UP across the thermal solve and this one was DOWN, which is the easy direction. | fixed v2.1.356-beta |
