| D14 | **Pluto and Charon are authored with the BARYCENTRE's heliocentric inclination instead of their own mutual orbit's, so the model has them eclipsing every orbit when really they do so twice in 248 years.** Found 2026-08-03 when [[G8]] began answering for barycentre partners. Both members carry `i_deg` 17.16 - which is Pluto's orbital inclination to the ECLIPTIC, the barycentre's own number, copied down onto them. Their mutual orbit is really inclined about 119 deg to the ecliptic, because that is Pluto's obliquity and Charon orbits in its equator. **The consequence is real and it is in the app, not just in a prediction:** with a 17 deg plane the pair sit permanently lined up with the Sun, so the eclipse row reads "every 5 d - total", where the truth is that mutual events happen only in seasons around Pluto's equinoxes - the famous 1985-1990 run, which is how Charon's radius was measured, and the next is not due until the 2100s. **This is DATA, not the engine**, which faithfully answers what it is told. It is also the one case [[C3]]'s rule cannot express, since barycentre members are system-framed by design and must not inherit a partner's tilt. **The fix belongs in `scripts/starmap-build/`**, and read [[D4]] before touching it: the kit can no longer simply be re-run. Whoever takes it should decide whether a barycentre member wants its own `orbit.frame` declaration - the same lever [[C3]] reached for, which does not exist for this case. Related: [[C3]], [[G8]], [[D3]], [[D4]]. **FIXED v2.1.510-beta, and the ECCENTRICITY was copied too - this entry only spotted the inclination.** Both members carried the barycentre's heliocentric `e` of 0.2488 as well as its `i_deg` of 17.16; the mutual orbit is very nearly circular, because the pair is doubly synchronous. Corrected in `static/examples/Sol_2030-System.json` (the kit's Sol input, per [[D4d]]) to `e: 0.0002` and `i_deg: 112.78`, and both bundled maps regenerated. **THE NUMBER IN THIS ENTRY IS WRONG AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT: it is 112.78, not 119.** 119.591 deg is Pluto's OBLIQUITY, referenced to Pluto's own orbital plane; the mutual orbit's inclination to the ECLIPTIC is 112.783 deg, and the ecliptic is the frame this field is in - Earth is authored `i_deg: 0` in the same file, so Sol's system plane IS the ecliptic. The two differ by about Pluto's own 17 deg orbital inclination, which is precisely the quantity the copy fault was about, so taking 119 would have re-introduced a smaller version of the same error. **MEASURED BEFORE AND AFTER, and the predicted consequence is confirmed:** the eclipse row read `every 6 d - total (Charon)`, with `everyOrbit: true` and no date at all; it now returns a DATED event with `everyOrbit: false`. Walking the predictor forward 550 years finds **five seasons - 2089-2093, 2214-2215, 2337-2341, 2462-2463, 2585 - spaced 123 to 125 years apart**, i.e. twice per 248-year orbit, each lasting one to four years and holding 80-230 events. That is the real behaviour, including the multi-year run that made Charon's radius measurable. **STILL OPEN, DELIBERATELY: the EPOCH is not anchored.** `Omega_deg` is 0 on both members, so the line of nodes is unauthored and the seasons land in the right PATTERN at the wrong DATES - the model's nearest is 2089 where the real run was 1985-1990 and the next is due around the 2100s. Two ways to close it, both wanting a decision: author Charon's published node (about 223 deg, ecliptic J2000), or SOLVE for the `Omega_deg` that puts a season on the known 1985-1990 run. Neither makes this an ephemeris - `eclipses.ts` says in its own header that it holds elements fixed and does not precess nodes. **THE `orbit.frame` QUESTION IS ANSWERED AND THE ANSWER IS NO NEW SCHEMA.** `satelliteTiltRad` already returns 0 whenever the parent is not a body, so a barycentre member is unconditionally system-framed and the lever would have nothing to switch. What was missing is not a declaration but a GUARD, and this fault has a mechanical fingerprint: a member whose `e` and `i_deg` are identical to its own barycentre's. That assertion belongs in [[D9]]'s invariant test. **SIDE EFFECT FOUND AND NOT FIXED - see the unnumbered seasonal-eccentricity finding below**, which is why Pluto's total temperature range moves from 6-66 K to 7-65 K here. | **fixed v2.1.510-beta - epoch not anchored, see the Omega note** |
| E2 | **Sessions share one git INDEX as well as one working tree, so `git add` followed by `git commit` is not atomic and one session's staged work lands in another's commit.** Observed three times on 2026-08-03 between the scene/grids stream and two others. Twice it went one way — a [[G9]] inbox entry and the whole of [[G10]] (eleven files, `niceInterval.ts`, the metric grid, the 43x ring-label fix) were swept into commits titled "docs(inbox): D6 sharpened..." and "Real-sky import phase 1..." — and once the other, when a concurrent inbox edit was carried into a [[G8]] commit. **NOTHING WAS LOST ANY OF THE THREE TIMES**, which is exactly why it is worth writing down: the failure is silent, the work is committed and pushed under a message that does not describe it, and the only symptom is `git commit` reporting "no changes added to commit" to the session that staged them. **The consequence is not corruption but ARCHAEOLOGY** — `git log -- <file>` and `git blame` now point at the wrong intent, and a future session reading "why did this change" is misled. It also breaks commit-per-item, which exists so one bad call can be rewound alone. **Cheap mitigations, in order of cost:** stage and commit in ONE shell invocation rather than two tool calls, so the window is milliseconds rather than minutes; check `git log -1 --stat` after committing rather than trusting the push result, which is the standing rule for the changelog already and should be generalised; and for anything larger, a session-per-worktree (`git worktree add`) removes the shared index entirely, which is the real fix if five streams are now normal. Related: the coordination rules above, which cover numbering, debt and duplication but not this. **CLOSED v2.1.411-beta: the worktree-per-session recipe is written into the standing rules above, and was proved by using it.** The whole of C9, E3 and this edit were done in `../sse2-frame-hygiene` on branch `wt/frame-hygiene`, pushed with `git push origin HEAD:beta`. A worktree closes BOTH races at once - its own index and its own working tree - and as a bonus each one regenerates its own `tests/output/solar-system-derived.json`, so a before/after diff finally means something. Two frictions found and written into the recipe: `beta` cannot be checked out twice (use `-b wt/<name> beta`, push `HEAD:beta`), and **do not junction `node_modules`** - it half-works, which is worse than not working. Also recorded: `npm ci` is ten seconds here, and the preview server needs its own port in `C:\Development\.claude\launch.json`. | closed v2.1.411-beta |

| B37 | **A belt carries an ascent Δv budget derived from a mass that is not a mass.** Found 2026-08-03 while sorting what legitimately applies to a belt for [[B11]]. `loDeltaVBudget_ms` is computed for belts and rings and shows in the info block as "Ascent Δv" — but a belt's `massKg` is a DEBRIS-DENSITY PROXY, not gravitational mass: `scripts/starmap-build/build-starmaps.mjs` sets it via `densityProxyMassKg()` and says so ("NOT gravitational mass (excluded from perturbers)"), and [[B19]]'s stability work excludes belts from gravitational pairing for the same reason. So the figure is an escape-velocity calculation on a number that was never a mass, for a body you cannot stand on to ascend from. **The `flight/ascent` TAG is correctly absent** — it is emitted inside the gated pass — so this is the value and the info-block row, not the tag. **Decide which of the two B26 readings applies**, exactly as that entry framed it: either a belt's Δv is meaningless like a giant's habitability and should be withheld, or it means "ascent from a typical fragment" and needs a fragment mass rather than the belt's proxy. **Do not simply hide the row** without answering that — the same choice was got right for the radiation figure by asking it explicitly. Related: [[B11]], [[B26]], [[B18]], [[B19]]. | **FIXED v2.1.886-beta - and THE ROW'S CAUSE IS WRONG, though its REASONING is right.** `loDeltaVBudget_ms` is NOT computed for belts: `calculateDeltaVBudgets` already returns early for anything that is not a planet or moon and writes **-1 as a not-applicable sentinel**. The fault is downstream and wider - **-1 is truthy**, and of four consumers two tested it that way (`bodyFacts.ts`, `ReportDocument.svelte`), so every belt and ring published **"Ascent Dv -0.0 km/s"**; `BodyTechnicalDetails.svelte` printed **"-1.0 m/s"**; and only the `flight/ascent` tag gated properly. **SO THE SAME ROW WAS ALSO LYING ABOUT GIANTS** - measured, Jupiter published 50.3 km/s while the tag beside it correctly said nothing, which is [[B18]]'s category error reaching a surface B18 did not. Worse, the panel's giant guard was a `classes` regex on "gas-giant", so URANUS AND NEPTUNE fell through it - the B11 class-regex fault alive in a copy. **FIX: one predicate, `orbits.ts ascentBudgetApplies`, and all four consumers now ask it** (the tag's own gate was the correct one, so it is the one they share). **THE B26 QUESTION IS ANSWERED: WITHHELD, not a fragment figure** - a belt's mass is a debris-density proxy (PHY-13) so escape velocity on it is arithmetic on a non-mass, and "ascent from a typical fragment" would mean INVENTING a body (the fragment has no radius, mass or gravity in the data) and reporting its figure as the belt's; a GM who wants that adds the asteroid and gets a real one. **NOT hidden** - the row stays and says *"not applicable - debris spread round an orbit, with no surface to leave"*, because a vanished row reads as a bug. **TAIL FOUND AND FIXED:** the row used a fixed km/s field, so Phobos (9 m/s) and Deimos (5 m/s) both read "0.0 km/s", which reads as free; now magnitude-aware via the existing `formatSpeedAuto`. Sol fixture unmoved. Engine map PHY-22; `physics/ascentApplicability.spec.ts` pins all of it. |

That trend IS the Kraft relation (1967) — specific angular momentum scaling with mass — and the sharp step at F5 is the braking switching off, not the birth angular momentum changing. **Below the break, mass enters through gyrochronology's colour term rather than separately: at a FIXED age, redder means longer period.** At roughly Solar age, G2 is ~25 d, K is ~35-40 d, and M runs to ~70-130 d. Overload remains possible but should be measured rather than assumed. **TWO HYPOTHESES WORTH THE NAME, each with the instrument that separates them — do not reason further without one of these.** **(1) THE CAMERA'S USER OFFSET IS BEING CANCELLED BY A CONTINUOUSLY REWRITTEN BASE.** This is RENDER-S12's exact subject — the camera is a BASE the system writes plus an OFFSET only the user writes — and the camera work already paid for three faults in this family (a re-frame reading its own motion back as user input and cancelling itself; a floating-origin rebase failing to move the rig's remembered shot; the camera being read when the user had not touched it). **If `setSystem` is storming, the base is rewritten repeatedly and user input is swallowed** — and [[P1]] measured exactly that storm, four full rebuilds in five seconds (RENDER-S22). **Instruments: `window.__camDebug = true` reports the shot, the chosen ladder level, the actual distance, whether the drive is armed, and `targetDrift`; `?perf=1` gives `holo.setSystem.same`, the wasted-rebuild count.** **(2) AN EXCEPTION KILLED THE ANIMATION LOOP.** "Lags, then nothing responds, refresh fixes it" is the textbook signature — the last frame stays painted while the loop is dead and handlers no longer fire. **RENDER-S7 exists for this family: never swallow an exception on the path that decides whether a thing renders.** Instrument: the console **AT THE MOMENT OF FAILURE**, which is precisely what was not captured. **WHAT TO ASK THE USER FOR, AND NOTE THE APP WAS BUILT FOR THIS EXACT SITUATION: the DIAGNOSTIC BUNDLE (Settings -> System -> "Reporting a problem") — shipped v2.1.489 because "a load hang is the one fault a user CANNOT usefully report".** `report.json` is the first thing to read. Also worth requesting: the console captured while it is stuck rather than after, `?perf=1` on the URL for the `[sse-perf]` line, and `window.__camDebug = true` set before it fails. **LIKELY ROOT CAUSE FOUND, 2026-08-13 — READ THIS FIRST; EVERYTHING BELOW IS THE TRAIL THAT LED HERE. THE RIG RECOGNISES A ZOOM ONLY FROM THE MOUSE WHEEL, AND A TOUCH PINCH FIRES NO WHEEL EVENT.** Narrowed by the owner to: renderer fine, rings still turning, **the map still TILTS in the last frames — so rotate works — and it is specifically PINCH ZOOM that fails, on mobile only.** That combination is diagnostic, because rotate and zoom are detected by two different listeners. **THE EVIDENCE, at `src/lib/holo/scene.ts:2052-2061`. The comment says one thing and the code does another:**
```
// The user driving zoom (wheel / pinch) takes the camera off auto-framing ...
canvas.addEventListener('wheel', (e) => {
  noteUserInput('wheel', Math.sign((e as WheelEvent).deltaY || 0));
  reframing = false;      // touching the zoom hands the camera over NOW; deriveOffset reads it
}, { passive: true, ... });
```
**The comment claims "wheel / pinch". The only listener is `wheel`. A touch pinch does not fire a `wheel` event** — it arrives as multiple pointers and OrbitControls consumes it as a dolly. Meanwhile the `pointermove` handler at `:2042-2051` notes the input as **`'drag'`**, which is the rotate kind, not the zoom kind. **So on a pinch, OrbitControls moves the camera in, the rig is never told a ZOOM happened, and its base/offset reconciliation puts the distance back — RENDER-S12's exact mechanism, and the same fault family the camera work already paid for three times** (a re-frame reading its own motion back as user input and cancelling itself; the camera being read when the user had not touched it). **A COMMIT MESSAGE FROM THAT VERY WORK STATES THE BUG OUT LOUD: `29362d9` "Zoom comes from the wheel alone; a drag rotates and nothing else."** That was correct for a mouse and silently excludes every touch device. **IT EXPLAINS EVERY SYMPTOM WITHOUT STRAIN:** mobile-only, because a laptop zooms with the wheel, which IS handled; pinch dead but tilt alive, because drag IS detected; renderer healthy throughout; and no exception anywhere, because nothing is broken — the camera is being politely corrected. **HONEST LIMIT ON THIS CLAIM: I read the LISTENERS, not `noteUserInput` or `deriveOffset`.** The final step — that the un-noted pinch is actually undone rather than merely un-flagged — is inferred from RENDER-S12's model and that commit message, and **must be confirmed in those two functions before anyone writes a fix.** `window.__camDebug = true` on a touch device, pinching, is the direct test: watch whether the distance changes and is then pulled back. **The likely fix is small — teach the rig that a multi-pointer gesture is a ZOOM, alongside the wheel — but it belongs to the Ship Model Handoff session, whose file this is and who holds RENDER-S12.**

**HYPOTHESIS (3) IS REFUTED BY THE VIDEO — READ THIS BEFORE THE PARAGRAPH BELOW IT, WHICH IS KEPT ONLY AS A RECORD OF A WRONG TURN.** The owner, watching the recording: **the orbit rings ARE STILL MOVING, slowly, AFTER the failure, while pan and zoom do nothing.** (Confirmed explicitly when asked — the motion is post-event, not before it.) **SO "CRASH" IS THE WRONG WORD AND IT HAS ALREADY SENT THIS INVESTIGATION DOWN ONE BLIND ALLEY: nothing has crashed.** The render loop survives the event and keeps producing frames; only the CONTROLS stop responding. Anyone picking this up should stop looking for exceptions, context loss or a dead rAF loop — all three are excluded by moving rings. That kills WebGL context loss outright — **a lost context repaints NOTHING, so anything still animating proves the render loop is alive and producing frames.** It equally kills hypothesis (2), a thrown exception killing the animation loop, for the same reason. **So the picture is NOT frozen; only the CONTROLS are dead.** That puts hypothesis (1) — the camera's user offset being cancelled by a continuously rewritten base, RENDER-S12's exact subject — back at the top, alongside a new and simpler candidate: **the app is ALIVE BUT SO SLOW that input is processed and the next frame is seconds away, which is indistinguishable from dead controls.** That second reading unifies the whole report with something already measured: [[P1]] clocked `holo.setSystem` at **four full scene rebuilds in five seconds** on a desktop (RENDER-S22). On a phone, with far less headroom, the same storm would drop the frame rate to a fraction of that — "lags when rendering" is the storm building, "can't zoom" is a frame rate near zero, "a refresh fixes it" is the storm not yet re-established, and "laptop is fine" is simply more headroom. **THE ONE OBSERVATION THAT DISCRIMINATES BETWEEN THE TWO, AND IT CAN BE TAKEN FROM THE VIDEO WE ALREADY HAVE WITHOUT GOING BACK TO THE USER: do the rings move SMOOTHLY but slowly, or in visible JERKS/STEPS?** Smooth-but-slow means the frame rate is healthy and the CLOCK is simply at a low rate — so rendering is fine and the fault is in the camera/input path (hypothesis 1). Jerky or stepping means a very low FRAME RATE — the app is drowning, and this is the P1 storm arriving on a device that cannot absorb it. **Watch for that first; it decides which of the two sessions this belongs to.** `?perf=1` settles it definitively, since the `[sse-perf]` line prints the frame rate alongside `holo.setSystem.same`.

**SUPERSEDED, KEPT AS A RECORD — the mobile-only reasoning below led to WebGL context loss, which the video refutes. The observation that the app has NO context-loss listeners is still true and still worth fixing as an instrument, but it is no longer the leading explanation.** "IT WORKS ON A LAPTOP BUT NOT ON MOBILE DEVICES". THE OWNER WAS TEMPTED TO CALL THAT NOISE. IT IS NOT — IT IS THE STRONGEST CLUE IN THE REPORT, AND IT PROMOTES A THIRD HYPOTHESIS ABOVE BOTH OF THE ABOVE.** **(3) WEBGL CONTEXT LOSS, and it fits EVERY symptom without strain.** Mobile GPUs drop the WebGL context under memory pressure; desktops almost never do. When it happens the canvas **keeps displaying the last rendered frame**, the render loop stops producing new ones, and **a page refresh creates a fresh context** — which is precisely "it lags while rendering, then I can't zoom, and a refresh fixes it", including the device split. **THE DETAIL THAT MAKES IT FIT BETTER THAN AN INPUT FAULT: if the context is lost, the user's pinch-zoom IS still being received — the scene simply never repaints. So "I can't zoom" and "the picture is frozen" are INDISTINGUISHABLE to the user**, and the report would read exactly as it does. Do not assume the input layer is at fault just because input is what the user noticed. **AND WE ARE COMPLETELY BLIND TO IT — VERIFIED, NOT ASSUMED: a grep of `src/` for `webglcontextlost` / `webglcontextrestored` / `loseContext` returns NOTHING** (the `closeContextMenu` hits are the right-click menu). So if this is the cause, it has been happening silently and would never appear in any console log or diagnostic bundle we have asked for. **THE CHEAP FIX IS AN INSTRUMENT, NOT A REPAIR, AND IT SHOULD COME FIRST: add `webglcontextlost` and `webglcontextrestored` listeners on the holo canvas.** That converts an unreportable freeze into a logged event, feeds it into `[sse-perf]` and the diagnostic bundle, and lets the app tell the user "graphics restarted" rather than appearing broken — three-ish lines for the listener, and the honest repair (rebuild the scene on restore) can follow once we know it is real. **This is also consistent with the project's demonstrated history rather than a fresh guess: mobile resource pressure is a PROVEN failure mode here** — [[P1]] began with a low-end mobile that could not load at all, and the memory watch exists because the app hit out-of-memory in a live session. **WHAT THE DEVICE SPLIT ALSO DOES IS DISCRIMINATE BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO HYPOTHESES:** a continuously-rewritten camera base (1) would be device-INDEPENDENT and should fail on the laptop too, so mobile-only argues against it; an exception or a dead loop (2) is resource-sensitive and stays live. **One secondary mobile-only path worth knowing but ranking below context loss: pinch/drag on the player view goes through three.js OrbitControls** (`HoloView.svelte:177`, `touch-action: none; /* let OrbitControls own pinch/drag */`), a different input path from the laptop's wheel-and-drag. Plausible, but OrbitControls' touch handling is mature and widely used, and it would not explain the lag that precedes the freeze. **Territory: the Ship Model Handoff session owns camera/framing and `holo/scene.ts`, and holds RENDER-S12 and S19.** **The coordinator deliberately did NOT add the context-loss listener — `holo/scene.ts` is that session's hot file and this board has recorded four working-tree sweeps.** Related: [[P1]], RENDER-S7, RENDER-S12, RENDER-S22, the open `liquids.json` 404 finding, `docs/dev/debug-tools.md`. **CONFIRMED IN CODE AND FIXED v2.1.549-beta - the coordinator's inference was RIGHT, and the un-noted pinch was genuinely UNDONE rather than merely un-flagged.** Verified in the two functions the trail said to check. `noteUserInput` only records a kind; the reversion is at `holo/scene.ts` in the frame loop: `if (lastInput.kind !== 'wheel' || nowMs > userInputUntil) viewOffset = { rot, zoom: zoomBeforeDerive }` - so on a pinch the freshly-derived zoom (which DID carry the gesture) was overwritten with the previous frame's, and `composeShot` then put the camera back. **THE CAMERA REALLY DOES MOVE FIRST**, which is why the gesture felt dead rather than ignored: `controls.touches.TWO` is three's `DOLLY_PAN` default and is never overridden here, so OrbitControls dollies and the rig undoes it a frame later. Note the failure is the same whether or not `pointermove` fires during the pinch - noted as `'drag'` the zoom is discarded by that line, and noted not at all `userDroveCamera` is false so the whole derive block is skipped and the old offset is re-composed. **THE FIX: the rule now names the SET of inputs that own the distance, `ownsDistance(kind)`, EXPORTED FROM `viewport/cameraRig.ts` and pinned in `cameraRig.spec.ts` (mutation-checked: restoring `kind === 'wheel'` fails the test).** The scene tracks live pointers, recognises a two-pointer span change as a `'pinch'` with a direction on the WHEEL'S sign convention (spreading = in = negative, matching -deltaY), clears `reframing` as the wheel does, and no longer mis-files a pinch as a drag. **THE OTHER SURFACES ARE CLEAN - CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED, and the reason is interesting: `holo/scene.ts` was the SOLE casualty precisely BECAUSE it is the only surface that reconciles the camera against intent.** The 2D orrery (`SystemVisualizer`) and the GM starmap (`Starmap.svelte`) both use the shared `input/gestures.ts` layer, which handles pinch properly and wires `onZoom` -> `zoomAt`; the 3D starmap (`starmapScene.ts`) has no base/offset rig at all (no `noteUserInput`/`deriveOffset`/`viewOffset`), so nothing second-guesses its dolly. **ALSO DONE, the cheap instrument this entry asked for: `webglcontextlost` / `webglcontextrestored` listeners on the holo canvas**, counted into `[sse-perf]` (`holo.glContextLost`/`Restored`) and the `gl` provider, with `preventDefault` on loss so a restore can fire. Recovery is deliberately NOT built - rebuild on restore when a counter proves it happens. Engine map: **RENDER-S23** (a working MOUSE path is no evidence at all about TOUCH). **NOT VERIFIED ON A DEVICE - and it cannot be from here** (RENDER-S19/S23: the Browser pane emulates touch points but a genuine two-finger pinch is not reliably reproducible, and it will not composite for a worker session). The handback test is one line: **open a system on a phone or tablet, pinch to zoom, and the view should STAY where you put it.** | **fixed v2.1.549-beta - awaiting a pinch on a real device** |
| G20 | **V3.1 FEATURE (MOVED OUT OF V4): SCALE THE MAP HIERARCHY UP TWO MORE LEVELS — galaxies placed on a map to form GALAXY CLUSTERS, and clusters placed into FILAMENTS on a COSMIC WEB.** Owner, 2026-08-07: *"the V4 star cluster map / galaxy idea is instead a V3.1 feature and we wanna scale up the hierarchy too. Pretty much EXACTLY the same abstraction & scalability for up two more levels - exactly the same physical design and concept… Just the scale and background visualisation change."* **THE TIER STACK BECOMES FIVE, ONE ABSTRACTION THROUGHOUT:** system (bodies about a star, AU) -> starmap (stars in a neighbourhood, ly) -> galaxy (clusters and stars, kpc) -> galaxy cluster (galaxies, Mpc) -> cosmic web (filaments of clusters, Gpc). **THE CLAIM IS SOUND AND THE GROUNDWORK IS ALREADY DONE** — the four scale-agnostic pieces named in `v4-scope.md` carry to any tier: the floating origin (precision across magnitudes, already solved once), the size law (`scaleLaw.ts`, RENDER-S11, "one tested module the scene binds, never restates"), `niceInterval.ts` (any scale lands on round numbers — it is what fixed the starmap rings being wrong by 43x), and `scale.pixelsPerUnit`. **AND [[D18]]'S FRAMING GENERALISES INTO THE TIER RULE, WHICH IS A NICE CONFIRMATION THE ABSTRACTION IS REAL: "it is a STARMAP importer — the planets are just a nice add-on" is the same sentence at every level.** At each tier the tier's OWN objects are the point and their contents are the enrichment. **FOUR THINGS DO NOT CARRY OVER, AND THEY ARE WHERE THIS WILL BITE — none is fatal and two are simplifications.** **(1) ORBITS STOP BEING THE MOTION MODEL, and this is the real physical discontinuity.** Bodies orbit a star; stars orbit a cluster centre loosely; but **galaxy clusters and the cosmic web are not bound in that way at all — the dominant motion is cosmological EXPANSION plus peculiar velocity, and a filament is not an orbit.** The abstraction holds perfectly for POSITION and HIERARCHY and breaks for MOTION. Decide per tier which motion model applies rather than assuming Kepler scales up. **(2) THE CLOCK HAS NOTHING TO SHOW UP THERE, WHICH IS A SIMPLIFICATION, NOT A PROBLEM.** The Milky Way's rotation is ~250 Myr and web evolution is Gyr-scale, so across any campaign's timespan **nothing at tiers 4-5 visibly moves.** Those tiers are navigable static backdrops; do not build animation for them. **(3) "ONE PARENT" GETS GENUINELY FUZZY AT THE TOP, and that is real astronomy, not a modelling failure.** A star sits in one system; a galaxy's membership does not work that way — the Milky Way is in the Local Group AND the Virgo Supercluster AND Laniakea depending on the definition used, and cluster boundaries are actively disputed. **Treat containment above the galaxy tier as an AUTHORING decision with a declared convention, not a derived fact.** **(4) THE DATA STORY DOES NOT EXTEND FOR FREE, and this is the one to scope BEFORE building.** The real-sky importer reads SIMBAD, Gaia and the Exoplanet Archive — all STELLAR catalogues. Galaxies need different sources entirely (NED, 2MASS, SDSS), and **cosmic-web filament structure is largely SIMULATION-DERIVED rather than observational**, so "import it like we import stars" is not available at the top tier. **RESOLVED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-07 — THE CATALOGUE QUESTION IS ANSWERED AND THE SCOPING NOTE IS NO LONGER NEEDED: "we would just use procgen as there is little real data we can really use."** So tiers 3-5 are **GENERATED, NOT IMPORTED**, and the importer's stellar-catalogue limitation stops being a constraint. **This is a large simplification** — it removes the top tiers' dependency on the astronomy/import stream entirely and makes G20 a rendering-and-generation job rather than a data one. **THREE MORE DECISIONS FROM THE SAME EXCHANGE, all of which shrink the work:** **(1) MOTION IS CAMERA, NOT CONTENT.** *"The 3D rotation would be camera panning rather than star movement as time is effectively not needed at that scale."* This confirms point (2) above as a decision: **nothing at these tiers is animated by the clock; the sense of three dimensions comes from moving the CAMERA.** No propagator, no per-object motion, no clock coupling. **(2) EACH TIER IS A PROCEDURAL FIELD OF POINTS OF LIGHT** of varying size and colour, arranged into the structure that tier represents — galaxy morphologies, cluster shapes, filaments. One generator shape parameterised per tier, which is the project mantra again. **(3a) THE GENERATOR IS NAMED — OWNER, 2026-08-07: 3D VORONOI TESSELLATION ("Voronoi foam"). AGREED, AND IT IS A BETTER CHOICE THAN IT LOOKS, because it is not a lookalike — the VORONOI FOAM IS A PUBLISHED MORPHOLOGICAL MODEL OF THE COSMIC WEB** (van de Weygaert & Icke and successors), so this satisfies plausible-and-fun by using the actual description rather than imitating a picture of it. **IT ALSO FORMALISES THE OWNER'S OWN BUBBLE INTUITION EXACTLY, which is a good sign both are right:** Voronoi CELLS are the voids, cell FACES are the walls/sheets, cell EDGES are the filaments, and cell VERTICES are the nodes where clusters sit. **THE HIERARCHY THEREFORE FALLS OUT OF ONE CONSTRUCTION — four levels of structure from a single seed field**, which is the project mantra again: place galaxy clusters at the vertices, string galaxies along the edges, scatter sparse ones across the faces, and leave the cells empty. Nothing needs to be authored per level. **THE PRACTICAL STEER, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH SAYING: DO NOT BUILD A TESSELLATION. SAMPLE A DISTANCE FIELD.** A true 3D Voronoi (the Delaunay dual, with cell topology) is fiddly and heavy, and for a FIELD OF POINTS none of that topology is needed. Instead: generate seeds, then for each candidate point take the distances to its nearest few seeds. Near-equidistant from **2** seeds means it lies on a wall; from **3**, on a filament; from **4**, at a node. **That is a distance test per point with no mesh construction, and the ratio between the first and second nearest distances gives a CONTINUOUS "how filament-y is this point" value that can drive brightness, size and colour directly** — so the points-of-light field is a straight function of the seed field. **This is Worley / cellular noise**, a standard well-trodden technique that is also GPU-implementable if it ever needs to be. **Two notes for whoever builds it.** Seeds must be generated **deterministically and on demand per region** (hash the coarse grid cell) rather than as one finite set, or the map cannot be unbounded — the same seeded-reproducibility rule the importer already follows. And the SAME seed field serves several tiers at different zoom: at cluster scale you are near one node, at cosmic-web scale you see the foam — tier reuse, again for free. **(3) THE COSMIC WEB HAS A STATED VISUAL MODEL, and it is the physically right one: a 3D BUBBLE model — the bubbles are the VOIDS and the film between them is the FILAMENTS.** Worth keeping because it is genuinely how the structure is described: voids bounded by sheets/walls, with filaments where those sheets intersect and clusters at the nodes. Generating voids and drawing their boundaries is also far cheaper than generating filaments directly, so the owner's mental model is the efficient implementation as well as the accurate one. Related: [[D18]], [[G9]], [[G10]], `docs/dev/v4-scope.md` (where this idea started and from which it is now removed), RENDER-S11. | captured, V3.1 - **scope the catalogue question first**, then design |

The full model is [[G18]]-adjacent and lives in `docs/dev/v4-scope.md`; do not start it here.** **V3 SCOPE:** a new Settings -> Planets -> Biospheres section; a **vegetation coverage slider, 0-100%**, tinting that proportion of a qualifying world's LAND; colour derived from the host star; and — from the discussion — **an on/off option, because some worlds should have life that never colonised the land.** Owner's steer on placement: skip the poles and (probably) the equator, clustering where temperature is optimal rather than painting uniformly. **THE DATA MODEL ALREADY ANSWERS EVERY QUESTION THIS FEATURE ASKS — no new fields are needed.** `types.ts:155-161`: `Biosphere { complexity, coverage, biochemistry, energy_source, morphologies }`, where **`morphologies` already includes `'flora'`** (and `'fungal'` and `'fauna'`, which is exactly what the owner said he would extend to in V4), `coverage` already exists as a number, and `biochemistry` already spans `water-carbon` / `ammonia-silicon` / `methane-carbon`. **AND THE SHARPEST ONE: `energy_source` is already `'photosynthesis' | 'chemosynthesis' | 'thermosynthesis'`, WHICH IS THE CORRECT GATE FOR THE WHOLE STAR-COLOUR IDEA.** Only photosynthetic life has any reason to be the colour of its star; a chemosynthetic vent biosphere does not care what the sky looks like. Gating on that field is free, is physically right, and immediately makes the feature smarter than "tint if alive". **DO NOT WRITE A SECOND STAR-COLOUR FUNCTION.** Star colour from temperature already exists — [[G9]] ships charted stars "at their true direction, brightness and colour" — so locate that derivation and reuse it. `rendering/colors.ts` carries `getClassColor` / `getPlanetColor` and is the likely home. **THE ONE REAL SCIENCE QUESTION, AND IT NEEDS THE OWNER, because the stated purpose of the feature is to teach the physics: is plant colour the band that is ABSORBED, or the band that is REFLECTED?** The two give opposite answers and the model must pick one and hold it. **Earth is the only anchor we have and it disambiguates: our peak is green-yellow and our plants are GREEN — i.e. they REFLECT near the peak rather than absorbing it.** That is the real and genuinely unresolved "green gap". So a rule of "plants take the colour of the star's peak, absorbed" would make EARTH's plants black, contradicting the one case everybody knows. **A rule that IS self-consistent and still gives the owner every outcome he named: absorb the wings, reflect near the peak.** A G-dwarf then yields green; an M-dwarf's peak sits in far red/IR, so broad absorption across red and IR leaves almost nothing visible reflected and the plants read **black or grey**, exactly as he described; an F-star pushes the reflected band bluewards toward blue/violet; and a binary can legitimately produce two overlapping answers. **Recommend that rule, but it is his call and it should be settled BEFORE anything ships, because the feature's whole justification is that a curious user can chase the reasoning and find it sound.** **PUT THE COLOUR TABLE IN RULE-PACK DATA FROM DAY ONE, even at V3 scale.** The owner's own plan is "an extensible system of rules the user can edit or add to… shake and bake your own colour schemes", and the standing architecture rule says a GM-editable look lever is pack DATA, never code. Fix or thread it deliberately rather than working around it. **SCOPE SHARPENED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-07, AND IT IS A BETTER DESIGN THAN THE FIRST SKETCH.** *"We need to make this TAG driven for the render engine to run off… stop these being checkboxes and instead make them autogenerated or manually added tags… This is a hierarchy - plant life covers fungal, fungal colours microbial, as each more sophisticated biosphere would gradually take over the previous… in V4 we will see planet colours change over time as biospheres evolve… while we have 4 morphologies we could make this extensible in the settings."* UI he described: **a coverage slider per morphology, a way to REORDER them to set the hierarchy, and colour options for each** — so adding `techno` as a fifth ("dark with lights") just works. **WHY THIS IS RIGHT: it is the standing architecture rule applied exactly** (physics and data drive tags; tags drive the image), and **the hierarchy is a PAINTER'S ALGORITHM** — coverage per layer plus an order is precisely how you would render it, and it is why the V4 time-evolution falls out for free rather than needing anything new. **This V3 feature is effectively the RENDERING HALF of the V4 life model, built early**, so its shape should be chosen to be V4-compatible: the epoch list in `v4-scope.md` sets coverages per epoch, and scrubbing then changes a planet's colour with no further machinery. **FOUR THINGS TO SETTLE FIRST, AND (1) IS A REAL TRAP.** **(1) DO NOT SYNC TAGS AND `morphologies` BIDIRECTIONALLY — PICK ONE AUTHORITY.** The owner's phrasing ("they turn tags on and off and obviously vice versa") describes two stores of one fact, which is this codebase's most recurring fault by its own stated test: *could these two answer the same question differently?* They could, and they will. **RECOMMEND THE TAGS ARE THE AUTHORITY and `Biosphere.morphologies` stops being stored at all** — the tag system has ALREADY solved the hard half of this, which is mixing derived and authored facts: provenance is declared by category (TAG-4), `authored` tags are removable and never come back (TAG-5), one module decides what may delete a tag (TAG-1), and [[A44]] fixed precisely the failure where a generator-written tag was presented as engine-derived. A GM adding `biosphere/flora` by hand and the engine deriving it are then the same mechanism with different provenance, and there is no sync to get wrong. **(2) `morphologies` IS A CLOSED UNION AND EXTENSIBILITY BREAKS IT.** `types.ts:160` is `('microbial'|'fungal'|'flora'|'fauna')[]`. A user-extensible list cannot be a closed union — it becomes a key into pack data, which is the same move gases and liquids already made. Everything is treated the same - differences (like no light for flora) is just defined in its definition."** One uniform record per morphology, one code path that reads it. **There must be no `if (morphology === 'sentient')` anywhere in the implementation**, and no notion of a render mode, a type, or a class of morphology. Flora having no lights is an EMPTY LIGHT RANGE in flora's definition, not a branch. Fauna contributing nothing visible is two empty ranges, not a `none` case. **THIS EXPLICITLY SUPERSEDES THE OWNER'S OWN EARLIER LINE THAT "`life/sentient` may require a different renderer" — it does not, and an implementer reading that sentence in isolation would build the one thing this principle forbids.** Sentient is simply a definition with a strong light range and a weak colour range; `techno` is one with a dark colour range and a bright light range. **This is the "build one system, parameterised, not three" rule from `v4-scope.md` applied at feature scale, and it is also the anti-duplication rule stated positively.** If a difference cannot be expressed in the definition, that is a signal the DEFINITION SCHEMA is missing a field — extend the schema, never add a branch. **SHIPPED v2.1.652-beta.** Built as specified with three recorded deviations, all argued in `docs/dev/biosphere-and-surface-light.md`. **(1) The ABSORB-vs-REFLECT question no longer needs an answer, and this entry's diagnosis of it was right about Earth and wrong about the shape of the fix.** Reflectance is not a rule to choose — you see what a pigment fails to absorb — and WHERE each pigment absorbs is now pack data per pigment. Chlorophyll's real bands bracket the green, so Earth comes out green with nothing in the code saying so, and "absorb the wings, reflect near the peak" turns out to be a DESCRIPTION of chlorophyll's authored bands rather than a law the engine applies. Reversing it for a pack is editing that pack's band centres. **(2) `Biosphere.morphologies` was WIDENED, not replaced by tags** — this entry recommended tags be the authority; [[B52]]'s own test overrules it (a GM setting flora to 60% cannot be re-derived, so it is DATA). The `biodiversity/*` tags are derived-only and never written back, so the bidirectional-sync trap this entry named does not exist. **Owner's call to overturn.** **(3) [[C2]] was threaded, not fixed:** `body.vegetation` carries resolved colours written in physics where the pack is in hand, the same move `auroraEmitters` already makes; C2 itself is untouched and still open for cloud decks. Everything else landed: coverage per morphology, reorderable order as the hierarchy, pack-data colour table, `energy_source` as the gate, no branch on any morphology anywhere, and `techno` shipped in the data as the extensibility proof. | **SHIPPED v2.1.652-beta** |

**OWNER'S DESIGN, 2026-08-07 — `morphologies` IS KILLED AND BECOMES A TAG GROUP.** `life/microbial`, `life/fungal`, `life/flora`, `life/fauna`, `life/sentient` — so a user can drive them from their own rule packs. **That settles trap (1) above in the strongest way: one authority, no sync.** `life/sentient` is expected to render DIFFERENTLY — mostly light points on coastlines — so the colour chooser wants a randomly-pickable colour RANGE and "coloured light points" as an option, plus **a special colour `mid-spectrum` meaning "derive from the star"**. **THE OWNER'S OWN GOTCHA, and he is right to raise it: tags have no concept of hierarchy.** His proposal is to use TAG VALUES as the order. **RECOMMEND A SPLIT INSTEAD — values are the right home for one thing and the wrong home for the other, and mixing them causes a real fault.** **(a) TAG VALUE = per-body COVERAGE.** That genuinely varies per planet, which is exactly what a value is for, and the precedent already ships: `feature/polar-vortex` carries `"8"`, and `hazard/radiation` carries a band. So `life/flora` with value `0.6` is idiomatic. **(b) THE STACK ORDER BELONGS IN PACK DATA, NOT IN TAG VALUES — RECOMMENDED, AND ACCEPTED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-07: "I agree - let settings define order." SO THIS IS DECIDED, NOT A SUGGESTION. The reason it matters is that the order is a property of the VOCABULARY and not of any planet.** Flora outranks microbial everywhere, always. Put it in per-planet values and: every body carries a redundant copy of one global fact; **two planets can disagree about whether flora outranks fungal**, which is this codebase's recurring fault stated exactly; and reordering the hierarchy means rewriting every life tag on every body in the campaign. **The owner already designed the right home for it in the previous message — the reorderable list in Settings.** Keep it there. **Tags say WHAT IS PRESENT and HOW MUCH; the pack says HOW THE VOCABULARY STACKS.** That is the same separation gases already use: the composition says which gas, the pack says what it does. **OWNER CONFIRMED 2026-08-07, closing this point: "keep it [the order] away from tags - if anything the tag value could define COVERAGE! So a planet can be tweaked individually - again possible in the definition you can have a range it starts with at random."** **So the model is complete and has three homes, each holding the thing that actually varies at that level:** **SETTINGS/PACK holds the vocabulary** — per morphology a colour range, a point-light range, **a COVERAGE RANGE to draw a starting value from**, and the stack order. **THE TAG VALUE holds this planet's actual coverage**, drawn from that range at generation and then **individually tweakable by the GM**. **THE TAG KEY says the life is there.** Nothing is stored twice. **ONE TRAP IN "RANDOM AT GENERATION", AND THERE IS A TEST THAT WILL CATCH IT: THE DRAW MUST HAPPEN ONCE AND BE PERSISTED — THE PROCESSOR MUST NEVER RE-ROLL IT.** If coverage were re-drawn on each pass, `process()` would stop being idempotent and `src/lib/system/idempotence.test.ts` goes red (PHY-1: nothing may read a value a later pass writes; [[B13]] found seven such edges at once). It would also silently overwrite the GM's own tweak on the next recalculation, which is the worse half. So the value is written at generation, and thereafter behaves as authored data — the tag system already has the machinery for exactly that distinction (TAG-5: `authored` tags are removable and never come back; [[A44]]: a generator-written tag must not be presented as engine-derived). **Seed the draw deterministically**, per the same rule the importer already follows for generated content, so a regenerate reproduces it rather than reshuffling every world. **(c) PACK DATA PER MORPHOLOGY should therefore carry: display name, colour options (including ranges), a coverage range, the STACK ORDER, and a RENDER MODE — `tint` | `lights` | `none`.** The render mode is what makes `life/sentient` and a future `techno` work, and it also solves the earlier problem that `fauna` should not tint a world seen from orbit: fauna is simply `none`. **(d) `mid-spectrum` SHOULD BE A DERIVATION MODE, NOT A MAGIC COLOUR STRING.** There will be more than one (an absorbed-band variant is the obvious second), so model it as a small enum of "derive the colour this way" rather than a sentinel hex. **This is also exactly where the absorbed-vs-reflected question above has to be answered** — `mid-spectrum` is that decision, wearing a name. **GROUNDING — TWO THINGS THIS CAN BUILD ON RATHER THAN INVENT.** `rendering/planetAppearance.ts` is **ALREADY TAG-DRIVEN** — it gates on `has('structure/subsurface-ocean')` and similar — so a tag-driven biosphere tint slots into an existing pipeline instead of creating a second one. And `rendering/planetTexture.ts` **already paints land against ocean at the true coverage fraction** (`:125-127`, "If the world is mostly ocean, paint ocean as the base and draw LAND patches instead, so the % reads right"). **So there IS land to tint, and coastlines already exist as the edges of those patches.** **REFINED BY THE OWNER, SAME DAY, AND IT SUPERSEDES THE `tint | lights | none` MODE ENUM SUGGESTED IN (c) — HIS IS SIMPLER AND MORE FLEXIBLE:** *"visually life will have a base colour range and a base point light range."* **So every morphology carries BOTH channels rather than choosing between them**, and either may be empty. **CONFIRMED EXPLICITLY BY THE OWNER, same day: "so lights and colour are both relevant… in every level of the hierarchy." DECIDED — there is no per-morphology mode switch anywhere in this design; colour and lights are two ranges present at EVERY level.** That removes a branch and expresses everything the mode enum could: flora is tint-only; `life/sentient` is a faint tint plus strong lights; a future `techno` is a DARK tint plus bright lights, which is exactly the owner's earlier description and is not expressible as a single mode; fauna is simply both-empty. **Drop the enum; use two optional ranges.** **AND THE PLACEMENT RULE, which is the other half:** *"assume life clusters between land and solvent - which is likely."* **It is more than likely, it is right** — littoral zones (estuaries, shallows, coastal shelves) are Earth's most productive by a wide margin, so this is the plausible-and-fun standard met without effort. **It also UNIFIES the design: one placement rule drives both channels.** Coverage then reads as *how far life has spread OUTWARD from the land/solvent boundary*, which is a far better meaning for the slider than a scatter or a latitude band — and it supersedes the first sketch's "skip the poles and equator" as the primary rule, though a temperature weighting can still modulate it. **THIS ESCALATES THE ONE OPEN QUESTION FROM A SIDE-ISSUE TO THE CENTRAL ONE, AND IT SHOULD BE ANSWERED FIRST.** `planetTexture.ts` paints land against ocean as PATCHES at the true coverage fraction — but **are those patch EDGES addressable, or are they only painted?** Under the original sketch that only affected sentient lights. Under this one **the land/solvent boundary drives every morphology's tint AND lights**, so if the edges are not recoverable, the whole feature needs the texture generator to expose its boundary rather than a small addition. **ANSWERED AND CLOSED BY THE OWNER, 2026-08-07: "planetTexture will need a rewrite - so don't sweat it."** So the edge-addressability question is moot; the rewrite will expose the land/solvent boundary this design needs. **CLARIFIED BY THE OWNER, correcting an over-reading in an earlier draft of this entry: the rewrite he means is OF `planetTexture`, FOR THIS FEATURE — it is IN SCOPE HERE, not a separate project and not a prerequisite.** His words: *"planetTexture will just require a rewrite for this - it shoves on patches of colour… it is not going to know about edges and lights, etc."* So there is **no phantom dependency to schedule around and no separate board entry to raise** — an earlier draft wrongly inferred a large unscoped texture project and recommended waiting for it. Ignore that. **WHAT IT DOES MEAN IS AN HONEST SIZE ESTIMATE, WHICH MATTERS FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: G19 IS NOT A SLIDER.** The UI and the data model are small — a settings section, pack definitions, tag values — but the item also **rewrites the planet texture generator** so that it (i) knows where the land/solvent boundary IS rather than only painting patches either side of it, and (ii) can place point lights at all, which it currently has no concept of. Scope it as a medium job with a rendering core, not as chrome. The two-factor placement score and the layered painter order are then specified against that new generator rather than bolted onto today's patch painter. **THE COVERAGE SEMANTICS, owner's worked example:** *"if you have plant coverage at 50% it will cluster to coastlines in bio-compatible temps on the surface (i.e. skip extremes)."* So placement is a **two-factor score per location — proximity to the land/solvent boundary, times temperature suitability — and the coverage percentage fills the best-scoring ground first**, spreading outward as it rises. That is a clean, statable rule and it should go in the design note verbatim. **DO NOT INVENT A "BIO-COMPATIBLE TEMPERATURE" CONSTANT — THE ENGINE ALREADY DERIVES THE RIGHT ANSWER TWICE OVER, AND HARDCODING A LIFE ZONE IS THE MISTAKE TO AVOID HERE.** (a) **The surface temperature RANGE already exists**: `surfaceTempProfile` publishes `totalMinK`/`totalMaxK`, which [[A5]] established brackets the mean by construction — so "the extremes of this world's surface" is a lookup, not new physics, and it gives the cold-pole/hot-subsolar spread the rule needs. (b) **The tolerable band should come from THE SOLVENT BEING LIQUID, not from a number.** `Biosphere.biochemistry` already distinguishes `water-carbon` / `ammonia-silicon` / `methane-carbon`, and the liquids overhaul already derives phase properly with pressure (`phaseAtP`, the `hydrosphere/*` phase tags). **So "bio-compatible" means "the solvent is liquid there" — which is physically exactly right, needs no constants, and handles ammonia and methane life correctly for free.** A hardcoded 0-40 C band would be wrong for three of the biochemistries the type already declares, and would silently contradict the phase tags shown two rows away in the same block — the [[A5]] fault class, repeated. It also ties this V3 feature to V4's substrate-agnostic life model rather than diverging from it. **THE SCIENCE DECISION, ANSWERED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-07: "absorbed vs reflected = green for earth - i.e. the most efficient colour to harvest energy." THE OUTCOME IS ACCEPTED AND CORRECT; THE STATED REASON NEEDS ONE ADJUSTMENT, AND IT MATTERS ONLY BECAUSE THIS FEATURE'S WHOLE PURPOSE IS THAT A CURIOUS USER CAN CHASE THE REASONING AND FIND IT SOUND.** **Green is not the colour Earth's plants harvest — it is the one band they THROW AWAY.** Chlorophyll absorbs hard in the blue (~430 nm) and the red (~660 nm) and REFLECTS green (~550 nm); a leaf looks green precisely because that light bounces off it. That is the real and still-unresolved "green gap". So a rule phrased literally as *"plants are the colour they harvest most efficiently"* makes **Earth's plants BLACK**, contradicting the one case every user can check by looking out of the window. **THE TWO RULES IN PLAY DO NOT AGREE, WHICH IS WORTH SEEING PLAINLY:** *colour = the star's peak* gives green for the Sun but RED for an M-dwarf; *plants absorb everything they can* gives BLACK for every star including ours. The owner wants green for the Sun AND black for an M-dwarf — which is one answer from each rule, so a third rule is needed to deliver both. **RECOMMENDED RULE, WHICH GIVES EVERY OUTCOME HE NAMED FROM A SINGLE PRINCIPLE AND IS REAL ASTROBIOLOGY: SELECTIVITY SCALES WITH AVAILABLE ENERGY.** Where light is abundant, photosynthesis SATURATES — there is more energy arriving than the machinery can use — so life can afford to discard a band, and discarding near the peak may even protect against overload. Where light is scarce, nothing can be discarded. Then: **a bright G-type is energy-rich, so plants are selective and REFLECT near the peak — GREEN, and Earth is explained rather than excepted; a dim M-dwarf is energy-poor, so life absorbs across red and IR and reflects almost nothing visible — BLACK or grey, exactly as the owner described; a hotter, brighter F-type is more energy-rich still, so selectivity increases and the reflected band moves bluewards — BLUE or VIOLET.** One principle, three outcomes, all his. **It also answers the user's "why?" with something satisfying instead of circular** — "because its sun is too dim to waste any light" is a better sentence than "because the physics says so", and it is the kind of answer the owner said he wants people to go looking for. **ACCEPTED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-07 ("Perfect!") — SO THIS IS THE RULE, NOT A SUGGESTION.** `mid-spectrum` is defined as *selectivity scales with available energy*: a bright star lets photosynthesis saturate, so life discards a band near the peak and REFLECTS it; a dim star forces broadband absorption, so almost nothing visible is reflected. **Earth is green because its sun is bright enough to waste light — it is explained by the rule rather than excepted from it, which is the property that makes the whole feature defensible to a user who checks.** Carry that sentence in `mid-spectrum`'s own definition and in whatever tooltip or explainer surface describes it, because that token IS this decision. **The colour table remains pack DATA**, so a GM who disagrees can still author their own scheme — the rule sets the shipped defaults, not a law.

**THE TARGET OUTCOME, owner's example: "Pandora may have glowing purple fungi spots against orange - that is fine!" IT IS MORE THAN FINE, AND THE POINT IS THAT IT NEEDS NO SPECIAL CASE — it is the model working through legitimate paths, which is the test of whether the design is right.** Two things it confirms. **(a) THE POINT-LIGHT CHANNEL IS AVAILABLE TO EVERY MORPHOLOGY, not just `life/sentient`.** Glowing fungi is bioluminescence, and it is REAL — foxfire (Armillaria, Panellus stipticus) glows on Earth — so a fungal layer using the light channel is plausible-and-fun met exactly. Do not implement lights as a sentient-only feature; that would break this example and would be wrong anyway. **(b) `mid-spectrum` IS ONE COLOUR OPTION AMONG SEVERAL AND MUST NOT BE THE DEFAULT FOR EVERYTHING.** Purple fungi are not derived from the star, and should not be: **only PHOTOSYNTHETIC life has any physical reason to track its star's spectrum, and `Biosphere.energy_source` already gates exactly that.** Fungi are heterotrophs; their colour is free. So the physics positively supports the artistic outcome rather than merely tolerating it — which is the standard this whole feature is meant to meet. **NOTE FOR WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP: this entry is now most of the design note.** Extract it to `docs/dev/biosphere-appearance-design.md` rather than re-deriving it, and settle the two open owner decisions at the top of that document. Related: [[C2]], [[G9]], [[G18]], [[A44]], TAG-1/TAG-3/TAG-4/TAG-5/TAG-7 in `engine-map.md`, [[B29]], `docs/dev/v4-scope.md`, `docs/dev/architecture-physics-tags-visuals.md`. | **SPLIT V3 / V4 BY THE OWNER, 2026-08-13 — "let's do what is practicable in V3 and make the initial changes; the move to tags kinda makes sense as it blends in with the tagging rewrite." THE SEAM IS DATA VERSUS RENDERING, and it is a clean one because the two halves were only ever bundled by arriving in the same conversation.** **V3 — THE DATA MODEL, and it belongs with the tagging rewrite because that is exactly what it is:** kill `Biosphere.morphologies` and replace it with the `life/*` tag group (`life/microbial`, `life/fungal`, `life/flora`, `life/fauna`, `life/sentient`), coverage carried as the TAG VALUE, and the vocabulary — stack order, colour range, light range, coverage range — as pack data with its Settings editor. **That is a tag-domain job done by a session already holding the tag domain, and it needs no renderer at all.** **V4 — THE PICTURE:** the layered painter, placement on the land/solvent boundary, point lights, and the `planetTexture` rewrite they require. Rides with the new generation engine. **WHY THIS ORDER IS RIGHT AND NOT JUST CHEAPER: the V3 half UNBLOCKS the V4 half and is useless to nobody in the meantime.** Once life is expressed as tags with coverages, every existing tag surface gets it free — the tag panel, Find-by-tag, map highlights, player redaction, rule packs — so a GM can author and query biospheres long before anything is drawn. | D18 | **The real-sky importer produces a "local neighbourhood" with NO SOL AND NO ALPHA CENTAURI — and both omissions are ONE root, which is a category error rather than a bug.** Owner, 2026-08-07, with a screenshot of an imported map: *"the NASA starmap importer misses Sol… kinda obvious why in retrospect — so local neighbourhood starmaps should offer to add it. Also I don't see alpha centauri either which IS weird."* **THE SINGLE ROOT: A CONFIRMED-PLANET-HOST CENSUS IS NOT A STELLAR CENSUS.** `query.mjs:19` selects from the NASA Exoplanet Archive's `pscomppars` — "every confirmed planet + host-star parameters" — and `convert.mjs:1` calls itself the "confirmed-only converter". So the importer returns **planet hosts**, and a star with no confirmed planet is not in the result set at all. Both famous absences follow immediately: **(a) Sol is not a planet host in an EXOPLANET archive** — our planets are not exoplanets — and it is additionally the coordinate ORIGIN (`presets.mjs:14`, `centre: { raDeg: 0, decDeg: 0, distLy: 0 }, centreLabel: 'Sol'`), so it is the reference point the map is measured FROM rather than a row in it. **(b) Alpha Centauri A and B have NO CONFIRMED PLANETS**, so they are correctly excluded by the same gate, while **Proxima does** (b/c/d) and therefore arrives. That is exactly what the screenshot shows: Proxima Cen present, its two bright companions absent. **AND THE SHARPEST SYMPTOM, FOUND IN THE SPECS: `convert.spec.js:90` asserts Proxima is "present as sys-alphacen"** — so the importer already knows the Alpha Centauri GROUPING and builds a system under that identity containing only its faintest member. **The map therefore has an Alpha Centauri with neither Alpha Centauri in it.** **THE IMPORTER IS DOING WHAT IT SAYS — this is not a defect to patch quietly.** `presets.mjs:16` is honest about it: "Every confirmed planet host within 16.5 light years of Sol… **the same census the bundled map curates by hand**, built fresh from the catalogue." The BUNDLED map has Sol and Alpha Centauri because a human put them there; the live importer has no such step. **So the two ship different neighbourhoods, and only one of them is believable to a user.** **THIS IS THE SESSION'S OWN NAMED NEXT PROBLEM, arriving as a user report:** the outgoing astronomy handover listed "Gaia population presets and **the census problem**" as its best-fit next work. This is that, with a concrete symptom attached. **THE MACHINERY TO FIX IT ALREADY EXISTS AND SHOULD NOT BE REBUILT: the session has SIMBAD and Gaia TAP queries.** A star with no planets is a Gaia/SIMBAD question, not an Exoplanet Archive one. **OWNER'S ASK IS THE MINIMUM: a local-neighbourhood import should OFFER TO ADD SOL.** Options to bring back with a recommendation rather than picking: (1) always inject Sol for a Sol-centred import, since it is the origin and its data is not catalogue-derived anyway; (2) offer "include notable nearby stars without confirmed planets", filled from Gaia/SIMBAD — which fixes Alpha Cen and everything like it, not just the two we noticed; (3) leave the census pure and say so plainly in the preset blurb and on the finished map. **THE GOVERNING FRAMING, OWNER 2026-08-07 — READ THIS FIRST, BECAUSE IT MAKES EVERY DECISION BELOW OBVIOUS RATHER THAN ARBITRARY: "This is a STARMAP importer - clue is in the name. The planets are just a nice add-on."** **The priority was inverted from the start.** What exists is a PLANET-HOST importer that happens to place stars; what it should be is a STAR importer that happens to attach planets. That single correction explains the whole item: the missing Sol and Alpha Centauri are not edge cases, they are what you get when the secondary thing is used as the selection criterion for the primary one. It is also why the fault read as "obvious in retrospect" — the name always said what it should do. **Anyone picking this up should re-read the design doc against that sentence**, because other decisions in the pipeline were probably made under the old framing too.

**DECIDED BY THE OWNER 2026-08-07, AND IT IS STRONGER THAN ANY OF THE THREE OPTIONS: "Always add nearby stars - even if no planets - the system can populate them. That should be the behaviour - no need to ask."** Which follows directly from the framing above: you do not ask permission to include the primary object. **CORRECTED 2026-08-07 — an earlier draft of this entry said "no toggle and no prompt… the generator filling out the rest", which CONFLATED TWO SEPARATE DECISIONS and would have misled whoever built it. The owner caught it. THE TWO ARE INDEPENDENT:** **(a) STAR INCLUSION is unconditional** — every star in the region arrives, planets or not, no toggle and no prompt. That is what "no need to ask" meant. **(b) FILL-OUT REMAINS A USER CHOICE, exactly as it is today.** It is not implied by (a) and must not become automatic. **THE FULL MATRIX, so it cannot be misread again:**

| | **Fill-out OFF** (straight import) | **Fill-out ON** |
|---|---|---|
| Star **with** confirmed planets | real star + its real planets, and nothing else | real planets held as fixed ANCHORS + generated extras (this is today's behaviour, unchanged) |
| Star **without** confirmed planets | **real star, BARE — no planets at all.** This is the new case for a straight import and it must be legal | real star + a fully generated system, no anchors |
| **Sol**, when in region | real star + the shipped preset | real star + the shipped preset — **the generator never touches Sol in either mode** |

**So the new star population is orthogonal to fill-out: it changes WHICH STARS ARRIVE, not what happens to them afterwards.** Note the consequence for a straight import: a bare star with no planets is now a normal, valid outcome, so nothing downstream may assume a system has at least one planet — worth a deliberate check, since the previous census guaranteed every system had one by construction. **THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS — EXTEND IT, DO NOT BUILD IT.** Fill-out mode shipped with the importer and today runs the generator around real stars *that have confirmed planets*, holding those as fixed anchors, tagging everything it invents `origin/generated`, deterministic per catalogue slug. The change is to let it run around stars with **NO** anchors at all. **That also settles the DATA-R4 provenance question for free:** the invention is already labelled, so the rule ("never invents and never overwrites") is satisfied by the existing tag rather than needing a new one. **THREE CONSEQUENCES THAT MUST BE HANDLED, and the first two will bite silently.** **(1) SOL IS SPECIAL-CASED — OWNER, 2026-08-07: "Always add Sol if on the map - use our preset to fill it."** This closes the trap the general rule would otherwise spring: Sol has no confirmed planets in an exoplanet archive, so "populate stars without planets" would hand it an INVENTED solar system, which is the one outcome nobody wants. Instead Sol is filled from the shipped preset — `static/examples/Sol_2030-System.json`, which the build kit already reads wholesale — and **never from the generator**. **Note the condition is "IF ON THE MAP", i.e. if Sol falls inside the imported region — it is not forced into every import.** A region centred on Sgr A*, or any cone that does not reach Sol, correctly has no Sol in it. Since Sol is also the coordinate origin, "is Sol in this region" is simply whether the region contains the origin, which the existing cone/shell maths already answers. **(2) THE COST MODEL IS CALIBRATED ON THE WRONG POPULATION AND WILL BE WRONG.** `costModel.mjs:4` states in as many words that it guards "against counts the real catalogue never produces: confirmed-planet hosts" — so its whole notion of a plausible result size is planet-host-shaped. A stellar census within the same radius is several times larger (order 60+ systems within ~16 ly against roughly 20 planet hosts), so the guardrails will either refuse a legitimate import or wave through something far bigger than intended. **Re-derive the cost model against stellar counts in the same commit; do not leave it as a follow-up.** **(3) THE PIPELINE INVERTS.** Today the Exoplanet Archive is the SOURCE. It becomes an ENRICHMENT JOIN: query Gaia/SIMBAD for the stars in the region first, then attach confirmed planets where they exist, then fill out the remainder. The session already has both query paths, so this is re-plumbing rather than new capability — but it is a genuine change of shape and should be recognised as one rather than bolted on. **Watch load cost as well:** `recalcAllSystems` runs 31-47 ms per system, so tripling the system count triples the physics pass; see [[P1]] and UI-L1..L7 for the instruments if it becomes noticeable. Territory: real-sky importer. Related: [[D7]], [[D17]], DATA-R4 (the importer never invents and never overwrites — note option 2 sits right against that rule and needs its provenance answered: an added star with no planets should presumably be tagged so it cannot be mistaken for a detection). **BUILT v2.1.547-beta.** The pipeline is inverted: `simbadStarsAdql` is the primary query, `convertRegion` is the entry point, and the Exoplanet Archive is joined onto the census by POSITION. **MEASURED, Local Neighbourhood (16.5 ly): 21 systems -> 56.** Sol present; Alpha Centauri present with all three stars (A, B and Proxima) and Proxima's planets attached; 34 of the 56 are bare stars, which is the new legal case. **WHERE THE STARS COME FROM:** SIMBAD, because DATA-R6 measured it as the one service that answers a browser directly. A stellar snapshot (`static/realsky/stars.json`, 866 rows to the same 12.7 pc bound the planet snapshot uses) is published beside it by `fetch-sources.mjs`, so an offline GM is not left worse off than before. **STELLAR PARAMETERS: the blocker nobody had spotted.** A general star catalogue gives a spectral type and astrometry and nothing else, while `starNodeFromRow` SKIPS a host missing mass/radius/Teff (DATA-R4) - so without a per-class table every planetless star would have been skipped and the item could not be delivered at all. Solved by REUSE, not invention: `statTemplates` in the rule pack is the same data the generator draws its own stars from. The figures are labelled typical-for-class in the body description, which is what DATA-R4 asks (estimate openly, never invent silently). **THE CENSUS IS THE REAL WORK, and both faults were measured rather than guessed - see DATA-R9.** A raw cone lists multiple-star CONTAINERS as well as stars, inconsistently (Alpha Cen returns three rows for two stars; Luhman 16 returns a container only), and its 3D positions CANNOT BE SUBTRACTED - Sirius A and B differ by 1.2% in parallax, which fabricates 6,856 AU for a pair genuinely ~20 AU apart. Projected separation recovers 16 AU. | B40 | **The Hayashi limit does not appear to be implemented, so an aged star can be given a physically impossible temperature.** Owner, 2026-08-07, after working with red giants. **CONFIRMED ABSENT: grep for "hayashi" over `src/` and `docs/` returns NOTHING.** **WHAT THE ENGINE DOES INSTEAD, and it predicts exactly the fault:** `physics/stellar-evolution.ts`, inside `ageStar`'s giant branch, cools a star by a MULTIPLIER of its own main-sequence temperature — `T = star.temperatureK * (1 - 0.55 * e)`, with a comment saying it "cools toward ~2600-3500 K (reddens)". **That comment is only true for a Sun-like progenitor.** Because the form is multiplicative, the floor a star can reach is proportional to where it STARTED: a 5,800 K G-type lands near 2,600 K, which is plausible, but a 3,000 K M-dwarf would be driven to about **1,350 K**, which is not a star. **The Hayashi limit is precisely the rule that forbids this** — a fully convective star in hydrostatic equilibrium has a MINIMUM effective temperature (roughly 3,000-4,000 K, weakly mass- and composition-dependent), and a red giant ascends its track at nearly CONSTANT temperature rather than cooling without bound. **The physical shape is a FLOOR, and the code has a RATIO.** So real giants converge to a similar 3,000-3,500 K regardless of progenitor, while this model spreads them proportionally to their starting point. **RECOMMENDED FIRST MEASUREMENT, not a fix: sweep progenitor masses from ~0.2 to ~8 solar through `ageStar` at several ages past the main sequence and plot the resulting temperature.** If the cool end goes below ~2,500 K the diagnosis is confirmed; if something downstream already clamps it, the fault is only the honesty of the intermediate value. **NOTE the one place a clamp DOES exist and why it is not this:** the same function carries an HR clamp of >=1500 K "needed for the radius/class math", explicitly described as not leaking into the displayed temperature for black holes — so there IS a floor in the vicinity, but it is a numerical guard at 1,500 K, not a physical limit at ~3,000 K. **ALSO WORTH DECIDING (owner's call, not a worker's): a low-mass M-dwarf cannot become a red giant within the age of the universe at all**, yet the slider will happily age one there. Whether the engine should refuse, warn, or simply play along is a product question — and it becomes a live one under [[G17]]. Territory: the physics session. Related: [[B9]](b), [[B11]], [[G17]], `docs/dev/v4-scope.md`. | **DONE v2.1.590-beta.** Measured first, as asked: a 0.2 Msun progenitor reached 1,500 K and a 0.5 Msun 2,019 K. The node is never deleted; being inside the star is a TAG at that age, and the body reappears when the slider moves back because nothing was ever destroyed. DO NOT BUILD IT.** **ONE THING WORTH SETTLING WHENEVER THIS OPENS, because it is a product question and not an engineering one: what does the slider do to a system IMPORTED FROM REAL ASTRONOMY, where the age is a MEASUREMENT rather than a generated parameter?** Sliding it is arguably falsifying data, and the answer changes whether the control is offered on those systems at all. | D17 | **"Epsilon Indi A b on the real starmap importer."** Owner, 2026-08-07 — captured verbatim because the fault is NOT yet stated and must not be guessed at; the observation is the system name plus the surface it was seen on. **AWAITING ONE DETAIL FROM THE OWNER: what is wrong with it?** Candidates, none of them assumed and all cheap to distinguish once he says: a wrong or missing radius (Eps Ind Ab is a ~3 Jupiter-mass RV/astrometric detection, so `pl_rade` is either absent or BACK-FILLED from a mass-radius relation — the very column the importer's own notes flag as lying); a mass that is really `msini`; a wildly long period (~45 yr) mis-scaled; a naming/id collision between the star `Epsilon Indi A` and its companion brown dwarfs `Eps Ind Ba/Bb`, which is a trap the stable-id/phase-hash coupling would feel; or it simply not arriving at all. **UNBLOCKED AND DIAGNOSED 2026-08-07 — the owner supplied a screenshot and the exported `eps_Ind_A-System.json`, and NONE of the candidates above was right.** **THE FAULT: `defaultMakeup` tests DENSITY BEFORE MASS, so a self-compressed giant is read as rock.** `src/lib/import/realsky/planets.mjs:16-21` is a four-branch ladder and the FIRST branch is `if (densityGcc != null && densityGcc > 4) return { rock: 0.62, metal: 0.33, ice: 0.05 }` — which is character-for-character the makeup in the exported file. **THE FUNCTION ALREADY CONTAINS THE RIGHT ANSWER AND NEVER REACHES IT:** its last branch returns `{ gas: 0.85, ice: 0.10, rock: 0.05 }` for anything over 40 Earth masses, and this body is **2,066 Earth masses** — but the density short-circuit fires four lines earlier and mass is never consulted. So it is not a missing model, it is an ORDERING fault, and the fix is to gate the density branch on mass rather than to invent anything. **THE DENSITY IS NOT WRONG AND MUST NOT BE "FIXED" — verify this before touching it.** Mass 1.2337e28 kg and radius 80,912 km give 5.56 g/cc, which the app displays and which is arithmetically right; both figures come straight from the catalogue (6.5 Jupiter masses, 12.7 Earth radii, i.e. 1.16 Jupiter radii). **A super-Jupiter genuinely IS that dense** — above about one Jupiter mass a giant's radius stops growing and then shrinks under degenerate compression, so mass keeps climbing into a near-constant volume. Jupiter is 1.33 g/cc; 6.5 M_J at 1.16 R_J really is ~5.6 g/cc. **`density > 4` is a sound proxy for "rocky" ONLY BELOW the giant threshold; above it, high density means hydrogen and helium squeezed by self-gravity.** The rule needs a mass ceiling, nothing more. **THE CLASSIFIER IS INNOCENT AND THIS IS WORTH KNOWING:** the type reads **Super Jupiter / Sub-Brown Dwarf** with `web20super-jupiter.jpg`, correctly derived from mass and radius. So the engine simultaneously calls it a super-Jupiter and says it is 62% rock and 33% metal — **two subsystems answering one question differently, which is [[D11]]'s exact shape arriving on real-sky data.** **THIS IS THE SAME ROOT AS [[D7]] AND THE TWO SHOULD BE ONE JOB.** D7 (every RV super-Earth authored 55% ice) is branch THREE of this same four-line function; D17 is branch one. `defaultMakeup` is the single composition inference for every imported planet, it is four lines long, it is consulted once at `convert.mjs:96`, and it is wrong at both ends of its range. **Fix them together, then re-import and diff, because this function has already written its verdict into the bundled maps.** **SECONDARY, NOTED NOT FIXED:** the same body carries `axial_tilt_deg: 90` with no `rotation_period_hours` and **no `spin/*-inferred` tag**, unlike every generated body in the file — a 90-degree obliquity presented as fact with no provenance, which is [[A44]]'s subject. Per [[B39]] the absent rotation reads as ZERO spin, so it will not deform; the issue is honesty, not shape. Related: [[D7]] (same function - MERGE), [[D11]] (same contradiction), [[A44]], [[B39]], DATA-R3, DATA-R4. **FIXED v2.1.508-beta.** The density branch now carries a mass ceiling, and the ceiling IS the function's own existing giant threshold rather than a second number — `massMe < GIANT_MASS_ME` where `GIANT_MASS_ME = 40`, used in both places it appears. The density is untouched, as the entry required. **MEASURED, not reasoned:** across the 182 committed cache rows exactly SIX change and no others — eps Ind A b, GJ 680 b, WISEP J121756.91+162640.2 A b, COCONUTS-2 b, HD 115404 A c, HD 222237 b, all 5.19–25.10 Jupiter masses, all `rock 0.62/metal 0.33/ice 0.05` to `gas 0.85/ice 0.10/rock 0.05`. Of those only **eps Ind A b is in a bundled map**; the other five reach a GM through the in-app importer, which shares the function. A whole-map before/after dump of all 226 non-star bodies in both shipped maps diffs to exactly TWO lines (the one body, twice) — nothing else moved, which is the intended shape of this change. Pinned by `src/lib/import/realsky/planets.spec.js`, including a catalogue-wide assertion that no row is called rocky while its mass says giant, and by the case that must NOT regress: HD 219134 b at 4.74 Me and a genuinely MEASURED 6.34 g/cc still reads rock, so the ceiling did not disarm the branch. New rule DATA-R7 records why the catalogue's density is usually not evidence. | **fixed v2.1.508-beta** |
